abstract: In the visual cortex of the monkey the horizontal organization of the preferred orientations of orientation-selective cells follows two opposing rules: 1) neighbors tend to have similar orientation preferences, and 2) many different orientations are observed in a local region. Several orientation models which satisfy these constraints are found to differ in the spacing and the topological index of their singularities. Using the rate of orientation change as a measure, the models are compared to published experimental results.
originalAbstract: In the visual cortex of the monkey the horizontal organization of the preferred orientations of orientation-selective cells follows two opposing rules: 1) neighbors tend to have similar orientation preferences, and 2) many different orientations are observed in a local region. Several orientation models which satisfy these constraints are found to differ in the spacing and the topological index of their singularities. Using the rate of orientation change as a measure, the models are compared to published experimental results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how preferred visual orientations are arranged across monkey primary visual cortex. The organization must satisfy two competing observations: nearby cells tend to prefer similar orientations, yet a small region contains cells preferring many different orientations. A useful model must explain local similarity together with local diversity.

Several orientation-map models meet both requirements, so those observations alone do not distinguish their spatial organization. The paper finds differences in the spacing and topological index of their singularities. These are features of how the orientation pattern is organized around special locations in the map, rather than simply which orientations are present.

To connect these structural differences with observations, the authors compare the models against published experimental results using the rate at which preferred orientation changes across the cortex. This gives the comparison a measurable spatial criterion. The contribution is a way to distinguish otherwise plausible maps by examining how rapidly orientation preferences vary and how the map's singularities organize that variation.
summary.tldr: The paper compares cortical orientation-map models through their singularities and the spatial rate of orientation change.

title: Centric Models of the Orientation Map in Primary Visual Cortex

abstract: We describe two expriments in optical neural computing. In the first a closed optical feedback loop is used to implement auto-associative image recall. In the second a perceptron-Iike learning algorithm is implemented with photorefractive holography.
originalAbstract: We describe two expriments in optical neural computing. In the first a closed optical feedback loop is used to implement auto-associative image recall. In the second a perceptron-Iike learning algorithm is implemented with photorefractive holography.
title: Experimental Demonstrations of Optical Neural Computers

This paper investigates the additional interactions introduced by the task of function learning. paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose receptive fields for networks whose units respond to localized regions of the input space. Receptive-field size, shape, and overlap determine how these units represent inputs. The authors ask how those choices affect learning a target function, with the objective of minimizing average performance error.

Their analysis identifies three interacting factors: noise in individual units, the density of training samples, and the structure of the function being learned. Radial basis function networks provide the framework for the discussion. Unit noise is included explicitly because the authors are interested in constraints relevant to biological systems.

The paper argues that the distribution of inputs alone need not determine a good receptive-field arrangement. The structure of the target function also provides useful guidance about how the representation should be organized. Based on the analysis, the authors propose an algorithm that changes receptive-field properties during learning. The contribution is a way to connect adaptive representation design with the examples available, the reliability of units, and the function the network must learn.
summary.tldr: An analysis of noise, sample density, and target-function structure motivates adapting receptive fields during neural learning.

title: How Receptive Field Parameters Affect Neural Learning

abstract: We have attempted to use information theoretic quantities for ana(cid:173) lyzing neuronal connection structure from spike trains. Two point mu tual information and its maximum value, channel capacity, be(cid:173) tween a pair of neurons were found to be useful for sensitive de(cid:173) tection of crosscorrelation and for estimation of synaptic strength, respectively. Three point mutual information among three neurons could give their interconnection structure. Therefore, our informa(cid:173) tion theoretic analysis was shown to be a very powerful technique for deducing neuronal connection structure. Some concrete exam(cid:173) ples of its application to simulated spike trains are presented.

Three point mutual information among three neurons could give their interconnection structure. Therefore, our informa(cid:173) tion theoretic analysis was shown to be a very powerful technique for deducing neuronal connection structure. paragraphs: The paper investigates how recordings of neural spikes can reveal the connections between neurons. Instead of examining connection structure directly, the authors analyze how much information different spike trains share. Their approach uses information measures at two scales: pairs of neurons and groups of three. These scales address different questions about the underlying network.

For pairs, mutual information measures statistical dependence between the two spike trains. The authors find it useful for detecting crosscorrelation sensitively. They also examine channel capacity, described here as the maximum mutual information between a pair, and find it useful for estimating synaptic strength. Thus, detecting a relationship and estimating its strength receive distinct information-based treatments.

For three neurons, the authors report that three-point mutual information can reveal their interconnection structure. This extends the analysis beyond individual pairs toward identifying how a small group is organized. Examples using simulated spike trains demonstrate the proposed applications. The stated contribution is a way to extract structural clues from neural activity through complementary information measures.
summary.tldr: Information measures between pairs and triples of spike trains provide clues about synaptic strength and neural connection structure.

title: Information Theoretic Analysis of Connection Structure from Spike Trains

abstract: In this paper, we will consider the problem of classifying electroencephalo(cid:173) gram (EEG) signals of normal subjects, and subjects suffering from psychi(cid:173) atric disorder, e.g., obsessive compulsive disorder, schizophrenia, using a class of artificial neural networks, viz., multi-layer perceptron. It is shown that the multilayer perceptron is capable of classifying unseen test EEG signals to a high degree of accuracy.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we will consider the problem of classifying electroencephalo(cid:173) gram (EEG) signals of normal subjects, and subjects suffering from psychi(cid:173) atric disorder, e.g., obsessive compulsive disorder, schizophrenia, using a class of artificial neural networks, viz., multi-layer perceptron. It is shown that the multilayer perceptron is capable of classifying unseen test EEG signals to a high degree of accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether an artificial neural network can classify electroencephalogram signals from different subject groups. The groups include normal subjects and subjects with psychiatric disorders, with obsessive compulsive disorder and schizophrenia given as examples. The task is to assign EEG signals to the relevant categories using patterns present in the recordings.

The chosen model is a multilayer perceptron. In this application, the network provides the connection between the EEG input and the classification decision. The research question concerns whether this class of network can learn distinctions that remain useful when it encounters signals outside the examples used to train it.

The authors report that the network classifies previously unseen test EEG signals with high accuracy. The use of unseen signals is central to the finding: the reported capability extends beyond handling the training examples themselves. The result supports multilayer perceptrons as an approach to this EEG classification problem, with the stated evidence focused on distinguishing the subject groups through their recorded signals.
summary.tldr: A multilayer perceptron reportedly classifies unseen EEG signals from normal subjects and subjects with psychiatric disorders with high accuracy.

title: Classification of Electroencephalogram using Artificial Neural Networks

abstract: Accounts of neurological disorders often posit damage to a specific functional pathway of the brain. Farah (1990) has proposed an alterna(cid:173) tive class of explanations involving partial damage to multiple path(cid:173) ways. We explore this explanation for optic aphasia, a disorder in which severe perfonnance deficits are observed when patients are asked to name visually presented objects, but surprisingly, performance is rela(cid:173) tively nonnal on naming objects from auditory cues and on gesturing the appropriate use of visually presented objects. We model this highly specific deficit through partial damage to two pathways-one that maps visual input to semantics, and the other that maps semantics to naming responses. The effect of this damage is superadditive, meaning that tasks which require one pathway or the other show little or no perfor(cid:173) mance deficit, but the damage is manifested when a task requires both pathways (i.e., naming visually presented objects). Our model explains other phenomena associated with optic aphasia, and makes testable experimental predictions. Neuropsychology is the study of disrupted cognition resulting from damage to functional systems in the brain. Generally, accounts of neuropsychological disorders posit damage to a particular functional system or a disconnection between systems. Farah (1990) sug(cid:173) gested an alternative class of explanations for neuropsychological disorders: partial dam(cid:173) age to multiple systems, which is manifested through interactions among the loci of damage. We explore this explanation for the neuropsychological disorder of optic aphasia. Optic aphasia, arising from unilateral left posterior lesions, including occipital cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum (Schnider, Benson, & Scharre, 1994), is marked by a deficit in naming visually presented objects, hereafter referred to as visual naming (Farah, 1990). However, patients can demonstrate recognition of visually presented objects nonverbally, for example, by gesturing the appropriate use of an object or sorting visual items into their proper superordinate categories (hereafter, visual gesturing). Patients can also name objects by nonvisual cues such as a verbal definition or typical sounds made by the objects (hereafter, auditory naming). Although optic aphasia cannot be explained by damage to the vision-to-semantics pathway or the semantics-ta-naming Farah (1990) proposed an explanation in terms of partial damage to both pathways (the X's).

paragraphs: Optic aphasia presents a striking pattern: someone may struggle to name an object they see, yet still demonstrate its use or name it from an auditory cue. The paper asks how a model can produce this selective impairment when the abilities needed for parts of the task appear relatively preserved.

The proposed explanation introduces partial damage to two pathways. One connects visual input to meaning, and the other connects meaning to a spoken name. Showing how to use a visible object relies on the first pathway, while naming from auditory cues can use the second. Naming a visible object requires both, making it vulnerable to their combined impairment.

The model produces a superadditive effect: the combined damage causes a disproportionately severe deficit on the task requiring both pathways. This matters because a highly specific behavioral impairment need not imply damage to a single specialized route. The authors also report explaining other associated phenomena and generating experimental predictions, extending the account beyond the central naming difficulty.
summary.tldr: Partial damage to two interacting pathways can explain severe visual naming difficulties alongside relatively preserved related abilities.

title: A Superadditive-Impairment Theory of Optic Aphasia

This paper demonstrates the possibility of replacing the numerical simulation of nontrivial dynamic models with a dramatically more efficient "NeuroAnimator" that exploits neural networks. Neu(cid:173) roAnimators are automatically trained off-line to emulate physical dy(cid:173) namics through the observation of physics-based models in action. De(cid:173) pending on the model, its neural network emulator can yield physically realistic animation one or two orders of magnitude faster than conven(cid:173) tional numerical simulation. We demonstrate NeuroAnimators for a va(cid:173) riety of physics-based models.

paragraphs: Physics-based animation can produce realistic motion, but numerically simulating the underlying dynamics can be computationally expensive. This paper explores replacing that numerical simulation with a neural-network emulator called a NeuroAnimator. The objective is to retain physically realistic animation while reducing the computation required to generate motion.

A NeuroAnimator is trained automatically offline by observing a physics-based model in action. The network learns to emulate the model's dynamics from those observations. This places the learning stage before the animation stage in which the emulator is used, allowing the trained network to serve as a faster substitute for conventional numerical simulation.

The authors demonstrate the approach on a variety of physics-based models, including nontrivial dynamic systems. Depending on the model, the emulator can produce physically realistic animation one or two orders of magnitude faster than conventional simulation. The result establishes the possibility of substantial speed improvements through learned emulation, with the size of the benefit explicitly depending on the model being animated.
summary.tldr: NeuroAnimators learn physical dynamics offline and can generate realistic animation 10–100 times faster than numerical simulation, depending on the model.

title: Fast Neural Network Emulation of Dynamical Systems for Computer Animation

abstract: Human reaction times during sensory-motor tasks vary consider(cid:173) ably. To begin to understand how this variability arises, we exam(cid:173) ined neuronal populational response time variability at early versus late visual processing stages. The conventional view is that pre(cid:173) cise temporal information is gradually lost as information is passed through a layered network of mean-rate "units." We tested in hu(cid:173) mans whether neuronal populations at different processing stages behave like mean-rate "units". A blind source separation algorithm was applied to MEG signals from sensory-motor integration tasks. Response time latency and variability for multiple visual sources were estimated by detecting single-trial stimulus-locked events for each source. In two subjects tested on four visual reaction time tasks, we reliably identified sources belonging to early and late vi(cid:173) sual processing stages. The standard deviation of response latency was smaller for early rather than late processing stages. This sup(cid:173) ports the hypothesis that human populational response time vari(cid:173) ability increases from early to late visual processing stages.

paragraphs: Human reaction times vary across repetitions of a sensory–motor task. This study examines one possible contributor: variation in the response timing of neuronal populations at different stages of visual processing. It tests a view in which precise timing information becomes less well preserved as signals pass through successive processing stages.

The researchers apply blind source separation to MEG recordings from sensory–motor integration tasks. For each recovered visual source, they detect stimulus-related events on individual trials and estimate response latency and its variability. This makes the comparison about the timing of source responses across trials, including sources associated with both early and late visual processing.

In two participants completing four visual reaction-time tasks, the researchers reliably identify early and late visual sources. The standard deviation of response latency is smaller at early stages than at later ones. This supports the hypothesis that population response-time variability increases along visual processing stages in the studied setting, connecting a measured timing difference to the proposed loss of temporal precision.
summary.tldr: MEG measurements in two participants support greater neuronal population response-time variability at later visual processing stages.

title: An MEG Study of Response Latency and Variability in the Human Visual System During a Visual-Motor Integration Task

abstract: In this article we study the effects of introducing structure in the input distribution of the data to be learnt by a simple perceptron. We determine the learning curves within the framework of Statis(cid:173) tical Mechanics. Stepwise generalization occurs as a function of the number of examples when the distribution of patterns is highly anisotropic. Although extremely simple, the model seems to cap(cid:173) ture the relevant features of a class of Support Vector Machines which was recently shown to present this behavior.
originalAbstract: In this article we study the effects of introducing structure in the input distribution of the data to be learnt by a simple perceptron. We determine the learning curves within the framework of Statis(cid:173) tical Mechanics. Stepwise generalization occurs as a function of the number of examples when the distribution of patterns is highly anisotropic. Although extremely simple, the model seems to cap(cid:173) ture the relevant features of a class of Support Vector Machines which was recently shown to present this behavior.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why learning performance can improve in stages as the number of training examples increases. It uses a simple perceptron as a toy model and introduces structure into the distribution of its inputs. The aim is to isolate how properties of the data distribution can shape the learning curve.

The authors determine learning curves using statistical mechanics. They find stepwise generalization when the pattern distribution is highly anisotropic, meaning that its structure differs strongly across directions. In this setting, increasing the number of examples produces distinct stages in generalization behavior. The stated condition concerns pronounced directional differences in the inputs.

Although deliberately simple, the model appears to capture relevant features of a class of support vector machines previously observed to behave this way. This is a qualified connection between a tractable model and a more complex learning method. The contribution is an explanation of how structured input distributions can generate stepwise learning, rather than a claim that all support vector machines must generalize in stages.
summary.tldr: A perceptron toy model links highly anisotropic input distributions to stepwise generalization resembling behavior in a class of SVMs.

title: Understanding Stepwise Generalization of Support Vector Machines: a Toy Model

abstract: We propose a new method for estimating intrinsic dimension of a dataset derived by applying the principle of maximum likelihood to the distances between close neighbors. We derive the estimator by a Poisson process approximation, assess its bias and variance theo- retically and by simulations, and apply it to a number of simulated and real datasets. We also show it has the best overall performance compared with two other intrinsic dimension estimators.
originalAbstract: We propose a new method for estimating intrinsic dimension of a dataset derived by applying the principle of maximum likelihood to the distances between close neighbors. We derive the estimator by a Poisson process approximation, assess its bias and variance theo- retically and by simulations, and apply it to a number of simulated and real datasets. We also show it has the best overall performance compared with two other intrinsic dimension estimators.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to estimate a dataset's intrinsic dimension from distances between nearby points. Intrinsic dimension concerns how many dimensions are needed to describe the structure present in the data. By focusing on close neighbors, the method uses local distance information as evidence about that structure.

The estimator is derived by applying maximum likelihood under a Poisson process approximation. This gives the distance-based calculation a probabilistic basis: dimension is estimated through a model for the observations used in the calculation. The authors assess both bias and variance, examining systematic error and variability through theoretical analysis and simulations.

They also apply the estimator to simulated and real datasets and compare it with two other intrinsic-dimension estimators. The paper reports the best overall performance among those three methods in its comparisons. That finding supports the proposed estimator in the evaluated settings. The contribution combines a local-distance construction, a likelihood-based derivation, analysis of statistical behavior, and empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: A maximum-likelihood estimator uses neighboring-point distances to estimate intrinsic dimension and performs best overall in the reported three-method comparison.

title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Intrinsic Dimension

abstract: Markov jump processes play an important role in a large number of application domains. However, realistic systems are analytically intractable and they have traditionally been analysed using simulation based techniques, which do not provide a framework for statistical inference. We propose a mean field approximation to perform posterior inference and parameter estimation. The approximation allows a practical solution to the inference problem, {while still retaining a good degree of accuracy.} We illustrate our approach on two biologically motivated systems.
originalAbstract: Markov jump processes play an important role in a large number of application domains. However, realistic systems are analytically intractable and they have traditionally been analysed using simulation based techniques, which do not provide a framework for statistical inference. We propose a mean field approximation to perform posterior inference and parameter estimation. The approximation allows a practical solution to the inference problem, {while still retaining a good degree of accuracy.} We illustrate our approach on two biologically motivated systems.

paragraphs: Markov jump processes describe stochastic systems whose states change through jumps. They are useful across many application areas, but realistic models can be analytically intractable. This paper focuses on making statistical inference practical for such systems, going beyond the simulation-based analysis traditionally used in the setting described by the authors.

The proposed method uses a mean field approximation to support both posterior inference and parameter estimation. Posterior inference concerns what can be inferred about the system given observations, while parameter estimation concerns the values governing its behavior. Addressing both within an approximation provides a route from a specified stochastic model to learning about the system represented by that model.

The authors report that the approximation makes the inference problem practically solvable while preserving a good degree of accuracy. They illustrate the approach on two biologically motivated systems. These examples demonstrate the intended use of the method, and the stated contribution is a workable approximate inference framework for jump-process models whose exact analysis is difficult.
summary.tldr: A mean field approximation makes posterior inference and parameter estimation practical for Markov jump processes while retaining reported accuracy.

title: Variational inference for Markov jump processes

abstract: The replica method is a non-rigorous but widely-used technique from statistical physics used in the asymptotic analysis of many large random nonlinear problems. This paper applies the replica method to non-Gaussian MAP estimation. It is shown that with large random linear measurements and Gaussian noise, the asymptotic behavior of the MAP estimate of an n-dimensional vector ``decouples as n scalar MAP estimators. The result is a counterpart to Guo and Verdus replica analysis on MMSE estimation. The replica MAP analysis can be readily applied to many estimators used in compressed sensing, including basis pursuit, lasso, linear estimation with thresholding and zero-norm estimation. In the case of lasso estimation, the scalar estimator reduces to a soft-thresholding operator and for zero-norm estimation it reduces to a hard-threshold. Among other benefits, the replica method provides a computationally tractable method for exactly computing various performance metrics including MSE and sparsity recovery.

paragraphs: Estimating a large vector from random linear measurements can involve a complicated nonlinear optimization problem. This paper analyzes maximum a posteriori, or MAP, estimation with non-Gaussian models and Gaussian measurement noise. It uses the replica method from statistical physics, which the authors explicitly describe as non-rigorous, to study behavior as the problem dimension becomes large.

The central result is a decoupling description: the asymptotic behavior of the vector estimate can be represented through scalar MAP estimators. This replaces a coupled, high-dimensional performance analysis with simpler one-dimensional calculations. The analysis provides a MAP counterpart to earlier replica work on minimum mean-squared-error estimation.

The framework applies to compressed-sensing estimators including basis pursuit, lasso, thresholded linear estimation, and zero-norm estimation. For lasso, the scalar rule becomes soft thresholding; for zero-norm estimation, it becomes hard thresholding. Within the replica analysis, these reductions make quantities such as mean-squared error and sparsity recovery computationally tractable to calculate exactly. That computational benefit should be understood within the method's stated non-rigorous, asymptotic setting.
summary.tldr: A non-rigorous replica analysis reduces large-system MAP estimation to scalar problems, enabling tractable compressed-sensing performance calculations.

title: Asymptotic Analysis of MAP Estimation via the Replica Method and Compressed Sensing

abstract: We study repeated zero-sum games against an adversary on a budget. Given that an adversary has some constraint on the sequence of actions that he plays, we consider what ought to be the player's best mixed strategy with knowledge of this budget. We show that, for a general class of normal-form games, the minimax strategy is indeed efficiently computable and relies on a random playout" technique. We give three diverse applications of this algorithmic template: a cost-sensitive "Hedge" setting, a particular problem in Metrical Task Systems, and the design of combinatorial prediction markets."

Given that an adversary has some constraint on the sequence of actions that he plays, we consider what ought to be the player's best mixed strategy with knowledge of this budget. We show that, for a general class of normal-form games, the minimax strategy is indeed efficiently computable and relies on a random playout" technique. We give three diverse applications of this algorithmic template: a cost-sensitive "Hedge" setting, a particular problem in Metrical Task Systems, and the design of combinatorial prediction markets."

paragraphs: In a repeated zero-sum game, a player's best strategy depends on what the opponent is allowed to do over time. This paper considers adversaries whose sequences of actions must obey a budget constraint. The player knows that constraint and seeks an appropriate mixed strategy, meaning a strategy that randomizes its choices.

The central question is how to exploit the budget while still protecting against the strongest permitted opponent. For a general class of normal-form games, the authors show that the minimax strategy can be computed efficiently. Their algorithm relies on a random-playout technique, providing a computational template for incorporating constraints on the adversary's overall sequence of actions.

The paper applies this template to three different settings: a cost-sensitive version of Hedge, a particular problem in metrical task systems, and combinatorial prediction-market design. These applications demonstrate the range of the formulation. The result gives known adversarial constraints a direct algorithmic role in selecting a strategy, with efficiency established for the stated class of games.
summary.tldr: Known constraints on an adversary's action sequence enable efficiently computable minimax strategies through a random-playout method.

title: Repeated Games against Budgeted Adversaries

abstract: Straightforward application of Deep Belief Nets (DBNs) to acoustic modeling produces a rich distributed representation of speech data that is useful for recognition and yields impressive results on the speaker-independent TIMIT phone recognition task. However, the first-layer Gaussian-Bernoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machine (GRBM) has an important limitation, shared with mixtures of diagonal-covariance Gaussians: GRBMs treat different components of the acoustic input vector as conditionally independent given the hidden state. The mean-covariance restricted Boltzmann machine (mcRBM), first introduced for modeling natural images, is a much more representationally efficient and powerful way of modeling the covariance structure of speech data. Every configuration of the precision units of the mcRBM specifies a different precision matrix for the conditional distribution over the acoustic space. In this work, we use the mcRBM to learn features of speech data that serve as input into a standard DBN. The mcRBM features combined with DBNs allow us to achieve a phone error rate of 20.5\%, which is superior to all published results on speaker-independent TIMIT to date.

paragraphs: Deep belief networks can learn useful speech representations, but a common first-layer model has a restrictive view of acoustic inputs. Given its hidden state, a Gaussian-Bernoulli restricted Boltzmann machine treats input components as conditionally independent. This paper addresses that restriction by learning features with a mean-covariance restricted Boltzmann machine before passing them into a standard deep belief network.

The mean-covariance model represents how acoustic components vary together. Different configurations of its precision units specify different precision matrices for the conditional acoustic distribution. This gives the model a more expressive and representationally efficient way to capture covariance structure. The architecture uses those learned features as the input representation for subsequent recognition.

The combined system achieves a phone error rate of 20.5% on the speaker-independent TIMIT task. The authors report that this exceeds the performance of all published results available at the time. The finding supports covariance-aware feature learning for this benchmark, connecting a richer model of acoustic dependencies to improved phone recognition.
summary.tldr: Covariance-aware speech features combined with a deep belief network achieve a reported 20.5% phone error rate on speaker-independent TIMIT.

title: Phone Recognition with the Mean-Covariance Restricted Boltzmann Machine

abstract: We study the fundamental problem of learning an unknown large-margin halfspace in the context of parallel computation. Our main positive result is a parallel algorithm for learning a large-margin halfspace that is based on interior point methods from convex optimization and fast parallel algorithms for matrix computations. We show that this algorithm learns an unknown gamma-margin halfspace over n dimensions using poly(n,1/gamma) processors and runs in time ~O(1/gamma) + O(log n). In contrast, naive parallel algorithms that learn a gamma-margin halfspace in time that depends polylogarithmically on n have Omega(1/gamma^2) runtime dependence on gamma. Our main negative result deals with boosting, which is a standard approach to learning large-margin halfspaces. We give an information-theoretic proof that in the original PAC framework, in which a weak learning algorithm is provided as an oracle that is called by the booster, boosting cannot be parallelized: the ability to call the weak learner multiple times in parallel within a single boosting stage does not reduce the overall number of successive stages of boosting that are required.

paragraphs: This paper asks how quickly parallel computation can learn a linear classification boundary when examples have a separating margin. The margin, denoted gamma, matters because the runtime can become much larger as it shrinks. The authors provide both an algorithm that improves this dependence and a limit on parallelizing a familiar alternative.

Their algorithm combines interior point methods from convex optimization with fast parallel matrix computations. Using a number of processors polynomial in the dimension n and in 1/gamma, it runs in approximately O(1/gamma) plus O(log n) time, with the first term stated in soft-O notation. The naive parallel methods considered have at least quadratic dependence on 1/gamma.

The negative result concerns boosting in the original PAC framework, where a booster accesses a weak learner as an oracle. Calling that oracle multiple times simultaneously does not reduce the required number of successive boosting stages. This establishes a specific barrier to parallelizing that oracle-based procedure, while the positive result shows that a different optimization strategy can improve parallel learning time.
summary.tldr: An optimization-based parallel learner improves margin-dependent runtime, while oracle-based boosting retains a sequential-stage barrier.

title: Algorithms and hardness results for parallel large margin learning

abstract: Renewal processes are generalizations of the Poisson process on the real line, whose intervals are drawn i.i.d. from some distribution. Modulated renewal processes allow these distributions to vary with time, allowing the introduction nonstationarity. In this work, we take a nonparametric Bayesian approach, modeling this nonstationarity with a Gaussian process. Our approach is based on the idea of uniformization, allowing us to draw exact samples from an otherwise intractable distribution. We develop a novel and efficient MCMC sampler for posterior inference. In our experiments, we test these on a number of synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequences of events occurring along a time axis. In an ordinary renewal process, intervals between events are independent draws from the same distribution. Modulated renewal processes allow that distribution to change with time, making them suitable for describing event patterns whose statistical behavior is not stationary.

The authors take a nonparametric Bayesian approach, using a Gaussian process to model the time variation. This places the changing behavior within a probabilistic framework rather than requiring a fixed, finite description of its temporal shape. The resulting model combines renewal-process interval structure with a flexible account of nonstationarity.

Computation is a central contribution. The approach uses uniformization to obtain exact samples from a distribution that would otherwise be intractable, and the authors develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler for posterior inference. They test their methods on synthetic and real datasets. The work therefore addresses both how to represent changing event statistics and how to perform inference in the resulting model.
summary.tldr: Gaussian processes model time variation in renewal processes, with uniformization supporting exact sampling and an efficient posterior inference algorithm.

title: Gaussian process modulated renewal processes

abstract: Finding contours in natural images is a fundamental problem that serves as the basis of many tasks such as image segmentation and object recognition. At the core of contour detection technologies are a set of hand-designed gradient features, used by most existing approaches including the state-of-the-art Global Pb (gPb) operator. In this work, we show that contour detection accuracy can be significantly improved by computing Sparse Code Gradients (SCG), which measure contrast using patch representations automatically learned through sparse coding. We use K-SVD and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit for efficient dictionary learning and encoding, and use multi-scale pooling and power transforms to code oriented local neighborhoods before computing gradients and applying linear SVM. By extracting rich representations from pixels and avoiding collapsing them prematurely, Sparse Code Gradients effectively learn how to measure local contrasts and find contours. We improve the F-measure metric on the BSDS500 benchmark to 0.74 (up from 0.71 of gPb contours). Moreover, our learning approach can easily adapt to novel sensor data such as Kinect-style RGB-D cameras: Sparse Code Gradients on depth images and surface normals lead to promising contour detection using depth and depth+color, as verified on the NYU Depth Dataset. Our work combines the concept of oriented gradients with sparse representation and opens up future possibilities for learning contour detection and segmentation.

paragraphs: Contour detection identifies boundaries in images and supports tasks such as segmentation and object recognition. Many approaches measure contrast with manually designed gradient features. This paper instead learns representations of image patches through sparse coding, then measures contrast between those representations. The resulting Sparse Code Gradients make the description of local appearance part of what is learned.

The method uses K-SVD to learn a dictionary and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit to encode patches. Multi-scale pooling and power transforms represent oriented local neighborhoods before gradients are computed and a linear support vector machine is applied. Keeping richer patch information until the contrast computation helps the method learn how to distinguish contour-relevant local differences.

On BSDS500, the reported F-measure rises from 0.71 for gPb contours to 0.74. The authors also apply the approach to depth images and surface normals, reporting promising depth-only and depth-plus-color results on the NYU Depth Dataset. These findings show that learned contrast representations can improve contour detection and adapt to additional sensor information.
summary.tldr: Sparse Code Gradients learn local contrast representations that improve contour detection and extend to depth-based imagery.

title: Discriminatively Trained Sparse Code Gradients for Contour Detection

abstract: We trained a large, deep convolutional neural network to classify the 1.3 million high-resolution images in the LSVRC-2010 ImageNet training set into the 1000 different classes. On the test data, we achieved top-1 and top-5 error rates of 39.7\% and 18.9\% which is considerably better than the previous state-of-the-art results. The neural network, which has 60 million parameters and 500,000 neurons, consists of five convolutional layers, some of which are followed by max-pooling layers, and two globally connected layers with a final 1000-way softmax. To make training faster, we used non-saturating neurons and a very efficient GPU implementation of convolutional nets. To reduce overfitting in the globally connected layers we employed a new regularization method that proved to be very effective.

To reduce overfitting in the globally connected layers we employed a new regularization method that proved to be very effective.

paragraphs: Large-scale image recognition requires learning visual features that distinguish many categories across varied high-resolution photographs. This paper trains a deep convolutional network on 1.3 million ImageNet images spanning 1,000 classes. The model brings together substantial capacity and a training implementation able to use that capacity effectively.

The network has about 60 million parameters and 500,000 neurons, with five convolutional layers, pooling in selected locations, and globally connected classification layers. Non-saturating neurons and an efficient GPU implementation accelerate training. A regularization method reduces overfitting in the globally connected portion.

On the LSVRC-2010 test data, top-1 error is 39.7% and top-5 error is 18.9%, substantially better than the preceding results cited by the paper. The contribution demonstrates the combined impact of deep learned features, computational scale, and regularization on a demanding recognition benchmark. The evidence concerns this integrated system rather than isolating one component as the sole cause of the gain.
summary.tldr: A large GPU-trained convolutional network substantially improves ImageNet classification through deep learned features and effective regularization.

title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Stacked sparse denoising auto-encoders (SSDAs) have recently been shown to be successful at removing noise from corrupted images. However, like most denoising techniques, the SSDA is not robust to variation in noise types beyond what it has seen during training. We present the multi-column stacked sparse denoising autoencoder, a novel technique of combining multiple SSDAs into a multi-column SSDA (MC-SSDA) by combining the outputs of each SSDA. We eliminate the need to determine the type of noise, let alone its statistics, at test time. We show that good denoising performance can be achieved with a single system on a variety of different noise types, including ones not seen in the training set. Additionally, we experimentally demonstrate the efficacy of MC-SSDA denoising by achieving MNIST digit error rates on denoised images at close to that of the uncorrupted images.

paragraphs: An image denoiser can work well on familiar corruption yet struggle when the kind of noise changes. This paper addresses that problem for stacked sparse denoising autoencoders, whose success at cleaning images does not by itself make them robust to noise beyond their training experience.

The proposed system combines several of these autoencoders into a multi-column architecture and combines their outputs to produce a denoised image. This arrangement removes the need to identify the noise type or determine its statistics when processing a new image. The practical aim is a single denoising system that can handle a range of corruptions without first requiring a separate diagnosis of the noise.

The experiments report good denoising across several noise types, including some absent from training. The authors also evaluate whether the cleaned images remain useful for recognition: classification error on denoised MNIST digits approaches that on uncorrupted images. This connects the denoising result to preservation of information needed by a subsequent task, while the reported robustness remains an empirical finding for the tested noise conditions.
summary.tldr: Combining several denoising autoencoders yields a single system that performs well across tested noise types, including some unseen during training.

title: Adaptive Multi-Column Deep Neural Networks with Application to Robust Image Denoising

abstract: We connect a broad class of generative models through their shared reliance on sequential decision making. Motivated by this view, we develop extensions to an existing model, and then explore the idea further in the context of data imputation -- perhaps the simplest setting in which to investigate the relation between unconditional and conditional generative modelling. We formulate data imputation as an MDP and develop models capable of representing effective policies for it. We construct the models using neural networks and train them using a form of guided policy search. Our models generate predictions through an iterative process of feedback and refinement. We show that this approach can learn effective policies for imputation problems of varying difficulty and across multiple datasets.

paragraphs: This paper views a broad class of generative models as systems that make a sequence of decisions. Under this perspective, producing data is a process with successive choices, rather than a single prediction. The authors use that connection to extend an existing model and then investigate it through data imputation, the task of filling in missing information.

They formulate imputation as a Markov decision process and build neural networks that represent policies for that process. Training uses a form of guided policy search. Predictions emerge through repeated feedback and refinement, so the model's decision-making procedure includes opportunities to revise its developing answer across multiple steps.

The experiments show that this approach learns effective imputation policies across multiple datasets and problems of varying difficulty. Imputation also provides a setting for examining the relationship between unconditional generation and generation conditioned on available information. The paper's contribution is therefore both a connecting viewpoint for generative models and a concrete learning approach that makes iterative refinement part of the prediction process.
summary.tldr: Treating imputation as sequential decision making lets neural policies generate predictions through feedback and repeated refinement.

title: Data Generation as Sequential Decision Making

abstract: Most recent results in matrix completion assume that the matrix under consideration is low-rank or that the columns are in a union of low-rank subspaces. In real-world settings, however, the linear structure underlying these models is distorted by a (typically unknown) nonlinear transformation. This paper addresses the challenge of matrix completion in the face of such nonlinearities. Given a few observations of a matrix that are obtained by applying a Lipschitz, monotonic function to a low rank matrix, our task is to estimate the remaining unobserved entries. We propose a novel matrix completion method that alternates between low-rank matrix estimation and monotonic function estimation to estimate the missing matrix elements. Mean squared error bounds provide insight into how well the matrix can be estimated based on the size, rank of the matrix and properties of the nonlinear transformation. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the competitiveness of the proposed approach.

This paper addresses the challenge of matrix completion in the face of such nonlinearities. Given a few observations of a matrix that are obtained by applying a Lipschitz, monotonic function to a low rank matrix, our task is to estimate the remaining unobserved entries. paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries from a limited set of observations. Many approaches assume that the matrix itself has low rank or related linear structure. This paper considers a different situation: an underlying low-rank matrix has been transformed by an unknown nonlinear function, so the observed entries need not retain the original linear structure.

The assumed transformation is monotonic and Lipschitz. These conditions constrain its ordering behavior and how sharply its values can change. The proposed method alternates between estimating the underlying low-rank matrix and estimating the monotonic function. It uses both estimates to reconstruct missing entries, explicitly accounting for the nonlinear transformation during completion.

The authors derive mean squared error bounds that connect estimation quality to matrix size, rank, and properties of the transformation. These bounds explain how both the hidden linear structure and the nonlinearity affect the problem. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show competitive performance. The result supports completion under this structured nonlinear model, with guarantees tied to its stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: An alternating method completes matrices modeled as a monotonic Lipschitz transformation of an underlying low-rank matrix.

title: Matrix Completion Under Monotonic Single Index Models

abstract: We propose two stochastic gradient MCMC methods for sampling from Bayesian posterior distributions defined on Riemann manifolds with a known geodesic flow, e.g. hyperspheres. Our methods are the first scalable sampling methods on these manifolds, with the aid of stochastic gradients. Novel dynamics are conceived and 2nd-order integrators are developed. By adopting embedding techniques and the geodesic integrator, the methods do not require a global coordinate system of the manifold and do not involve inner iterations. Synthetic experiments show the validity of the method, and its application to the challenging inference for spherical topic models indicate practical usability and efficiency.
originalAbstract: We propose two stochastic gradient MCMC methods for sampling from Bayesian posterior distributions defined on Riemann manifolds with a known geodesic flow, e.g. hyperspheres. Our methods are the first scalable sampling methods on these manifolds, with the aid of stochastic gradients. Novel dynamics are conceived and 2nd-order integrators are developed. By adopting embedding techniques and the geodesic integrator, the methods do not require a global coordinate system of the manifold and do not involve inner iterations. Synthetic experiments show the validity of the method, and its application to the challenging inference for spherical topic models indicate practical usability and efficiency.

paragraphs: Some Bayesian posterior distributions live on curved spaces, such as hyperspheres, rather than unrestricted flat parameter spaces. The paper proposes two stochastic-gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for sampling on such manifolds. Their stated setting requires a known geodesic flow, which describes how motion proceeds along the manifold's geometry.

The authors introduce sampling dynamics and develop second-order numerical integrators for them. Embedding techniques and a geodesic integrator let the methods operate without a global coordinate system for the manifold. They also avoid inner iterations. Together with stochastic gradients, these choices provide the basis for scalable sampling on the curved spaces considered.

Synthetic experiments demonstrate the methods' validity, while an application to spherical topic models indicates practical usability and efficiency on a challenging inference problem. The contribution thus combines geometry-aware numerical methods with a scalable Bayesian sampling approach. Its applicability is tied to the available geodesic flow, and the reported experiments support the methods in that setting rather than establishing a sampler for arbitrary curved spaces.
summary.tldr: Two stochastic-gradient MCMC methods enable scalable posterior sampling on manifolds with known geodesic flow.

title: Stochastic Gradient Geodesic MCMC Methods

abstract: Graphs are a useful abstraction of image content. Not only can graphs represent details about individual objects in a scene but they can capture the interactions between pairs of objects. We present a method for training a convolutional neural network such that it takes in an input image and produces a full graph definition. This is done end-to-end in a single stage with the use of associative embeddings. The network learns to simultaneously identify all of the elements that make up a graph and piece them together. We benchmark on the Visual Genome dataset, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the challenging task of scene graph generation.

Not only can graphs represent details about individual objects in a scene but they can capture the interactions between pairs of objects. We present a method for training a convolutional neural network such that it takes in an input image and produces a full graph definition. This is done end-to-end in a single stage with the use of associative embeddings. The network learns to simultaneously identify all of the elements that make up a graph and piece them together. We benchmark on the Visual Genome dataset, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the challenging task of scene graph generation.

paragraphs: An image contains both individual objects and relationships between them. A graph can represent these two kinds of information together, making it a useful description of a scene. This paper develops a convolutional neural network that takes an image as input and outputs a complete graph definition.

The method uses associative embeddings to identify the graph's constituent elements and connect them. Both jobs are learned together in a single stage, with training carried out end to end. This joint formulation makes assembling the graph part of the network's learned task, alongside recognizing the elements that need to appear in it.

The authors evaluate the system on Visual Genome and report state-of-the-art performance for scene graph generation. The result supports the use of associative embeddings for producing structured descriptions directly from images. More broadly, the paper demonstrates a concrete way for an image-processing network to output interconnected scene information, extending its output beyond a collection of separately identified objects.
summary.tldr: A single-stage convolutional network uses associative embeddings to jointly identify and connect scene-graph elements from an image.

title: Pixels to Graphs by Associative Embedding

abstract: The problem of selecting the best $k$-element subset from a universe is involved in many applications. While previous studies assumed a noise-free environment or a noisy monotone submodular objective function, this paper considers a more realistic and general situation where the evaluation of a subset is a noisy monotone function (not necessarily submodular), with both multiplicative and additive noises. To understand the impact of the noise, we firstly show the approximation ratio of the greedy algorithm and POSS, two powerful algorithms for noise-free subset selection, in the noisy environments. We then propose to incorporate a noise-aware strategy into POSS, resulting in the new PONSS algorithm. We prove that PONSS can achieve a better approximation ratio under some assumption such as i.i.d. noise distribution. The empirical results on influence maximization and sparse regression problems show the superior performance of PONSS.

While previous studies assumed a noise-free environment or a noisy monotone submodular objective function, this paper considers a more realistic and general situation where the evaluation of a subset is a noisy monotone function (not necessarily submodular), with both multiplicative and additive noises. To understand the impact of the noise, we firstly show the approximation ratio of the greedy algorithm and POSS, two powerful algorithms for noise-free subset selection, in the noisy environments. We then propose to incorporate a noise-aware strategy into POSS, resulting in the new PONSS algorithm. We prove that PONSS can achieve a better approximation ratio under some assumption such as i.i.d. noise distribution. The empirical results on influence maximization and sparse regression problems show the superior performance of PONSS.

paragraphs: Selecting the best fixed-size subset becomes harder when evaluating a candidate gives an unreliable score. This paper studies noisy monotone objectives, allowing both additive and multiplicative noise. It does not require submodularity, the diminishing-returns property assumed in some earlier work, so its setting covers a broader class of subset-selection objectives.

The authors first analyze how noise affects approximation ratios for greedy selection and POSS, two methods used in noise-free settings. They then introduce PONSS by adding a noise-aware strategy to POSS. Its improved approximation guarantee depends on assumptions that include independently and identically distributed noise; the theoretical improvement is therefore conditional on the stated noise setting.

Experiments on influence maximization and sparse regression report superior performance for PONSS. These results complement the analysis by showing benefits in two application areas. The central contribution is to treat unreliable evaluations as part of algorithm design, rather than assuming that methods effective with exact scores retain the same behavior when those scores are disturbed.
summary.tldr: PONSS adapts subset selection to noisy evaluations, improving approximation guarantees under stated noise assumptions and performance in two application settings.

title: Subset Selection under Noise

abstract: This paper proposes a novel deep reinforcement learning (RL) architecture, called Value Prediction Network (VPN), which integrates model-free and model-based RL methods into a single neural network. In contrast to typical model-based RL methods, VPN learns a dynamics model whose abstract states are trained to make option-conditional predictions of future values (discounted sum of rewards) rather than of future observations. Our experimental results show that VPN has several advantages over both model-free and model-based baselines in a stochastic environment where careful planning is required but building an accurate observation-prediction model is difficult. Furthermore, VPN outperforms Deep Q-Network (DQN) on several Atari games even with short-lookahead planning, demonstrating its potential as a new way of learning a good state representation.
originalAbstract: This paper proposes a novel deep reinforcement learning (RL) architecture, called Value Prediction Network (VPN), which integrates model-free and model-based RL methods into a single neural network. In contrast to typical model-based RL methods, VPN learns a dynamics model whose abstract states are trained to make option-conditional predictions of future values (discounted sum of rewards) rather than of future observations. Our experimental results show that VPN has several advantages over both model-free and model-based baselines in a stochastic environment where careful planning is required but building an accurate observation-prediction model is difficult. Furthermore, VPN outperforms Deep Q-Network (DQN) on several Atari games even with short-lookahead planning, demonstrating its potential as a new way of learning a good state representation.

paragraphs: Planning in reinforcement learning can be difficult when an agent needs to anticipate outcomes but cannot easily predict its future observations. The Value Prediction Network addresses this problem by combining model-free and model-based learning within one neural network. Its central choice concerns what the learned model is trained to predict.

VPN learns a dynamics model over abstract states whose predictions concern future value: the discounted sum of rewards. These predictions are conditional on options, tying the representation to the choices being considered. Training the abstract states around value makes them directly relevant to planning, without requiring them to support detailed predictions of future observations.

Experiments show advantages over both model-free and model-based baselines in a stochastic environment where planning matters and observation prediction is difficult. VPN also outperforms Deep Q-Network on several Atari games with only short-lookahead planning. These results suggest that value-focused prediction can produce useful state representations and support effective planning even when looking ahead only a short distance.
summary.tldr: Value Prediction Networks plan through abstract states trained to predict future rewards, showing advantages in a stochastic environment and several Atari games.

title: Value Prediction Network

abstract: Goal-oriented dialog has been given attention due to its numerous applications in artificial intelligence. Goal-oriented dialogue tasks occur when a questioner asks an action-oriented question and an answerer responds with the intent of letting the questioner know a correct action to take. To ask the adequate question, deep learning and reinforcement learning have been recently applied. However, these approaches struggle to find a competent recurrent neural questioner, owing to the complexity of learning a series of sentences. Motivated by theory of mind, we propose "Answerer in Questioner's Mind" (AQM), a novel information theoretic algorithm for goal-oriented dialog. With AQM, a questioner asks and infers based on an approximated probabilistic model of the answerer. The questioner figures out the answerer’s intention via selecting a plausible question by explicitly calculating the information gain of the candidate intentions and possible answers to each question. We test our framework on two goal-oriented visual dialog tasks: "MNIST Counting Dialog" and "GuessWhat?!". In our experiments, AQM outperforms comparative algorithms by a large margin.

Motivated by theory of mind, we propose "Answerer in Questioner's Mind" (AQM), a novel information theoretic algorithm for goal-oriented dialog. With AQM, a questioner asks and infers based on an approximated probabilistic model of the answerer. The questioner figures out the answerer’s intention via selecting a plausible question by explicitly calculating the information gain of the candidate intentions and possible answers to each question. We test our framework on two goal-oriented visual dialog tasks: "MNIST Counting Dialog" and "GuessWhat?!". In our experiments, AQM outperforms comparative algorithms by a large margin.

paragraphs: In goal-oriented dialog, questions serve a practical purpose: their answers should help the questioner identify an appropriate action. Learning a capable questioner is difficult when it requires learning whole sequences of sentences. This paper proposes choosing questions by explicitly reasoning about what an answerer is likely to say.

The method, Answerer in Questioner's Mind, equips the questioner with an approximate probabilistic model of the answerer. For a possible question, it considers candidate intentions and possible responses, then calculates the information gain. This makes question selection depend on how much an answer could clarify the intention the questioner is trying to identify.

The authors evaluate the framework on MNIST Counting Dialog and GuessWhat?!, two goal-oriented visual dialog tasks. It outperforms the comparison algorithms by a large margin in their experiments. These findings support the usefulness of explicitly modeling the conversational partner and evaluating the informativeness of questions. The approximate answerer model is central to the approach: it supplies the predictions on which both questioning and inference rely.
summary.tldr: AQM selects informative visual-dialog questions by predicting possible answers with an approximate model of the answerer.

title: Answerer in Questioner's Mind: Information Theoretic Approach to Goal-Oriented Visual Dialog

abstract: We study the decentralized distributed computation of discrete approximations for the regularized Wasserstein barycenter of a finite set of continuous probability measures distributedly stored over a network. We assume there is a network of agents/machines/computers, and each agent holds a private continuous probability measure and seeks to compute the barycenter of all the measures in the network by getting samples from its local measure and exchanging information with its neighbors. Motivated by this problem, we develop, and analyze, a novel accelerated primal-dual stochastic gradient method for general stochastic convex optimization problems with linear equality constraints. Then, we apply this method to the decen- tralized distributed optimization setting to obtain a new algorithm for the distributed semi-discrete regularized Wasserstein barycenter problem. Moreover, we show explicit non-asymptotic complexity for the proposed algorithm. Finally, we show the effectiveness of our method on the distributed computation of the regularized Wasserstein barycenter of univariate Gaussian and von Mises distributions, as well as some applications to image aggregation.

To solve this problem, the authors develop an accelerated stochastic primal-dual gradient method for convex optimization with linear equality constraints. The method addresses a broader optimization setting before being applied to decentralized barycenter computation. Its analysis provides explicit non-asymptotic complexity bounds, describing computational requirements beyond a statement about eventual convergence.

The authors demonstrate the approach on univariate Gaussian and von Mises distributions, together with image aggregation applications. These examples show its effectiveness in the distributed setting considered. The formulation matters because it accommodates locally held distributions and neighbor communication while coordinating a shared result. Its target remains the regularized, semi-discrete problem, which combines continuous input distributions with a discrete barycenter approximation.
summary.tldr: An accelerated stochastic optimization method computes regularized Wasserstein barycenter approximations through local sampling and communication between neighboring machines.

title: Decentralize and Randomize: Faster Algorithm for Wasserstein Barycenters

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are one of the most practical methods for learning data distributions. A popular GAN formulation is based on the use of Wasserstein distance as a metric between probability distributions. Unfortunately, minimizing the Wasserstein distance between the data distribution and the generative model distribution is a computationally challenging problem as its objective is non-convex, non-smooth, and even hard to compute. In this work, we show that obtaining gradient information of the smoothed Wasserstein GAN formulation, which is based on regularized Optimal Transport (OT), is computationally effortless and hence one can apply first order optimization methods to minimize this objective. Consequently, we establish theoretical convergence guarantee to stationarity for a proposed class of GAN optimization algorithms. Unlike the original non-smooth formulation, our algorithm only requires solving the discriminator to approximate optimality. We apply our method to learning MNIST digits as well as CIFAR-10 images. Our experiments show that our method is computationally efficient and generates images comparable to the state of the art algorithms given the same architecture and computational power.

paragraphs: Wasserstein-based GANs compare generated and real data distributions using a distance with appealing modeling properties. Optimizing that distance is difficult, however, because the objective is nonconvex, nonsmooth, and hard to compute. This paper studies a smoothed formulation based on regularized optimal transport as a way to make training more tractable.

The authors show that gradient information for the smoothed objective is easy to obtain computationally, making first-order optimization applicable. They establish convergence to stationarity for a proposed class of GAN training algorithms. A useful feature is that the discriminator only needs to be solved approximately, rather than to exact optimality.

Experiments generate MNIST digits and CIFAR-10 images. The method is reported to be computationally efficient and to produce images comparable to state-of-the-art methods when architecture and computational power are held equal. The theoretical result concerns reaching stationarity, while the empirical results address the practical quality and efficiency of generated images under those matched resources.
summary.tldr: Regularized optimal transport makes GAN gradients tractable and supports convergence to stationarity with only approximately optimized discriminators.

title: On the Convergence and Robustness of Training GANs with Regularized Optimal Transport

abstract: Generalization has been one of the major challenges for learning dynamics models in model-based reinforcement learning. However, previous work on action-conditioned dynamics prediction focuses on learning the pixel-level motion and thus does not generalize well to novel environments with different object layouts. In this paper, we present a novel object-oriented framework, called object-oriented dynamics predictor (OODP), which decomposes the environment into objects and predicts the dynamics of objects conditioned on both actions and object-to-object relations. It is an end-to-end neural network and can be trained in an unsupervised manner. To enable the generalization ability of dynamics learning, we design a novel CNN-based relation mechanism that is class-specific (rather than object-specific) and exploits the locality principle. Empirical results show that OODP significantly outperforms previous methods in terms of generalization over novel environments with various object layouts. OODP is able to learn from very few environments and accurately predict dynamics in a large number of unseen environments. In addition, OODP learns semantically and visually interpretable dynamics models.

paragraphs: A learned dynamics model predicts how an environment changes after an action. Models focused on pixel-level motion can struggle when familiar objects appear in unfamiliar arrangements. This paper introduces the Object-Oriented Dynamics Predictor, or OODP, which represents an environment through objects and predicts their behavior using actions and relationships among those objects.

OODP is an end-to-end neural network that can be trained without supervision. Its convolutional relation mechanism is specific to object classes rather than individual objects and uses a locality principle. This design supports transferring learned relationships across arrangements, instead of tying every interaction pattern to the particular objects encountered during training.

Experiments show substantially better generalization than previous methods across environments with different object layouts. The model learns from very few environments and accurately predicts dynamics in many unseen ones. Its learned dynamics are also semantically and visually interpretable. Together, these findings support object-based relational structure as a useful way to organize predictions for transfer to new layouts.
summary.tldr: OODP predicts action-dependent object dynamics through class-based local relations, improving generalization to unfamiliar object layouts.

title: Object-Oriented Dynamics Predictor

abstract: Stochastic gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo (SGMCMC) has become a popular method for scalable Bayesian inference. These methods are based on sampling a discrete-time approximation to a continuous time process, such as the Langevin diffusion. When applied to distributions defined on a constrained space the time-discretization error can dominate when we are near the boundary of the space. We demonstrate that because of this, current SGMCMC methods for the simplex struggle with sparse simplex spaces; when many of the components are close to zero. Unfortunately, many popular large-scale Bayesian models, such as network or topic models, require inference on sparse simplex spaces. To avoid the biases caused by this discretization error, we propose the stochastic Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process (SCIR), which removes all discretization error and we prove that samples from the SCIR process are asymptotically unbiased. We discuss how this idea can be extended to target other constrained spaces. Use of the SCIR process within a SGMCMC algorithm is shown to give substantially better performance for a topic model and a Dirichlet process mixture model than existing SGMCMC approaches.

The paper shows why this approximation is troublesome on a probability simplex, where components are nonnegative and sum to one. Its main contribution is to address a specific source of sampling bias that becomes especially consequential when probability mass lies near a constraint boundary.
summary.tldr: SCIR removes time-discretization error in sparse-simplex sampling, provides asymptotic unbiasedness, and improves the reported Bayesian modeling results.

title: Large-Scale Stochastic Sampling from the Probability Simplex

abstract: Archetypal analysis represents instances as linear mixtures of prototypes (the archetypes) that lie on the boundary of the convex hull of the data. Archetypes are thus often better interpretable than factors computed by other matrix factorization techniques. However, the interpretability comes with high computational cost due to additional convexity-preserving constraints. In this paper, we propose efficient coresets for archetypal analysis. Theoretical guarantees are derived by showing that quantization errors of k-means upper bound archetypal analysis; the computation of a provable absolute-coreset can be performed in only two passes over the data. Empirically, we show that the coresets lead to improved performance on several data sets.

paragraphs: Archetypal analysis describes each data instance as a mixture of representative prototypes called archetypes. These prototypes sit on the boundary of the data's convex hull, giving them a geometric connection to the observed examples. This often makes them easier to interpret than factors from other matrix factorization methods, but enforcing the required convexity constraints adds computational cost.

The paper addresses that cost by constructing coresets: compact representations that allow the analysis to work with less data while retaining a provable approximation guarantee. Its central theoretical connection uses the quantization error of k-means to upper-bound the archetypal analysis error. This provides a way to control what is lost when the original data are summarized.

The authors show that a provable absolute-coreset can be computed in two passes over the data. They also report improved empirical performance on several datasets. The contribution therefore links an interpretable representation method to an efficient summarization strategy, supporting its use without requiring every stage of the analysis to operate on the complete dataset.
summary.tldr: Two-pass coresets make archetypal analysis more efficient while providing approximation guarantees derived from k-means quantization error.

title: Coresets for Archetypal Analysis

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the parameters of a $d$-dimensional rectified Gaussian distribution from i.i.d. samples. A rectified Gaussian distribution is defined by passing a standard Gaussian distribution through a one-layer ReLU neural network. We give a simple algorithm to estimate the parameters (i.e., the weight matrix and bias vector of the ReLU neural network) up to an error $\eps\norm{W}_F$ using $\widetilde{O}(1/\eps^2)$ samples and $\widetilde{O}(d^2/\eps^2)$ time (log factors are ignored for simplicity). This implies that we can estimate the distribution up to $\eps$ in total variation distance using $\widetilde{O}(\kappa^2d^2/\eps^2)$ samples, where $\kappa$ is the condition number of the covariance matrix. Our only assumption is that the bias vector is non-negative. Without this non-negativity assumption, we show that estimating the bias vector within any error requires the number of samples at least exponential in the infinity norm of the bias vector. Our algorithm is based on the key observation that vector norms and pairwise angles can be estimated separately. We use a recent result on learning from truncated samples. We also prove two sample complexity lower bounds: $\Omega(1/\eps^2)$ samples are required to estimate the parameters up to error $\eps$, while $\Omega(d/\eps^2)$ samples are necessary to estimate the distribution up to $\eps$ in total variation distance. The first lower bound implies that our algorithm is optimal for parameter estimation. Finally, we show an interesting connection between learning a two-layer generative model and non-negative matrix factorization. Experimental results are provided to support our analysis.
