paragraphs: VICE learns numerical representations of object concepts from human judgments. Its data come from a triplet odd-one-out task, in which people identify which object differs from the other two. The goal is to turn those behavioral choices into interpretable vectors that capture aspects of how people organize object concepts.

The method uses approximate Bayesian inference to learn sparse, non-negative embeddings. It also estimates uncertainty in the embedding values, and uses those estimates to select dimensions that best explain the data. This connects representation size to uncertainty-aware evidence about which dimensions are useful, rather than treating every learned dimension as equally supported.

The authors derive a PAC learning bound that can estimate generalization performance or provide a sufficient sample size for experimental design. In predicting human odd-one-out choices, VICE matches or exceeds its predecessor, SPoSE. Its representations are also more reproducible across random initializations. Together, these findings support using uncertainty estimates to obtain interpretable embeddings that predict behavior and remain more consistent across repeated fits.
summary.tldr: VICE learns sparse, uncertainty-aware object embeddings from human judgments, improving reproducibility while matching or exceeding SPoSE's predictive performance.

title: VICE: Variational Interpretable Concept Embeddings

abstract: Feature fusion plays a crucial role in unconstrained face recognition where inputs (probes) comprise of a set of $N$ low quality images whose individual qualities vary. Advances in attention and recurrent modules have led to feature fusion that can model the relationship among the images in the input set. However, attention mechanisms cannot scale to large $N$ due to their quadratic complexity and recurrent modules suffer from input order sensitivity. We propose a two-stage feature fusion paradigm, Cluster and Aggregate, that can both scale to large $N$ and maintain the ability to perform sequential inference with order invariance. Specifically, Cluster stage is a linear assignment of $N$ inputs to $M$ global cluster centers, and Aggregation stage is a fusion over $M$ clustered features. The clustered features play an integral role when the inputs are sequential as they can serve as a summarization of past features. By leveraging the order-invariance of incremental averaging operation, we design an update rule that achieves batch-order invariance, which guarantees that the contributions of early image in the sequence do not diminish as time steps increase. Experiments on IJB-B and IJB-S benchmark datasets show the superiority of the proposed two-stage paradigm in unconstrained face recognition.

paragraphs: Face recognition sometimes receives a collection of low-quality images rather than one clear photograph. Combining their features can improve recognition, but the combination must handle varying image quality and relationships among images. Attention mechanisms have quadratic complexity in the number of inputs, while recurrent approaches can make the result depend on input order.

Cluster and Aggregate divides feature fusion into two stages. First, it assigns the input features to a set of global cluster centers. Then, it combines the resulting cluster features. Aggregation therefore operates on the cluster summaries rather than directly on the entire collection. Those summaries also retain information from earlier images when new images arrive sequentially.

The update rule uses incremental averaging to achieve batch-order invariance. Consequently, processing images in differently ordered batches does not change their contributions, and earlier images do not lose influence simply because more time steps pass. Experiments on IJB-B and IJB-S support the effectiveness of this approach, combining scalability to large image sets with order-invariant sequential processing.
summary.tldr: Clustering image features before aggregation enables scalable face recognition with sequential updates that preserve batch-order invariance.

title: Cluster and Aggregate: Face Recognition with Large Probe Set

abstract: This work identifies the existence and cause of a type of posterior collapse that frequently occurs in the Bayesian deep learning practice. For a general linear latent variable model that includes linear variational autoencoders as a special case, we precisely identify the nature of posterior collapse to be the competition between the likelihood and the regularization of the mean due to the prior. Our result also suggests that posterior collapse may be a general problem of learning for deeper architectures and deepens our understanding of Bayesian deep learning.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a form of posterior collapse encountered in Bayesian deep learning. It analyzes a general linear latent-variable model that includes linear variational autoencoders as a special case. This gives the authors a setting in which they can identify the mechanism precisely rather than merely observe that collapse occurs.

The identified cause is competition between the likelihood and the prior's regularization of the mean. These two parts of learning exert competing pressures: the likelihood concerns explaining the observations, while the prior contributes the regularization. The result locates the source of the studied collapse in their interaction, making the balance between them central to understanding the phenomenon.

Because the analyzed model contains linear variational autoencoders, the explanation applies beyond a single narrowly chosen linear architecture. The authors further suggest that posterior collapse may be a broader learning problem in deeper architectures. That extension remains a suggestion in the stated findings; the precise causal identification is established for the general linear model under study.
summary.tldr: A linear latent-variable analysis attributes a form of posterior collapse to competition between likelihood fitting and prior-induced mean regularization.

title: Posterior Collapse of a Linear Latent Variable Model

abstract: Learning high-level causal representations together with a causal model from unstructured low-level data such as pixels is impossible from observational data alone. We prove under mild assumptions that this representation is however identifiable in a weakly supervised setting. This involves a dataset with paired samples before and after random, unknown interventions, but no further labels. We then introduce implicit latent causal models, variational autoencoders that represent causal variables and causal structure without having to optimize an explicit discrete graph structure. On simple image data, including a novel dataset of simulated robotic manipulation, we demonstrate that such models can reliably identify the causal structure and disentangle causal variables.

paragraphs: Recovering high-level causal variables and their relationships directly from pixels is not possible from observational data alone in the setting described by this paper. The authors investigate what additional information can make that recovery identifiable. Their weak supervision consists of paired observations taken before and after random interventions, without labels describing those interventions.

Under mild assumptions, they prove that this paired setting makes the causal representation identifiable. The pairing supplies information about change even though the intervention itself is unknown. This is the theoretical contribution: the authors establish that a particular form of limited supervision can resolve an obstacle that ordinary observations leave unresolved.

They then introduce implicit latent causal models, implemented as variational autoencoders that represent causal variables and structure without optimizing an explicit discrete graph. On simple image data, including a new simulated robotic-manipulation dataset, the models reliably recover causal structure and disentangle causal variables. The experiments support the approach within these image settings, alongside the conditional identifiability result.
summary.tldr: Under mild assumptions, paired observations before and after unknown interventions make causal representations identifiable and support learning them from simple images.

title: Weakly supervised causal representation learning

abstract: In the field of phase change phenomena, the lack of accessible and diverse datasets suitable for machine learning (ML) training poses a significant challenge. Existing experimental datasets are often restricted, with limited availability and sparse ground truth, impeding our understanding of this complex multiphysics phenomena. To bridge this gap, we present the BubbleML dataset which leverages physics-driven simulations to provide accurate ground truth information for various boiling scenarios, encompassing nucleate pool boiling, flow boiling, and sub-cooled boiling. This extensive dataset covers a wide range of parameters, including varying gravity conditions, flow rates, sub-cooling levels, and wall superheat, comprising 79 simulations. BubbleML is validated against experimental observations and trends, establishing it as an invaluable resource for ML research. Furthermore, we showcase its potential to facilitate the exploration of diverse downstream tasks by introducing two benchmarks: (a) optical flow analysis to capture bubble dynamics, and (b) neural PDE solvers for learning temperature and flow dynamics. The BubbleML dataset and its benchmarks aim to catalyze progress in ML-driven research on multiphysics phase change phenomena, providing robust baselines for the development and comparison of state-of-the-art techniques and models.

paragraphs: BubbleML addresses a data shortage in machine learning research on boiling and other phase-change phenomena. Experimental datasets can be difficult to access and may contain only sparse ground-truth measurements. That makes it harder to train and compare methods for systems in which temperature, fluid motion, and changes of phase interact.

The dataset supplies ground truth through physics-driven simulations of nucleate pool boiling, flow boiling, and sub-cooled boiling. Its 79 simulations vary gravity, flow rate, sub-cooling, and wall superheat. The authors validate the simulated data against experimental observations and trends. This gives researchers a collection with varied physical conditions and a connection to observed behavior, while retaining the detailed information available from simulation.

The paper also introduces two benchmarks. One uses optical flow to analyze bubble motion; the other tests neural partial differential equation solvers on temperature and flow dynamics. Together, these tasks make the dataset useful for both motion analysis and learning physical evolution. The contribution is a shared experimental resource and comparison framework for machine learning methods in multiphysics phase change.
summary.tldr: BubbleML provides 79 physics-driven boiling simulations and benchmarks for learning bubble motion, temperature, and flow dynamics.

title: BubbleML: A Multiphase Multiphysics Dataset and Benchmarks for Machine Learning

abstract: Multi-objective optimization (MOO) has become an influential framework in many machine learning problems with multiple objectives such as learning with multiple criteria and multi-task learning (MTL). In this paper, we propose a new direction-oriented multi-objective formulation by regularizing the common descent direction within a neighborhood of a direction that optimizes a linear combination of objectives such as the average loss in MTL or a weighted loss that places higher emphasis on some tasks than the others. This formulation includes GD and MGDA as special cases, enjoys the direction-oriented benefit as in CAGrad, and facilitates the design of stochastic algorithms. To solve this problem, we propose Stochastic Direction-oriented Multi-objective Gradient descent (SDMGrad) with simple SGD type of updates, and its variant SDMGrad-OS with an efficient objective sampling. We develop a comprehensive convergence analysis for the proposed methods with different loop sizes and regularization coefficients. We show that both SDMGrad and SDMGrad-OS achieve improved sample complexities to find an $\epsilon$-accurate Pareto stationary point while achieving a small $\epsilon$-level distance toward a conflict-avoidant (CA) direction. For a constant-level CA distance, their sample complexities match the best known $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ without bounded function value assumption. Extensive experiments show that our methods achieve competitive or improved performance compared to existing gradient manipulation approaches in a series of tasks on multi-task supervised learning and reinforcement learning. Code is available at https://github.com/ml-opt-lab/sdmgrad.

paragraphs: Learning several tasks at once creates an optimization problem in which improvements to different objectives can pull updates in competing directions. This paper proposes choosing a common descent direction while regularizing it toward a direction that improves a chosen linear combination of objectives. That combination can represent average performance or place greater emphasis on selected tasks.

The formulation includes gradient descent and the multiple-gradient descent algorithm as special cases. It leads to SDMGrad, which uses simple stochastic-gradient-style updates, and SDMGrad-OS, which samples objectives for efficiency. The authors analyze convergence across different choices of loop size and regularization strength, connecting algorithm design to the desired control over update direction.

With a constant permitted distance from that direction, they match the best-known O(ε⁻²) complexity without assuming bounded function values. Experiments on supervised multi-task learning and reinforcement learning show competitive or improved performance relative to existing gradient-manipulation approaches.
summary.tldr: SDMGrad offers simple stochastic updates with convergence guarantees for balancing multiple objectives and controlling conflicts between their update directions.

title: Direction-oriented Multi-objective Learning: Simple and Provable Stochastic Algorithms

abstract: Estimation of a complete univariate distribution from a sequence of observations is a useful primitive for both manual and automated decision making. This problem has received extensive attention in the i.i.d. setting, but the arbitrary data dependent setting remains largely unaddressed. We present computationally felicitous time-uniform and value-uniform bounds on the CDF of the running averaged conditional distribution of a sequence of real-valued random variables. Consistent with known impossibility results, our CDF bounds are always valid but sometimes trivial when the instance is too hard, and we give an instance-dependent convergence guarantee. The importance-weighted extension is appropriate for estimating complete counterfactual distributions of rewards given data from a randomized experiment, e.g., from an A/B test or a contextual bandit.

paragraphs: Estimating an entire distribution provides more information than estimating a single average, but standard results often assume independent observations from an unchanged distribution. This paper studies sequences with arbitrary data dependence. Its target is the cumulative distribution function of the running average of the observations’ conditional distributions.

The proposed confidence bands are uniform in both time and value. They cover uncertainty across the distribution’s thresholds while supporting continued observation over time. The authors also make the computational procedures practical and provide an instance-dependent convergence guarantee, linking how informative the bands become to the difficulty of the particular sequence.

A stated limitation is essential to interpreting the result: the bands remain valid but can become trivial on sufficiently hard instances, consistent with known impossibility results. An importance-weighted extension estimates complete counterfactual reward distributions from randomized data, including A/B tests and contextual bandits. The contribution combines broad statistical validity with explicit recognition that validity does not always imply informative bounds.
summary.tldr: Time- and value-uniform confidence bands estimate running-average conditional distributions under nonstationarity, remaining valid even when hard instances make them uninformative.

title: Time-uniform confidence bands for the CDF under nonstationarity

abstract: We study the problem of collaboratively learning least squares estimates for $m$ agents. Each agent observes a different subset of the features---e.g., containing data collected from sensors of varying resolution. Our goal is to determine how to coordinate the agents in order to produce the best estimator for each agent. We propose a distributed, semi-supervised algorithm Collab, consisting of three steps: local training, aggregation, and distribution. Our procedure does not require communicating the labeled data, making it communication efficient and useful in settings where the labeled data is inaccessible. Despite this handicap, our procedure is nearly asymptotically, local-minimax optimal---even among estimators allowed to communicate the labeled data such as imputation methods. We test our method on US Census data. We also discuss generalizations of our method to non-Gaussian feature settings, non-linear settings, and Federated Learning.

Our procedure does not require communicating the labeled data, making it communication efficient and useful in settings where the labeled data is inaccessible. Despite this handicap, our procedure is nearly asymptotically, local-minimax optimal---even among estimators allowed to communicate the labeled data such as imputation methods. We test our method on US Census data. We also discuss generalizations of our method to non-Gaussian feature settings, non-linear settings, and Federated Learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies collaboration among agents that each observe a different subset of the available features. Such differences can arise when sensors collect information at different resolutions. The objective is to coordinate learning so that each agent obtains a strong least-squares estimator, despite having only a partial view of the features.

The proposed semi-supervised procedure, Collab, has three stages: agents train locally, their results are aggregated, and information is distributed back to them. Labeled examples do not need to be communicated. This makes the procedure useful when those examples cannot be accessed centrally and reduces the communication burden associated with sharing them.

The main theoretical result says that Collab is nearly optimal in an asymptotic, local-minimax sense, even compared with estimators allowed to exchange labeled data, including imputation methods. The qualification matters: this is a specific statistical optimality statement, not a claim of best performance in every finite dataset. The authors also test Collab on US Census data and discuss extensions involving non-Gaussian features, nonlinear models, and federated learning.
summary.tldr: Collab coordinates linear estimation across agents with different feature subsets without exchanging labeled data, while achieving a qualified near-optimality guarantee.

title: Collaboratively Learning Linear Models with Structured Missing Data

abstract: In many reinforcement learning tasks, the agent has to learn to interact with many objects of different types and generalize to unseen combinations and numbers of objects. Often a task is a composition of previously learned tasks (e.g. block stacking).These are examples of compositional generalization, in which we compose object-centric representations to solve complex tasks. Recent works have shown the benefits of object-factored representations and hierarchical abstractions for improving sample efficiency in these settings. On the other hand, these methods do not fully exploit the benefits of factorization in terms of object attributes. In this paper, we address this opportunity and introduce the Dynamic Attribute FacTored RL (DAFT-RL) framework. In DAFT-RL, we leverage object-centric representation learning to extract objects from visual inputs. We learn to classify them into classes and infer their latent parameters. For each class of object, we learn a class template graph that describes how the dynamics and reward of an object of this class factorize according to its attributes. We also learn an interaction pattern graph that describes how objects of different classes interact with each other at the attribute level. Through these graphs and a dynamic interaction graph that models the interactions between objects, we can learn a policy that can then be directly applied in a new environment by estimating the interactions and latent parameters.We evaluate DAFT-RL in three benchmark datasets and show our framework outperforms the state-of-the-art in generalizing across unseen objects with varying attributes and latent parameters, as well as in the composition of previously learned tasks.

paragraphs: An agent interacting with multiple objects may encounter new combinations, unfamiliar object properties, or tasks assembled from previously learned tasks. Representing each object separately helps, but the authors argue that further structure is available within objects themselves. DAFT-RL learns how individual object attributes contribute to dynamics, rewards, and interactions.

The framework extracts objects from visual inputs, assigns them to classes, and infers their latent parameters. For each class, a template graph describes how dynamics and rewards factor across attributes. Another graph describes attribute-level interactions between object classes. A dynamic interaction graph then represents the interactions among the objects present in a particular environment.

Together, these structures support a policy that can be applied in a new environment by estimating its interactions and latent parameters. This connects reusable class-level knowledge to the particular objects currently encountered. Evaluation on three benchmark datasets reports better generalization than state-of-the-art methods for unseen objects with varying attributes and latent parameters, as well as for tasks composed from previously learned tasks.
summary.tldr: DAFT-RL models object attributes and their interactions to improve generalization to unfamiliar objects and composed tasks.

title: Learning Dynamic Attribute-factored World Models for Efficient Multi-object Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Most neural networks assume that input images have a fixed number of channels (three for RGB images). However, there are many settings where the number of channels may vary, such as microscopy images where the number of channels changes depending on instruments and experimental goals. Yet, there has not been a systemic attempt to create and evaluate neural networks that are invariant to the number and type of channels. As a result, trained models remain specific to individual studies and are hardly reusable for other microscopy settings. In this paper, we present a benchmark for investigating channel-adaptive models in microscopy imaging, which consists of 1) a dataset of varied-channel single-cell images, and 2) a biologically relevant evaluation framework. In addition, we adapted several existing techniques to create channel-adaptive models and compared their performance on this benchmark to fixed-channel, baseline models. We find that channel-adaptive models can generalize better to out-of-domain tasks and can be computationally efficient. We contribute a curated dataset and an evaluation API to facilitate objective comparisons in future research and applications.

paragraphs: Many image models expect a fixed set of input channels, such as the three channels in an RGB image. Microscopy does not always fit that arrangement: instruments and experimental goals can change both the number and type of channels collected. Models tied to one channel configuration can consequently be difficult to reuse across studies.

CHAMMI provides a benchmark for investigating models that adapt to these changes. It combines a curated dataset of single-cell images with varying channel counts and an evaluation framework built around biologically relevant tasks. The authors also adapt several existing techniques into channel-adaptive models and compare them with models that use fixed channel configurations.

The findings show that channel-adaptive models can generalize better to tasks outside their original domain and can be computationally efficient. These are demonstrated possibilities rather than a claim that every adaptive design is superior. By supplying both data and an evaluation API, CHAMMI gives future work a common basis for comparing whether flexibility in image inputs translates into useful biological predictions.
summary.tldr: CHAMMI benchmarks microscopy models that adapt to varying image channels and shows potential benefits for generalization and efficiency.

title: CHAMMI: A benchmark for channel-adaptive models in microscopy imaging

abstract: Aligning language models (LMs) with preferences is an important problem in natural language generation. A key challenge is that preferences are typically provided at the *sequence level* while LM training and generation both occur at the *token level*. There is, therefore, a *granularity mismatch* between the preference and the LM training losses, which may complicate the learning problem. In this paper, we address this issue by developing an alternate training process, where we iterate between grounding the sequence-level preference into token-level training guidance, and improving the LM with the learned guidance. For guidance learning, we design a framework that extends the pairwise-preference learning in imitation learning to both variable-length LM generation and the utilization of the preference among multiple generations. For LM training, based on the amount of supervised data, we present two *minimalist* learning objectives that utilize the learned guidance. In experiments, our method performs competitively on two distinct representative LM tasks --- discrete-prompt generation and text summarization.

paragraphs: Human preferences often judge complete generated answers, while a language model trains and generates one token at a time. This mismatch in granularity can complicate learning because an overall preference does not directly specify guidance for individual token decisions. The paper develops a training process that explicitly connects these two levels.

The process alternates between learning token-level guidance from sequence-level preferences and improving the language model using that guidance. Its guidance framework extends pairwise preference learning from imitation learning to variable-length text and preferences involving multiple generations. This lets the method accommodate the structure of language-model outputs and make use of comparisons beyond a single pair.

For updating the language model, the authors present two simple objectives suited to different amounts of supervised data. Experiments on discrete-prompt generation and text summarization show competitive performance. The findings support the usefulness of translating whole-output preferences into finer-grained training guidance, with an alternating procedure that learns the guidance and then applies it to model improvement.
summary.tldr: The method alternates between converting sequence-level preferences into token-level guidance and fine-tuning a language model with that guidance.

title: Preference-grounded Token-level Guidance for Language Model Fine-tuning

abstract: Collaborative machine learning (ML) is widely used to enable institutions to learn better models from distributed data. While collaborative approaches to learning intuitively protect user data, they remain vulnerable to either the server, the clients, or both, deviating from the protocol. Indeed, because the protocol is asymmetric, a malicious server can abuse its power to reconstruct client data points. Conversely, malicious clients can corrupt learning with malicious updates. Thus, both clients and servers require a guarantee when the other cannot be trusted to fully cooperate. In this work, we propose a peer-to-peer (P2P) learning scheme that is secure against malicious servers and robust to malicious clients. Our core contribution is a generic framework that transforms any (compatible) algorithm for robust aggregation of model updates to the setting where servers and clients can act maliciously. Finally, we demonstrate the computational efficiency of our approach even with 1-million parameter models trained by 100s of peers on standard datasets.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning lets institutions train together on distributed data, but keeping data local does not resolve every trust problem. A malicious server may exploit its role to reconstruct client data, while malicious clients may submit updates that corrupt learning. This paper addresses both kinds of deliberate protocol deviation.

The authors propose a peer-to-peer learning scheme that is secure against malicious servers and robust to malicious clients. Its central contribution is a generic framework for transforming compatible robust aggregation algorithms into this adversarial setting. Robust aggregation concerns how model updates are combined when some updates may be malicious.

The compatibility qualification matters: the transformation applies to aggregation algorithms that fit the framework. The authors also demonstrate computational efficiency with models containing one million parameters and training involving hundreds of peers on standard datasets. This evidence supports the practicality of combining protection against malicious coordination with resistance to harmful participant updates, rather than addressing only one side of collaborative learning's trust problem.
summary.tldr: A peer-to-peer framework adapts compatible robust aggregation algorithms to learning with malicious servers and clients.

title: Robust and Actively Secure Serverless Collaborative Learning

abstract: We study the parameterized complexity of training two-layer neural networks with respect to the dimension of the input data and the number of hidden neurons, considering ReLU and linear threshold activation functions. Albeit the computational complexity of these problems has been studied numerous times in recent years, several questions are still open. We answer questions by Arora et al. (ICLR 2018) and Khalife and Basu (IPCO 2022) showing that both problems are NP-hard for two dimensions, which excludes any polynomial-time algorithm for constant dimension. We also answer a question by Froese et al. (JAIR 2022) proving W[1]-hardness for four ReLUs (or two linear threshold neurons) with zero training error. Finally, in the ReLU case, we show fixed-parameter tractability for the combined parameter number of dimensions and number of ReLUs if the network is assumed to compute a convex map. Our results settle the complexity status regarding these parameters almost completely.

paragraphs: This paper asks how the difficulty of training two-layer neural networks depends on input dimension and the number of hidden neurons. It considers ReLU and linear threshold activations. The focus is computational complexity: identifying which restrictions on a training problem make it tractable and which still leave formal hardness barriers.

The authors prove NP-hardness for both activation types even with two-dimensional inputs. Thus, fixing the input dimension alone does not remove the stated complexity barrier. They also establish W[1]-hardness for zero-training-error problems with four ReLUs or two linear threshold neurons, further clarifying how small network size interacts with the difficulty of training.

A positive result appears when a ReLU network is assumed to compute a convex map. Under that restriction, training is fixed-parameter tractable in the combined parameter consisting of input dimension and number of ReLUs. Together, the results map out both hardness and tractability under explicit architectural and functional restrictions, nearly completing the classification for the parameters studied.
summary.tldr: Training two-layer networks remains NP-hard in two dimensions, while convex ReLU maps admit a combined-parameter tractability result.

title: Training Neural Networks is NP-Hard in Fixed Dimension

abstract: The widespread adoption of Transformer architectures in various data modalities has opened new avenues for the applications in molecular modeling. Nevertheless, it remains elusive that whether the Transformer-based architecture can do molecular modeling as good as equivariant GNNs. In this paper, by designing Interatomic Positional Encoding (IPE) thatparameterizes atomic environments as Transformer's positional encodings,we propose Geoformer, a novel geometric Transformer to effectively model molecular structures for various molecular property prediction. We evaluate Geoformer on several benchmarks, including the QM9 dataset and the recently proposed Molecule3D dataset. Compared with both Transformers and equivariant GNN models, Geoformer outperforms the state-of-the-art (SoTA) algorithms on QM9, and achieves the best performance on Molecule3D for both random and scaffold splits.By introducing IPE, Geoformer paves the way for molecular geometric modeling based on Transformer architecture.Codes are available at https://github.com/microsoft/AI2BMD/tree/Geoformer.

paragraphs: Molecular property prediction requires a model to make effective use of molecular structure. Transformers have succeeded across many kinds of data, but the paper asks whether they can compete with equivariant graph neural networks in molecular modeling. Its answer centers on giving the Transformer a positional representation designed around atomic environments.

The proposed Interatomic Positional Encoding, or IPE, parameterizes those environments as positional encodings. Geoformer incorporates IPE into a geometric Transformer for predicting molecular properties. The key design choice is to bring structural information into the architecture through its positional encoding, making molecular geometry part of how the Transformer represents its input.

The authors evaluate Geoformer on benchmarks including QM9 and Molecule3D, comparing it with both Transformers and equivariant graph neural networks. They report state-of-the-art performance on QM9 and the best results on Molecule3D under both random and scaffold splits. These findings support IPE as an effective route to geometric molecular modeling with Transformers, with the reported advantage demonstrated across the stated datasets and evaluation splits.
summary.tldr: Geoformer encodes atomic environments as Transformer positional information and achieves leading molecular-property prediction results on the reported benchmarks.

title: Geometric Transformer with Interatomic Positional Encoding

abstract: Reasoning on large-scale knowledge graphs has been long dominated by embedding methods. While path-based methods possess the inductive capacity that embeddings lack, their scalability is limited by the exponential number of paths. Here we present A\*Net, a scalable path-based method for knowledge graph reasoning. Inspired by the A\* algorithm for shortest path problems, our A\*Net learns a priority function to select important nodes and edges at each iteration, to reduce time and memory footprint for both training and inference. The ratio of selected nodes and edges can be specified to trade off between performance and efficiency. Experiments on both transductive and inductive knowledge graph reasoning benchmarks show that A\*Net achieves competitive performance with existing state-of-the-art path-based methods, while merely visiting 10% nodes and 10% edges at each iteration. On a million-scale dataset ogbl-wikikg2, A\*Net not only achieves a new state-of-the-art result, but also converges faster than embedding methods. A\*Net is the first path-based method for knowledge graph reasoning at such scale.

paragraphs: A*Net tackles a scaling problem in knowledge graph reasoning: following paths through a graph can support reasoning beyond learned entity embeddings, but the number of possible paths grows exponentially. This makes path exploration expensive in both memory and computation, helping explain why embedding methods have dominated reasoning on large knowledge graphs.

Inspired by the A* shortest-path algorithm, the method learns a priority function that selects important nodes and edges at each iteration. Training and inference therefore concentrate on a chosen portion of the graph. The selection ratios are adjustable, giving users a direct way to trade reasoning performance against computational efficiency.

On benchmarks covering both transductive and inductive reasoning, A*Net remains competitive with leading path-based approaches while visiting only 10% of nodes and edges per iteration. On the million-scale ogbl-wikikg2 dataset, it reports a new state-of-the-art result and faster convergence than embedding methods. These findings show that selective exploration can make path-based reasoning workable at a scale previously inaccessible to such methods.
summary.tldr: A*Net learns which graph paths to prioritize, enabling competitive knowledge graph reasoning while exploring far fewer nodes and edges.

title: A*Net: A Scalable Path-based Reasoning Approach for Knowledge Graphs

abstract: Binary Balanced Tree Recursive Neural Networks (BBT-RvNNs) enforce sequence composition according to a preset balanced binary tree structure. Thus, their non-linear recursion depth (which is the tree depth) is just $\log_2 n$ ($n$ being the sequence length). Such logarithmic scaling makes BBT-RvNNs efficient and scalable on long sequence tasks such as Long Range Arena (LRA). However, such computational efficiency comes at a cost because BBT-RvNNs cannot solve simple arithmetic tasks like ListOps. On the flip side, RvNN models (e.g., Beam Tree RvNN) that do succeed on ListOps (and other structure-sensitive tasks like formal logical inference) are generally several times more expensive (in time and space) than even Recurrent Neural Networks. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework --- Recursion in Recursion (RIR) to strike a balance between the two sides - getting some of the benefits from both worlds. In RIR, we use a form of two-level nested recursion - where the outer recursion is a $k$-ary balanced tree model with another recursive model (inner recursion) implementing its cell function. For the inner recursion, we choose Beam Tree RvNNs. To adjust Beam Tree RvNNs within RIR we also propose a novel strategy of beam alignment. Overall, this entails that the total recursive depth in RIR is upper-bounded by $k \log_k n$. Our best RIR-based model is the first model that demonstrates high ($\geq 90\%$) length-generalization performance on ListOps while at the same time being scalable enough to be trainable on long sequence inputs from LRA (it can reduce the memory usage of the original Beam Tree RvNN by hundreds of times). Moreover, in terms of accuracy in the LRA language tasks, it performs competitively with Structured State Space Models (SSMs) without any special initialization - outperforming Transformers by a large margin. On the other hand, while SSMs can marginally outperform RIR on LRA, they (SSMs) fail to length-generalize on ListOps. Our code is available at: https://github.com/JRC1995/BeamRecursionFamily/

However, their fixed composition structure struggles with structure-sensitive tasks such as ListOps. More flexible recursive models can solve these tasks but demand much more time and memory. Recursion in Recursion, or RIR, combines the two approaches.

RIR uses a balanced k-ary tree as its outer recursion and a Beam Tree recursive network inside each cell. A proposed beam-alignment strategy adapts the inner model to this arrangement. The resulting total recursive depth is bounded above by k log base k of n. This architecture retains a scalable outer organization while allowing richer composition within its individual recursive operations.

The best RIR model achieves at least 90% length-generalization performance on ListOps while remaining trainable on long Long Range Arena inputs. It can reduce the original Beam Tree model's memory use by hundreds of times. On LRA language tasks it is competitive with structured state-space models and substantially outperforms Transformers. State-space models can slightly surpass it on LRA, but fail the reported ListOps length-generalization test.
summary.tldr: RIR nests flexible recursion inside a balanced tree to combine strong ListOps length generalization with scalable long-sequence processing.

title: Recursion in Recursion: Two-Level Nested Recursion for Length Generalization with Scalability

abstract: In this paper, we consider the optimization problem Submodular Cover (SCP), which is to find a minimum cardinality subset of a finite universe $U$ such that the value of a submodular function $f$ is above an input threshold $\tau$. In particular, we consider several variants of SCP including the general case, the case where $f$ is additionally assumed to be monotone, and finally the case where $f$ is a regularized monotone submodular function. Our most significant contributions are that: (i) We propose a scalable algorithm for monotone SCP that achieves nearly the same approximation guarantees as the standard greedy algorithm in significantly faster time; (ii) We are the first to develop an algorithm for general SCP that achieves a solution arbitrarily close to being feasible; and finally (iii) we are the first to develop algorithms for regularized SCP. Our algorithms are then demonstrated to be effective in an extensive experimental section on data summarization and graph cut, two applications of SCP.

In particular, we consider several variants of SCP including the general case, the case where $f$ is additionally assumed to be monotone, and finally the case where $f$ is a regularized monotone submodular function. Our most significant contributions are that: (i) We propose a scalable algorithm for monotone SCP that achieves nearly the same approximation guarantees as the standard greedy algorithm in significantly faster time; (ii) We are the first to develop an algorithm for general SCP that achieves a solution arbitrarily close to being feasible; and finally (iii) we are the first to develop algorithms for regularized SCP. paragraphs: Submodular Cover asks for the smallest subset of available items whose function value reaches a specified threshold. The challenge is to keep the selected set small while achieving enough value. This paper studies several versions of that problem: general submodular functions, monotone functions, and regularized monotone functions.

For the monotone case, the authors introduce a scalable algorithm with approximation guarantees nearly matching those of the standard greedy method, but with substantially faster execution. For the general case, they provide an algorithm whose solution can come arbitrarily close to feasibility. That distinction matters: approaching the threshold arbitrarily closely is a different guarantee from always satisfying it exactly.

The paper also introduces algorithms for the regularized version, which the authors identify as a previously unaddressed setting. Experiments on data summarization and graph cut demonstrate the proposed methods' effectiveness in two applications. The contributions therefore address both computational efficiency in a familiar case and the availability of approximation methods for broader variants, with guarantees tailored to each problem's structure.
summary.tldr: New Submodular Cover algorithms improve scalability for monotone functions and extend approximation guarantees to general and regularized variants.

title: Bicriteria Approximation Algorithms for the Submodular Cover Problem

abstract: Modern deep policy gradient methods achieve effective performance on simulated robotic tasks, but they all require large replay buffers or expensive batch updates, or both, making them incompatible for real systems with resource-limited computers. We show that these methods fail catastrophically when limited to small replay buffers or during *incremental learning*, where updates only use the most recent sample without batch updates or a replay buffer. We propose a novel incremental deep policy gradient method --- *Action Value Gradient (AVG)* and a set of normalization and scaling techniques to address the challenges of instability in incremental learning. On robotic simulation benchmarks, we show that AVG is the only incremental method that learns effectively, often achieving final performance comparable to batch policy gradient methods. This advancement enabled us to show for the first time effective deep reinforcement learning with real robots using only incremental updates, employing a robotic manipulator and a mobile robot.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement-learning methods for robotic control often depend on stored experience or costly updates using batches of samples. Those requirements create difficulties for robots with limited computing resources. The authors show that the methods they examine can fail severely when replay buffers are small or when learning uses only the latest observation.

Their proposed Action Value Gradient method, or AVG, is designed for this incremental setting. Each update uses the most recent sample without a replay buffer or batch update. A set of normalization and scaling techniques addresses the instability that otherwise makes this form of deep policy-gradient learning difficult. The paper also removes reliance on target networks.

On robotic simulation benchmarks, AVG is the only incremental method in the reported comparison that learns effectively, often reaching final performance comparable to batch methods. The authors also demonstrate incremental deep reinforcement learning on a robotic manipulator and a mobile robot. These findings show that useful learning can occur under the paper's much leaner update regime.
summary.tldr: AVG enables effective deep policy-gradient learning from individual recent samples, with demonstrations in simulation and on two real robotic systems.

title: Deep Policy Gradient Methods Without Batch Updates, Target Networks, or Replay Buffers

abstract: This paper concerns the problem of aligning samples from large language models to human preferences using *best-of-$n$* sampling, where we draw $n$ samples, rank them, and return the best one. We consider two fundamental problems. First: what is the relationship between best-of-$n$ and other (RLHF-type) approaches to aligning LLMs? In particular, when should one be preferred to the other? We show that the best-of-$n$ sampling distribution is essentially equivalent to the policy learned by RLHF if we apply a particular monotone transformation to the reward function. Moreover, we show that this transformation yields the best possible trade-off between win-rate against the base model vs KL distance from the base model. Then, best-of-$n$ is a Pareto-optimal win-rate vs KL solution.The second problem we consider is how to fine-tune a model to mimic the best-of-$n$ sampling distribution, to avoid drawing $n$ samples for each inference. We derive *BonBon Alignment* as a method for achieving this. Experiments show that BonBon alignment yields a model that achieves high win rates while minimally affecting off-target aspects of the generations.

paragraphs: Best-of-n sampling aligns language-model outputs by generating several candidates, ranking them, and returning the best. This paper examines how that selection procedure relates to reinforcement learning from human feedback. It also asks whether a model can learn the resulting output distribution so that generating multiple candidates is no longer required at every inference.

The theoretical result connects best-of-n sampling to an RLHF policy under a particular monotone transformation of the reward function. With that transformation, the distribution achieves an optimal trade-off between beating the base model in preference comparisons and remaining close to its distribution, measured by KL distance. This is a specific Pareto-optimality result for win rate and distributional change, rather than a claim of optimality for every alignment objective.

The authors derive BoNBoN Alignment to fine-tune a model toward the best-of-n distribution. This transfers the benefit of selection into the model's sampling behavior. Experiments report high win rates with minimal effects on aspects of generation outside the alignment target, supporting the practical value of preserving base-model behavior while improving preferred responses.
summary.tldr: BoNBoN trains models to imitate best-of-n sampling, supported by a theoretical connection to an optimal win-rate-versus-KL alignment trade-off.

title: BoNBoN Alignment for Large Language Models and the Sweetness of Best-of-n Sampling

abstract: Visual representations become progressively more abstract along the cortical hierarchy. These abstract representations define notions like objects and shapes, but at the cost of spatial specificity. By contrast, low-level regions represent spatially local but simple input features. How do spatially non-specific representations of abstract concepts in high-level areas flexibly modulate the low-level sensory representations in appropriate ways to guide context-driven and goal-directed behaviors across a range of tasks? We build a biologically motivated and trainable neural network model of dynamics in the visual pathway, incorporating local, lateral, and feedforward synaptic connections, excitatory and inhibitory neurons, and long-range top-down inputs conceptualized as low-rank modulations of the input-driven sensory responses by high-level areas. We study this ${\bf D}$ynamical ${\bf C}$ortical ${\bf net}$work ($DCnet$) in a visual cue-delay-search task and show that the model uses its own cue representations to adaptively modulate its perceptual responses to solve the task, outperforming state-of-the-art DNN vision and LLM models. The model's population states over time shed light on the nature of contextual modulatory dynamics, generating predictions for experiments. We fine-tune the same model on classic psychophysics attention tasks, and find that the model closely replicates known reaction time results. This work represents a promising new foundation for understanding and making predictions about perturbations to visual processing in the brain.

paragraphs: High-level visual representations capture abstract concepts but lose precise spatial detail, while lower-level representations retain location and simpler features. This paper investigates how abstract context can guide those local sensory responses. It introduces DCnet, a trainable model of visual pathway dynamics designed around biologically motivated connections and neuron types.

DCnet includes local, lateral, and feedforward connections, excitatory and inhibitory neurons, and long-range top-down inputs. These top-down signals act as low-rank modulations of sensory responses. In a cue-delay-search task, the network uses its own representation of the cue to adapt its subsequent perceptual processing. The authors report that it outperforms the state-of-the-art vision and language models evaluated on that task.

The evolution of the model’s population activity provides an account of contextual modulation and generates predictions for experiments. After fine-tuning on classic attention tasks, the same model closely reproduces known reaction time findings. These results position DCnet as a promising tool for investigating context-dependent vision and predicting the effects of perturbations to visual processing.
summary.tldr: DCnet models how high-level context dynamically modulates sensory processing, with strong task performance and close matches to known attention reaction times.

title: Flexible Context-Driven Sensory Processing in Dynamical Vision Models

abstract: We analyze the capabilities of Transformer language models in learning compositional discrete tasks. To this end, we evaluate training LLaMA models and prompting GPT-4 and Gemini on four tasks demanding to learn a composition of several discrete sub-tasks. In particular, we measure how well these models can reuse primitives observable in the sub-tasks to learn the composition task. Our results indicate that compositional learning in state-of-the-art Transformer language models is highly sample inefficient: LLaMA requires more data samples than relearning all sub-tasks from scratch to learn the compositional task; in-context prompting with few samples is unreliable and fails at executing the sub-tasks or correcting the errors in multi-round code generation. Further, by leveraging complexity theory, we support these findings with a theoretical analysis focused on the sample inefficiency of gradient descent in memorizing feedforward models. We open source our code at https://github.com/IBM/limitations-lm-algorithmic-compositional-learning.

paragraphs: Learning several component procedures does not automatically mean a model can efficiently learn to combine them. This paper examines that distinction using four discrete tasks, each requiring a composition of smaller subtasks. The study trains LLaMA models and prompts GPT-4 and Gemini to measure how effectively they reuse primitives available in the component tasks.

The results reveal substantial sample inefficiency in the evaluated settings. LLaMA needs more examples to learn the composed task than would be required to relearn all its subtasks from scratch. Few-example prompting is also unreliable, with failures in executing subtasks and in correcting errors during multiple rounds of code generation.

A complexity-theoretic analysis supports these observations by studying the sample inefficiency of gradient descent in memorizing feedforward models. The combined evidence highlights a gap between exposure to reusable primitives and efficient composition. Its scope is the studied tasks, models, and theoretical setting; the contribution is an empirical and analytical account of that gap, rather than a claim that Transformers cannot compose algorithms.
summary.tldr: Across four discrete tasks, tested Transformer language models struggle to efficiently reuse component procedures when learning their composition.

title: Limits of Transformer Language Models on Learning to Compose Algorithms

abstract: Recent research has made significant progress in optimizing diffusion models for downstream objectives, which is an important pursuit in fields such as graph generation for drug design. However, directly applying these models to graph presents challenges, resulting in suboptimal performance. This paper introduces graph diffusion policy optimization (GDPO), a novel approach to optimize graph diffusion models for arbitrary (e.g., non-differentiable) objectives using reinforcement learning. GDPO is based on an eager policy gradient tailored for graph diffusion models, developed through meticulous analysis and promising improved performance. Experimental results show that GDPO achieves state-of-the-art performance in various graph generation tasks with complex and diverse objectives. Code is available at https://github.com/sail-sg/GDPO.

paragraphs: The paper concerns graph generation when the generated outputs must satisfy downstream objectives. Drug design is one motivating application. Their focus is therefore on adapting the optimization method to the graph setting.

Graph Diffusion Policy Optimization, or GDPO, uses reinforcement learning to optimize graph diffusion models for arbitrary objectives, including objectives that are not differentiable. Supporting such objectives matters because the desired evaluation criterion need not supply a gradient that a model can follow directly. The method centers on an eager policy gradient specifically developed for graph diffusion models through analysis of this setting.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across several graph-generation tasks with complex and varied objectives. These results support the proposed policy-gradient approach as an effective way to connect graph diffusion generation to downstream goals. The empirical claim concerns the tasks evaluated, while the broader methodological contribution is an optimization framework that accommodates objectives beyond differentiable training losses.
summary.tldr: GDPO uses a graph-specific reinforcement-learning update to optimize diffusion generators for objectives that can be non-differentiable.

title: Graph Diffusion Policy Optimization

abstract: Second-order optimization algorithms, such as the Newton method and the natural gradient descent (NGD) method exhibit excellent convergence properties for training deep neural networks, but the high computational cost limits its practical application. In this paper, we focus on the NGD method and propose a novel layer-wise natural gradient descent (LNGD) method to further reduce computational costs and accelerate the training process. Specifically, based on the block diagonal approximation of the Fisher information matrix, we first propose the layer-wise sample method to compute each block matrix without performing a complete back-propagation. Then, each block matrix is approximated as a Kronecker product of two smaller matrices, one of which is a diagonal matrix, while keeping the traces equal before and after approximation. By these two steps, we provide a new approximation for the Fisher information matrix, which can effectively reduce the computational cost while preserving the main information of each block matrix. Moreover, we propose a new adaptive layer-wise learning rate to further accelerate training. Based on these new approaches, we propose the LNGD optimizer. The global convergence analysis of LNGD is established under some assumptions. Experiments on image classification and machine translation tasks show that our method is quite competitive compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Natural gradient descent can offer favorable convergence behavior, but computing the information needed for its updates is expensive. This paper introduces LNGD, a layer-wise optimizer that reduces that expense by approximating the Fisher information matrix. The aim is to retain useful information for choosing updates while making training more practical.

The method starts with a block diagonal approximation and computes the blocks using layer-wise sampling, without requiring a complete backward pass for each block. It then replaces each block with a Kronecker product of two smaller matrices, one diagonal. This approximation preserves the block’s trace, giving the compression a specific mathematical constraint rather than simply discarding entries.

LNGD also adjusts learning rates separately by layer to accelerate training. The authors establish a global convergence analysis under assumptions and report competitive results on image classification and machine translation. Together, these contributions address both the cost of constructing natural gradient updates and the choice of update size, with empirical support across two different kinds of learning tasks.
summary.tldr: LNGD makes natural gradient training cheaper through layer-wise Fisher approximations and adaptive learning rates, with competitive results on classification and translation.

title: A Layer-Wise Natural Gradient Optimizer for Training Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Diverse human motion prediction (HMP) is a fundamental application in computer vision that has recently attracted considerable interest. Prior methods primarily focus on the stochastic nature of human motion, while neglecting the specific impact of external environment, leading to the pronounced artifacts in prediction when applied to real-world scenarios. To fill this gap, this work introduces a novel task: predicting diverse human motion within real-world 3D scenes. In contrast to prior works, it requires harmonizing the deterministic constraints imposed by the surrounding 3D scenes with the stochastic aspect of human motion. For this purpose, we propose DiMoP3D, a diverse motion prediction framework with 3D scene awareness, which leverages the 3D point cloud and observed sequence to generate diverse and high-fidelity predictions. DiMoP3D is able to comprehend the 3D scene, and determines the probable target objects and their desired interactive pose based on the historical motion. Then, it plans the obstacle-free trajectory towards these interested objects, and generates diverse and physically-consistent future motions. On top of that, DiMoP3D identifies deterministic factors in the scene and integrates them into the stochastic modeling, making the diverse HMP in realistic scenes become a controllable stochastic generation process. On two real-captured benchmarks, DiMoP3D has demonstrated significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its effectiveness in generating diverse and physically-consistent motion predictions within real-world 3D environments.

paragraphs: Predicting human movement involves uncertainty because several future motions may be plausible. But a person's surroundings also impose constraints on where and how they can move. This paper introduces the task of predicting diverse human motions inside real-world 3D scenes, addressing artifacts that arise when motion prediction emphasizes variability while neglecting the physical environment.

The proposed DiMoP3D framework takes a scene point cloud together with observed movement. It uses that history to infer likely target objects and the poses needed to interact with them. It then plans an obstacle-free route toward those objects and generates multiple possible future motions. Scene understanding therefore shapes both the intended interaction and the movement leading to it.

DiMoP3D incorporates deterministic environmental factors into its stochastic generation process, making variation responsive to the scene. On two benchmarks captured in real environments, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining diversity with physical consistency: the model aims to preserve multiple plausible futures while making those futures compatible with the surrounding 3D environment.
summary.tldr: DiMoP3D combines scene constraints with stochastic prediction to generate diverse, physically consistent human motions in real 3D environments.

title: Harmonizing Stochasticity and Determinism: Scene-responsive Diverse Human Motion Prediction

abstract: Zero- and few-shot visual anomaly segmentation relies on powerful vision-language models that detect unseen anomalies using manually designed textual prompts. However, visual representations are inherently independent of language. In this paper, we explore the potential of a pure visual foundation model as an alternative to widely used vision-language models for universal visual anomaly segmentation.We present a novel paradigm that unifies anomaly segmentation into change segmentation. This paradigm enables us to leverage large-scale synthetic image pairs, featuring object-level and local region changes, derived from existing image datasets, which are independent of target anomaly datasets. We propose a one-prompt Meta-learning framework for Universal Anomaly Segmentation (MetaUAS) that is trained on this synthetic dataset and then generalizes well to segment any novel or unseen visual anomalies in the real world. To handle geometrical variations between prompt and query images, we propose a soft feature alignment module that bridges paired-image change perception and single-image semantic segmentation. This is the first work to achieve universal anomaly segmentation using a pure vision model without relying on special anomaly detection datasets and pre-trained visual-language models. Our method effectively and efficiently segments any anomalies with only one normal image prompt and enjoys training-free without guidance from language. Our MetaUAS significantly outperforms previous zero-shot, few-shot, and even full-shot anomaly segmentation methods. Code and Models: https://github.com/gaobb/MetaUAS.

paragraphs: MetaUAS investigates whether a purely visual foundation model can locate unfamiliar anomalies without language prompts. Its central move is to reformulate anomaly segmentation as change segmentation. A normal image supplies the reference, and the model identifies anomalous regions in a query image through its learned ability to perceive differences between paired images.

The authors train a one-prompt meta-learning framework on synthetic image pairs created from existing datasets. These pairs contain changes to entire objects and to local regions, without depending on the target anomaly datasets. A soft feature alignment module handles geometric differences between the reference and query, connecting paired-image change perception with the segmentation of regions within an individual image.

After this training, MetaUAS uses one normal image as its prompt without further training or language guidance. The authors report strong generalization to unseen anomalies and significant improvements over previous zero-shot, few-shot, and even full-shot methods. The approach matters because its preparation relies on synthetic visual changes, while its use requires only a normal visual example of the target setting.
summary.tldr: MetaUAS learns anomaly segmentation from synthetic visual changes and identifies unseen anomalies using a single normal-image prompt.

title: MetaUAS: Universal Anomaly Segmentation with One-Prompt Meta-Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of active learning for global sensitivity analysis of expensive black-box functions. Our aim is to efficiently learn the importance of different input variables, e.g., in vehicle safety experimentation, we study the impact of the thickness of various components on safety objectives. Since function evaluations are expensive, we use active learning to prioritize experimental resources where they yield the most value. We propose novel active learning acquisition functions that directly target key quantities of derivative-based global sensitivity measures (DGSMs) under Gaussian process surrogate models.We showcase the first application of active learning directly to DGSMs, and develop tractable uncertainty reduction and information gain acquisition functions for these measures. Through comprehensive evaluation on synthetic and real-world problems, our study demonstrates how these active learning acquisition strategies substantially enhance the sample efficiency of DGSM estimation, particularly with limited evaluation budgets. Our work paves the way for more efficient and accurate sensitivity analysis in various scientific and engineering applications.

paragraphs: When evaluating a function requires an expensive experiment or simulation, discovering which inputs matter most can consume a large budget. This paper studies how to select evaluations specifically for sensitivity analysis. Its motivating example asks how changes in the thickness of vehicle components affect safety objectives.

The method uses a Gaussian process as a surrogate for the expensive function and targets derivative-based global sensitivity measures. These measures summarize how strongly the output changes with different inputs. Instead of choosing experiments only to improve general predictions, the proposed acquisition functions prioritize evaluations expected to reduce uncertainty or provide information about the sensitivity quantities themselves.

The authors develop computationally tractable ways to make these choices and describe this as the first direct application of active learning to these measures. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world problems show substantial gains in sample efficiency, especially with small evaluation budgets. The practical contribution is a closer match between the information an experiment collects and the input-importance question the analysis needs to answer.
summary.tldr: Targeting experiments directly at derivative-based sensitivity measures improves how efficiently input importance can be estimated.

title: Active Learning for Derivative-Based Global Sensitivity Analysis with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Despite the recent observation that large language models (LLMs) can store substantial factual knowledge, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms of how they acquire factual knowledge through pretraining. This work addresses this gap by studying how LLMs acquire factual knowledge during pretraining. The findings reveal several important insights into the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during pretraining. First, counterintuitively, we observe that pretraining on more data shows no significant improvement in the model's capability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. Next, LLMs undergo forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge, and LLMs trained with duplicated training data exhibit faster forgetting. Third, training LLMs with larger batch sizes can enhance the models' robustness to forgetting. Overall, our observations suggest that factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining occurs by progressively increasing the probability of factual knowledge presented in the pretraining data at each step. However, this increase is diluted by subsequent forgetting. Based on this interpretation, we demonstrate that we can provide plausible explanations on recently observed behaviors of LLMs, such as the poor performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge and the benefits of deduplicating the pretraining corpus.

paragraphs: Language models can retain substantial factual knowledge, but the process by which pretraining builds and preserves that knowledge is less understood. This paper examines factual learning as a changing process during training. It considers both the acquisition of facts and the forgetting that can follow as the model continues to encounter training data.

The authors observe that pretraining on more data does not significantly improve the studied ability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. They find forgetting in both memorization and generalization, with faster forgetting in models trained on duplicated data. Larger training batches, by contrast, can improve robustness to forgetting in their observations.

Their interpretation is that exposure gradually raises the probability assigned to factual information, while subsequent training dilutes those gains through forgetting. This account offers plausible explanations for weak performance on long-tail knowledge and for benefits from deduplicating pretraining data. The findings frame factual knowledge as a balance between repeated learning gains and later losses, rather than a simple consequence of accumulating more training data.
summary.tldr: The study describes factual learning during pretraining as incremental acquisition offset by forgetting, with data duplication and batch size affecting retention.

title: How Do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?

abstract: Correspondences in point cloud registration are prone to outliers, significantly reducing registration accuracy and highlighting the need for precise inlier identification. In this paper, we propose a robust inlier identification algorithm for point cloud registration by reformulating the conventional registration problem as an alignment error $\ell_0$-minimization problem. The $\ell_0$-minimization problem is formulated for each local set, where those local sets are built on a compatibility graph of input correspondences. To resolve the $\ell_0$-minimization, we develop a novel two-stage decoupling strategy, which first decouples the alignment error into a rotation fitting error and a translation fitting error. Second, null-space matrices are employed to decouple inlier identification from the estimation of rotation and translation respectively, thereby applying Bayesian theory to $\ell_0$-minimization problems and solving for fitting errors. Correspondences with the smallest errors are identified as inliers to generate a transformation hypothesis for each local set. The best hypothesis is selected to perform registration. We demonstrate that the proposed inlier identification algorithm is robust under high outlier ratios and noise through experiments. Extensive results on the KITTI, 3DMatch, and 3DLoMatch datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to both traditional and learning-based methods in various indoor and outdoor scenes.

paragraphs: Point cloud registration aligns two collections of 3D points using proposed matches between them. Incorrect matches can distort the estimated alignment, so identifying the trustworthy matches is a central part of the problem. This paper reformulates alignment as an ℓ0-minimization problem, organizing the search around local groups of correspondences built from a compatibility graph.

The algorithm separates two intertwined tasks in stages. First, it divides alignment error into rotation and translation fitting errors. It then uses null-space matrices to separate identifying reliable matches from estimating those transformations. This makes it possible to apply Bayesian reasoning to solve for the fitting errors. Matches with the smallest errors produce a candidate transformation for each local group.

The method selects the best candidate to perform registration. Experiments report robustness to high proportions of incorrect matches and to noise. Results on KITTI, 3DMatch, and 3DLoMatch show state-of-the-art performance against traditional and learning-based methods across the tested indoor and outdoor scenes.
summary.tldr: The method identifies reliable point matches by separating alignment errors and transformation estimation, improving registration in noisy, outlier-heavy experiments.

title: A robust inlier identification algorithm for point cloud registration via $\mathbf{\ell_0}$-minimization

abstract: Various linear complexity models, such as Linear Transformer (LinFormer), State Space Model (SSM), and Linear RNN (LinRNN), have been proposed to replace the conventional softmax attention in Transformer structures. However, the optimal design of these linear models is still an open question. In this work, we attempt to answer this question by finding the best linear approximation to softmax attention from a theoretical perspective. We start by unifying existing linear complexity models as the linear attention form and then identify three conditions for the optimal linear attention design: (1) Dynamic memory ability; (2) Static approximation ability; (3) Least parameter approximation. We find that none of the current linear models meet all three conditions, resulting in suboptimal performance. Instead, we propose Meta Linear Attention (MetaLA) as a solution that satisfies these conditions. Our experiments on Multi-Query Associative Recall (MQAR) task, language modeling, image classification, and Long-Range Arena (LRA) benchmark demonstrate that MetaLA is more effective than the existing linear models.

Its optimality framing concerns those approximation conditions, while the empirical findings demonstrate effectiveness across the reported tasks.
summary.tldr: MetaLA unifies linear attention designs and satisfies three proposed criteria for approximating softmax attention efficiently.

title: MetaLA: Unified Optimal Linear Approximation to Softmax Attention Map

abstract: Models for student reading performance can empower educators and institutions to proactively identify at-risk students, thereby enabling early and tailored instructional interventions. However, there are no suitable publicly available educational datasets for modeling and predicting future reading performance. In this work, we introduce the Enhanced Core Reading Instruction (ECRI) dataset, a novel large-scale longitudinal tabular dataset collected across 44 schools with 6,916 students and 172 teachers. We leverage the dataset to empirically evaluate the ability of state-of-the-art machine learning models to recognize early childhood educational patterns in multivariate and partial measurements. Specifically, we demonstrate a simple self-supervised strategy in which a Multi-Layer Perception (MLP) network is pre-trained over masked inputs to outperform several strong baselines while generalizing over diverse educational settings. To facilitate future developments in precise modeling and responsible use of models for individualized and early intervention strategies, our data and code are available at https://ecri-data.github.io/.
