paragraphs: This paper introduces object tracking that combines visible images, depth, and thermal infrared signals. Existing approaches commonly use only two of these modalities, leaving challenges in complex scenes. The work supplies both a dataset for studying the three-modality setting and a tracker designed to combine the complementary information without discarding an existing RGB tracking model.

The RGBDT500 dataset contains 500 videos with synchronized frames across all three modalities. The images are spatially aligned, and object bounding boxes provide tracking annotations. The proposed tracker, RDTTrack, first combines thermal and depth information under an orthogonal projection constraint. It then supplies the combined information alongside RGB as prompts to a pretrained RGB-only tracker.

This design makes prompt learning the connection between additional sensors and an established tracking model. Experiments report significant improvements in accuracy and robustness over existing dual-modal approaches in complex scenarios. The dataset makes the new tracking setting available for further study, while the algorithm demonstrates how a pretrained visual tracker can incorporate two additional sources of information.
summary.tldr: RGBDT500 and RDTTrack combine aligned RGB, depth, and thermal data to improve reported tracking accuracy and robustness.

title: Collaborating Vision, Depth, and Thermal Signals for Multi-Modal Tracking: Dataset and Algorithm

abstract: Effective decision-making and problem-solving in conversational systems require the ability to identify and acquire missing information through targeted questioning. A key challenge lies in efficiently narrowing down a large space of possible outcomes by posing questions that minimize uncertainty. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate information-seeking questions, with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to strategically select questions that maximize information gain, as a part of inference-time planning. Our primary contribution includes a hierarchical feedback mechanism that exploits past interaction patterns to guide future strategy. Specifically, each new problem is mapped to a cluster based on semantic similarity, and our UCT (Upper Confidence bound for Trees) formulation employs a cluster-specific bonus reward to prioritize successful question trajectories that have proven effective for similar problems in the past. Extensive empirical evaluation across medical diagnosis and technical troubleshooting domains shows that our method achieves an average of 12\% improvement in success rates and about 10x reduction in the number of LLM calls made for planning per conversation, compared to the state of the art. An additional 8\% gain in success rate is observed on average when we start with a constrained set of possibilities. Our results underscore the efficacy of feedback-aware MCTS in enhancing information-seeking in goal-oriented dialogues.

paragraphs: A useful conversational system must sometimes ask for missing information before it can solve a problem. The challenge is choosing questions that efficiently narrow the possible answers. This paper combines language-model question generation with Monte Carlo Tree Search, allowing the system to plan which questions should provide the most information.

Its main addition is feedback from previous conversations. Each new problem is assigned to a cluster of semantically similar problems. A cluster-specific bonus in the tree-search selection rule favors question trajectories that worked well for related cases. This lets planning draw on past interaction patterns rather than relying only on the current conversation.

Starting with a constrained set of possibilities produces an additional average 8% success-rate gain. The findings connect more effective questioning with substantially reduced planning effort.
summary.tldr: Feedback-aware tree search reuses successful questioning patterns to improve conversational problem solving while reducing planning calls.

title: Feedback-Aware MCTS for Goal-Oriented Information Seeking

abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) focuses on classifying known categories while simultaneously discovering novel categories from unlabeled data. However, previous GCD methods face challenges due to inconsistent optimization objectives and category confusion. This leads to feature overlap and ultimately hinders performance on novel categories. To address these issues, we propose the Neural Collapse-inspired Generalized Category Discovery (NC-GCD) framework. By pre-assigning and fixing Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) prototypes, our method ensures an optimal geometric structure and a consistent optimization objective for both known and novel categories. We introduce a Consistent ETF Alignment Loss that unifies supervised and unsupervised ETF alignment and enhances category separability. Additionally, a Semantic Consistency Matcher (SCM) is designed to maintain stable and consistent label assignments across clustering iterations. Our method significantly enhancing novel category accuracy and demonstrating its effectiveness.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery combines two tasks: recognizing categories with available labels and discovering new categories within unlabeled examples. These tasks can pull a model's representations in inconsistent directions. The paper links that inconsistency and confusion between categories to overlapping features, which particularly harms recognition of newly discovered categories.

NC-GCD gives both tasks a common geometric target. Before learning, it fixes category prototypes in an Equiangular Tight Frame, a structured arrangement with evenly organized angular relationships. A shared alignment loss then brings labeled and unlabeled examples toward these prototypes. This provides a consistent objective while encouraging different categories to occupy more clearly separated regions of the representation.

A Semantic Consistency Matcher additionally stabilizes category assignments across successive clustering iterations. This addresses the changing assignments that can otherwise undermine consistency during discovery. The authors report significant gains in novel-category accuracy. Together, the components show how coordinated feature geometry and stable assignments can improve the joint treatment of known and unknown categories.
summary.tldr: NC-GCD aligns labeled and unlabeled examples to shared fixed prototypes, improving separation and recognition of newly discovered categories.

title: Consistent Supervised-Unsupervised Alignment for Generalized Category Discovery

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved strong performance across a range of graph representation learning tasks, yet their adversarial robustness in graph classification remains underexplored compared to node classification. While most existing defenses focus on the message-passing component, this work investigates the overlooked role of pooling operations in shaping robustness. We present a theoretical analysis of standard flat pooling methods (sum, average and max), deriving upper bounds on their adversarial risk and identifying their vulnerabilities under different attack scenarios and graph structures. Motivated by these insights, we propose Robust Singular Pooling (RS-Pool), a novel pooling strategy that leverages the dominant singular vector of the node embedding matrix to construct a robust graph-level representation. We theoretically investigate the robustness of RS-Pool and interpret the resulting bound leading to improved understanding of our proposed pooling operator. While our analysis centers on Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), RS-Pool is model-agnostic and can be implemented efficiently via power iteration. Empirical results on real-world benchmarks show that RS-Pool provides better robustness than the considered pooling methods when subject to state-of-the-art adversarial attacks while maintaining competitive clean accuracy.

paragraphs: Classifying an entire graph requires combining its node representations into a graph-level summary. This pooling step can influence how vulnerable the final prediction is to adversarial changes. While many defenses concentrate on message passing between nodes, this paper examines pooling itself as a source of vulnerability and an opportunity for stronger defenses.

The authors derive upper bounds on adversarial risk for sum, average, and maximum pooling, identifying weaknesses associated with different attacks and graph structures. Their proposed Robust Singular Pooling constructs a graph representation using the dominant singular vector of the node-embedding matrix. They analyze its robustness theoretically and explain the resulting bound. Power iteration provides an efficient way to implement the operation.

The theoretical analysis focuses on Graph Convolutional Networks, although the pooling method can be used with other models. On real-world benchmarks under the evaluated adversarial attacks, it provides better robustness than the pooling alternatives considered while retaining competitive accuracy on unmodified data. The contribution makes graph summarization an explicit part of robustness design.
summary.tldr: Robust Singular Pooling improves evaluated graph-classification robustness by building graph summaries from the dominant singular vector of node embeddings.

title: Enhancing Graph Classification Robustness with Singular Pooling

abstract: Gated Linear Units (GLUs) have become essential components in the feed-forward networks of state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs). However, they require twice as many memory reads compared to feed-forward layers without gating, due to the use of separate weight matrices for the gate and value streams. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Masked Gated Linear Units (MGLUs), a novel family of GLUs with an efficient kernel implementation. The core contribution of MGLUs include: (1) the Mixture of Element-wise Gating (MoEG) architecture that learns multiple binary masks, each determining gate or value assignments at the element level on a single shared weight matrix resulting in reduced memory transfer, and (2) FlashMGLU, a hardware-friendly kernel that yields up to a 19.7$\times$ inference-time speed-up over a na\"ive PyTorch MGLU and is 47\% more memory-efficient and 34\% faster than standard GLUs despite added architectural complexity on an RTX5090 GPU. In LLM experiments, the Swish-activated variant SwiMGLU preserves its memory advantages while matching—or even surpassing—the downstream accuracy of the SwiGLU baseline.

paragraphs: Gated linear units improve the feedforward networks used in large language models, but their separate gate and value weight matrices increase memory reads. The paper introduces Masked Gated Linear Units, or MGLUs, to reduce this data movement while retaining gating. The design combines a changed architecture with a specialized implementation.

Its Mixture of Element-wise Gating architecture learns several binary masks over one shared weight matrix. Each mask assigns individual elements to gate or value roles, replacing the need for separate matrices for those streams. FlashMGLU supplies a hardware-friendly kernel so that the added masking machinery can translate into efficient execution rather than merely a compact representation.

On an RTX5090 GPU, the kernel achieves up to a 19.7-fold inference speedup over a naive PyTorch MGLU implementation. Compared with standard GLUs, the abstract reports 47% greater memory efficiency and 34% faster execution. Language-model experiments show that the Swish-based SwiMGLU variant retains its memory advantages while matching or exceeding SwiGLU downstream accuracy. These results connect reduced memory transfer with measured speed and predictive performance.
summary.tldr: MGLUs share gate and value weights through learned masks, reducing memory costs while preserving language-model accuracy.

title: Masked Gated Linear Unit

abstract: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) learning is a central task in structure discovery and causal inference. Although the field has witnessed remarkable advances over the past few years, it remains statistically and computationally challenging to learn a single (point estimate) DAG from data, let alone provide uncertainty quantification. We address the difficult task of quantifying graph uncertainty by developing a Bayesian variational inference framework based on novel, provably valid distributions that have support directly on the space of sparse DAGs. These distributions, which we use to define our prior and variational posterior, are induced by a projection operation that maps an arbitrary continuous distribution onto the space of sparse weighted acyclic adjacency matrices. While this projection is combinatorial, it can be solved efficiently using recent continuous reformulations of acyclicity constraints. We empirically demonstrate that our method, \texttt{ProDAG}, can outperform state-of-the-art alternatives in both accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph from data is difficult even when the goal is only one estimated structure. Quantifying uncertainty requires representing multiple possible graphs while ensuring that none contains a directed cycle. ProDAG addresses this problem with a Bayesian variational inference framework whose probability distributions live directly on the space of sparse acyclic graphs.

The key construction projects an arbitrary continuous distribution onto sparse weighted adjacency matrices that satisfy acyclicity. The authors use the resulting, provably valid distributions for both the prior and the approximate posterior. This gives the uncertainty representation the required graph structure by construction. Although the projection is combinatorial, recent continuous formulations of acyclicity constraints allow it to be solved efficiently.

Empirical results show that ProDAG can outperform state-of-the-art alternatives in both accuracy and uncertainty quantification. Its contribution is therefore more than a method for selecting a single graph: it provides a way to express uncertainty over structurally valid candidates. That directly addresses the added statistical and computational difficulty of uncertainty-aware structure discovery.
summary.tldr: ProDAG represents uncertainty over sparse directed acyclic graphs by projecting continuous distributions onto valid graph structures.

title: ProDAG: Projected Variational Inference for Directed Acyclic Graphs

abstract: Structure-agnostic causal inference studies the statistical limits of treatment effect estimation, when given access to black-box ML models that estimate nuisance components of the data generating process, such as estimates of the outcome regression and the treatment propensity. Here, we find that the answer depends in a surprising way on the distribution of the treatment noise. Focusing on the partially linear outcome model of \citet{robinson1988root}, we first show that the widely adopted double machine learning (DML) estimator is minimax rate-optimal for Gaussian treatment noise, resolving an open problem of \citet{mackey2018orthogonal}. Meanwhile, for independent non-Gaussian treatment noise, we show that DML is always suboptimal by constructing new practical procedures with higher-order robustness to nuisance errors. These *ACE* procedures use structure-agnostic cumulant estimators to achieve $r$-th order insensitivity to nuisance errors whenever the $(r+1)$-st treatment cumulant is non-zero. We complement these core results with novel minimax guarantees for binary treatments in the partially linear outcome model. Finally, using synthetic demand estimation experiments, we demonstrate the practical benefits of our higher-order robust estimators.

Focusing on the partially linear outcome model of \citet{robinson1988root}, we first show that the widely adopted double machine learning (DML) estimator is minimax rate-optimal for Gaussian treatment noise, resolving an open problem of \citet{mackey2018orthogonal}. Meanwhile, for independent non-Gaussian treatment noise, we show that DML is always suboptimal by constructing new practical procedures with higher-order robustness to nuisance errors. These *ACE* procedures use structure-agnostic cumulant estimators to achieve $r$-th order insensitivity to nuisance errors whenever the $(r+1)$-st treatment cumulant is non-zero. Finally, using synthetic demand estimation experiments, we demonstrate the practical benefits of our higher-order robust estimators.

paragraphs: Treatment-effect estimation often relies on machine-learning estimates of supporting quantities, such as outcome regressions and treatment propensities. Structure-agnostic analysis studies what can be achieved when those estimates are treated as black boxes. This paper shows that, in a partially linear outcome model, the distribution of treatment noise changes the statistical limits.

For Gaussian treatment noise, the authors prove that double machine learning achieves the minimax-optimal rate. For independent non-Gaussian treatment noise, they show that it is suboptimal in the studied setting. They construct alternative ACE procedures that offer higher-order protection against errors in the supporting estimates, using structure-agnostic estimators of cumulants.

The robustness guarantee is conditional: ACE achieves r-th order insensitivity to nuisance errors whenever the treatment's (r+1)-st cumulant is nonzero. The paper also supplies minimax guarantees for binary treatments. Synthetic demand-estimation experiments demonstrate practical benefits from the higher-order estimators. Together, these results show why the treatment-noise distribution matters when choosing an estimator, even when nuisance models remain black boxes.
summary.tldr: Treatment-noise distributions determine whether double machine learning is rate-optimal or can be improved by higher-order robust estimators.

title: It’s Hard to Be Normal: The Impact of Noise on Structure-agnostic Estimation

abstract: We prove that for any VC class, it is possible to transform any passive learning algorithm into an active learning algorithm with strong asymptotic improvements in label complexity for every nontrivial distribution satisfying a uniform classification noise condition. This generalizes a similar result proven by (Hanneke, 2009;2012) for the realizable case, and is the first result establishing that such general improvement guarantees are possible in the presence of restricted types of classification noise.
originalAbstract: We prove that for any VC class, it is possible to transform any passive learning algorithm into an active learning algorithm with strong asymptotic improvements in label complexity for every nontrivial distribution satisfying a uniform classification noise condition. This generalizes a similar result proven by (Hanneke, 2009;2012) for the realizable case, and is the first result establishing that such general improvement guarantees are possible in the presence of restricted types of classification noise.

paragraphs: Passive learning receives labeled examples without choosing which labels to request. Active learning instead selects examples for labeling, aiming to reach a desired accuracy with fewer labels. This paper asks whether an existing passive learning algorithm can be transformed into an active one that has a provable advantage even when some training labels are incorrect.

The authors prove that such a transformation is possible for any VC class, a family of classifiers whose complexity is described through its ability to fit label patterns. The improvement applies to every nontrivial distribution satisfying a uniform classification noise condition. Its scope is therefore broad across classifier families but explicitly restricted in the kind of label noise it permits.

The guarantee concerns strong asymptotic improvements in label complexity: how labeling requirements compare as learning becomes increasingly demanding. It extends a corresponding result for the realizable setting to a noisy setting. The significance is that restricted classification noise still permits a general theoretical advantage from choosing which examples to label.
summary.tldr: A general transformation gives passive learners asymptotically better label efficiency through active learning under uniform classification noise.

title: Activized Learning with Uniform Classification Noise

abstract: We consider the following signal recovery problem: given a measurement matrix Φ∈\mathbbR^n\times p and a noisy observation vector c∈\mathbbR^n constructed from c = Φθ^* + εwhere ε∈\mathbbR^n is the noise vector whose entries follow i.i.d. centered sub-Gaussian distribution, how to recover the signal θ^* if Dθ^* is sparse \rca under a linear transformation D∈\mathbbR^m\times p? One natural method using convex optimization is to solve the following problem: $\min_θ 1\over 2\|Φθ- c\|^2 + λ\|Dθ\|_1. This paper provides an upper bound of the estimate error and shows the consistency property of this method by assuming that the design matrix Φis a Gaussian random matrix. Specifically, we show 1) in the noiseless case, if the condition number of D is bounded and the measurement number n≥Ω(s\log(p)) where s is the sparsity number, then the true solution can be recovered with high probability; and 2) in the noisy case, if the condition number of D is bounded and the measurement increases faster than s\log(p), that is, s\log(p)=o(n), the estimate error converges to zero with probability 1 when p and s go to infinity. Our results are consistent with those for the special case D=\boldI_p\times p (equivalently LASSO) and improve the existing analysis. The condition number of D plays a critical role in our analysis. We consider the condition numbers in two cases including the fused LASSO and the random graph: the condition number in the fused LASSO case is bounded by a constant, while the condition number in the random graph case is bounded with high probability if m\over p (i.e., #\textedge\over #\textvertex$) is larger than a certain constant. Numerical simulations are consistent with our theoretical results.

paragraphs: A signal need not be sparse in its original coordinates to have useful sparse structure. This paper studies recovery when applying a linear transformation D produces a sparse vector. The estimator combines a squared measurement-error term with an absolute-value penalty on the transformed signal, encouraging sparsity in Dθ while fitting the observations.

The analysis assumes a Gaussian random measurement matrix and, for noisy observations, independent centered sub-Gaussian noise. With a bounded condition number for D, the authors establish high-probability exact recovery in the noiseless case using measurements on the order of s log p. In the noisy case, estimation error converges to zero almost surely when s log p grows more slowly than the measurement count.

The results agree with the LASSO special case where D is the identity and improve existing analysis. The condition number of D is central: the paper examines bounds for fused LASSO and random-graph transformations, including a graph-density condition for the latter. Numerical simulations are consistent with the theoretical findings.
summary.tldr: The paper proves conditional recovery guarantees for signals that become sparse under a linear transformation.

title: Guaranteed Sparse Recovery under Linear Transformation

abstract: This paper presents a new class of tensor factorization called positive semidefinite tensor factorization (PSDTF) that decomposes a set of positive semidefinite (PSD) matrices into the convex combinations of fewer PSD basis matrices. PSDTF can be viewed as a natural extension of nonnegative matrix factorization. One of the main problems of PSDTF is that an appropriate number of bases should be given in advance. To solve this problem, we propose a nonparametric Bayesian model based on a gamma process that can instantiate only a limited number of necessary bases from the infinitely many bases assumed to exist. We derive a variational Bayesian algorithm for closed-form posterior inference and a multiplicative update rule for maximum-likelihood estimation. We evaluated PSDTF on both synthetic data and real music recordings to show its superiority.

PSDTF can be viewed as a natural extension of nonnegative matrix factorization. One of the main problems of PSDTF is that an appropriate number of bases should be given in advance. To solve this problem, we propose a nonparametric Bayesian model based on a gamma process that can instantiate only a limited number of necessary bases from the infinitely many bases assumed to exist. We derive a variational Bayesian algorithm for closed-form posterior inference and a multiplicative update rule for maximum-likelihood estimation. We evaluated PSDTF on both synthetic data and real music recordings to show its superiority.

paragraphs: This paper introduces positive semidefinite tensor factorization, a method that represents a collection of positive semidefinite matrices using fewer basis matrices of the same kind. Each original matrix is expressed as a convex combination of those bases. The authors present this construction as a natural extension of nonnegative matrix factorization for separating sources in mixture signals.

A central modeling problem is deciding how many bases to use. The proposed nonparametric Bayesian model assumes an unlimited collection of potential bases but uses a gamma process to instantiate only a limited number that are needed. This moves the choice of an appropriate basis count into the modeling procedure.

The authors derive a variational Bayesian algorithm with closed-form posterior inference and also provide a multiplicative update rule for maximum-likelihood estimation. Evaluations on synthetic data and real music recordings show the reported superiority of PSDTF. These results support both the matrix-based representation and its use for modeling mixtures without fixing the number of bases in advance.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian tensor factorization represents mixture signals with positive semidefinite bases while adapting how many bases are used.

title: Infinite Positive Semidefinite Tensor Factorization for Source Separation of Mixture Signals

abstract: Although the MapReduce framework is now the \emphde facto standard for analyzing massive data sets, many algorithms (in particular, many iterative algorithms popular in machine learning, optimization, and linear algebra) are hard to fit into MapReduce. Consider, \emphe.g., the \ell_p regression problem: given a matrix A ∈\mathbbR^m \times n and a vector b ∈\mathbbR^m, find a vector x^* ∈\mathbbR^n that minimizes f(x) = \|A x - b\|_p. The widely-used \ell_2 regression, \emphi.e., linear least-squares, is known to be highly sensitive to outliers; and choosing p ∈[1, 2) can help improve robustness. In this work, we propose an efficient algorithm for solving strongly over-determined (m ≫n) robust \ell_p regression problems to moderate precision on MapReduce. Our empirical results on data up to the terabyte scale demonstrate that our algorithm is a significant improvement over traditional iterative algorithms on MapReduce for \ell_1 regression, even for a fairly small number of iterations. In addition, our proposed interior-point cutting-plane method can also be extended to solving more general convex problems on MapReduce.

paragraphs: Many iterative optimization algorithms are difficult to fit efficiently into MapReduce. The paper examines this issue for regression that minimizes an lp norm of prediction residuals. Least squares corresponds to p equal to two and is sensitive to outliers; choosing p between one and two, excluding two, can improve robustness.

The authors propose an efficient algorithm for robust regression when there are far more observations than variables and moderate solution precision is sufficient. The method is designed for MapReduce and uses an interior-point cutting-plane approach. Its target is therefore a specific combination of statistical robustness, strongly over-determined data, and distributed computation.

Experiments on data up to terabyte scale show a substantial improvement over traditional iterative MapReduce algorithms for l1 regression, even with relatively few iterations. The authors also state that the interior-point cutting-plane method can extend to more general convex problems. The results demonstrate practical benefits for the evaluated regression setting and suggest broader computational applicability.
summary.tldr: An interior-point cutting-plane method improves MapReduce robust regression for strongly over-determined problems requiring moderate precision.

title: Robust Regression on MapReduce

abstract: The problem of maximizing precision at the top of a ranked list, often dubbed Precision@k (prec@k), finds relevance in myriad learning applications such as ranking, multi-label classification, and learning with severe label imbalance. However, despite its popularity, there exist significant gaps in our understanding of this problem and its associated performance measure. The most notable of these is the lack of a convex upper bounding surrogate for prec@k. We also lack scalable perceptron and stochastic gradient descent algorithms for optimizing this performance measure. In this paper we make key contributions in these directions. At the heart of our results is a family of truly upper bounding surrogates for prec@k. These surrogates are motivated in a principled manner and enjoy attractive properties such as consistency to prec@k under various natural margin/noise conditions. These surrogates are then used to design a class of novel perceptron algorithms for optimizing prec@k with provable mistake bounds. We also devise scalable stochastic gradient descent style methods for this problem with provable convergence bounds. Our proofs rely on novel uniform convergence bounds which require an in-depth analysis of the structural properties of prec@k and its surrogates. We conclude with experimental results comparing our algorithms with state-of-the-art cutting plane and stochastic gradient algorithms for maximizing prec@k.

paragraphs: Precision at k measures how many of the top k ranked results are relevant. Optimizing this focus on the top of a list is useful in ranking, multilabel classification, and strongly imbalanced learning. The paper addresses gaps in both the theoretical understanding of this objective and scalable algorithms for optimizing it.

Its core contribution is a family of surrogate objectives with genuine upper-bounding properties for the precision-at-k learning problem. Such surrogates provide an alternative objective that can support optimization and analysis. The paper establishes consistency relationships with precision at k under various margin or noise conditions, so those relationships depend on the stated conditions rather than holding universally.

The surrogates lead to new perceptron algorithms with mistake bounds and stochastic-gradient-style methods with convergence bounds. Their analysis uses new uniform convergence results tailored to the structure of precision at k and its surrogates. Experiments compare the resulting algorithms with leading cutting-plane and stochastic-gradient approaches. Together, these contributions connect surrogate design, statistical justification, and scalable training for a ranking measure concentrated on top results.
summary.tldr: Upper-bounding surrogates for precision at k enable scalable perceptron and stochastic-gradient methods with conditional consistency and optimization guarantees.

title: Surrogate Functions for Maximizing Precision at the Top

abstract: Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent is a popular method for solving regularized loss minimization for the case of convex losses. We describe variants of SDCA that do not require explicit regularization and do not rely on duality. We prove linear convergence rates even if individual loss functions are non-convex, as long as the expected loss is strongly convex.
originalAbstract: Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent is a popular method for solving regularized loss minimization for the case of convex losses. We describe variants of SDCA that do not require explicit regularization and do not rely on duality. We prove linear convergence rates even if individual loss functions are non-convex, as long as the expected loss is strongly convex.

paragraphs: Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent is commonly used to minimize regularized objectives built from convex losses. This paper describes variants that broaden that setting in several ways. The methods do not rely on duality and do not require an explicit regularization term, changing two features associated with the usual SDCA formulation.

The analysis also allows individual loss functions to be nonconvex. The crucial condition is that their expected loss remains strongly convex. This separates the shape of each component from the shape of the combined objective: unfavorable curvature in individual losses is compatible with the aggregate property required by the result.

Under that condition, the authors prove linear convergence rates, meaning that the convergence guarantee has a geometric rate. The result broadens the applicability of SDCA-style methods while keeping strong convexity at the expected-loss level central to the theory. Its significance lies in identifying which familiar ingredients can be removed without losing the stated rate, and which aggregate property still supports the guarantee.
summary.tldr: SDCA variants achieve linear convergence without duality or explicit regularization when the expected loss is strongly convex, even with nonconvex components.

title: SDCA without Duality, Regularization, and Individual Convexity

abstract: Distributed clustering has attracted significant attention in recent years. In this paper, we study the k-means problem in the distributed dimension setting, where the dimensions of the data are partitioned across multiple machines. We provide new approximation algorithms, which incur low communication costs and achieve constant approximation ratios. The communication complexity of our algorithms significantly improve on existing algorithms. We also provide the first communication lower bound, which nearly matches our upper bound in a certain range of parameter setting. Our experimental results show that our algorithms outperform existing algorithms on real data-sets in the distributed dimension setting.
originalAbstract: Distributed clustering has attracted significant attention in recent years. In this paper, we study the k-means problem in the distributed dimension setting, where the dimensions of the data are partitioned across multiple machines. We provide new approximation algorithms, which incur low communication costs and achieve constant approximation ratios. The communication complexity of our algorithms significantly improve on existing algorithms. We also provide the first communication lower bound, which nearly matches our upper bound in a certain range of parameter setting. Our experimental results show that our algorithms outperform existing algorithms on real data-sets in the distributed dimension setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies k-means clustering when different dimensions of the data reside on different machines. Each machine therefore holds only part of the feature description needed for clustering. The central challenge is to coordinate a useful clustering solution while keeping the amount of information exchanged between machines low.

The authors provide approximation algorithms with constant approximation ratios and low communication costs. A constant ratio bounds solution quality relative to the optimal clustering objective, rather than requiring exact optimization. The stated communication complexity significantly improves on existing algorithms, connecting a guarantee about clustering quality with a guarantee about the cost of distributed coordination.

The paper also establishes a communication lower bound that nearly matches its upper bound within a particular range of parameter settings. This identifies a regime where the algorithms’ communication requirements are close to unavoidable, without claiming that conclusion for every regime. Experiments on real datasets show the proposed algorithms outperforming existing methods in the distributed-dimension setting, complementing the theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: New k-means approximation algorithms reduce communication when data features are split across machines.

title: K-Means Clustering with Distributed Dimensions

abstract: The past decade has seen a significant interest in learning tractable probabilistic representations. Arithmetic circuits (ACs) were among the first proposed tractable representations, with some subsequent representations being instances of ACs with weaker or stronger properties. In this paper, we provide a formal basis under which variants on ACs can be compared, and where the precise roles and semantics of their various properties can be made more transparent. This allows us to place some recent developments on ACs in a clearer perspective and to also derive new results for ACs. This includes an exponential separation between ACs with and without determinism; completeness and incompleteness results; and tractability results (or lack thereof) when computing most probable explanations (MPEs).
originalAbstract: The past decade has seen a significant interest in learning tractable probabilistic representations. Arithmetic circuits (ACs) were among the first proposed tractable representations, with some subsequent representations being instances of ACs with weaker or stronger properties. In this paper, we provide a formal basis under which variants on ACs can be compared, and where the precise roles and semantics of their various properties can be made more transparent. This allows us to place some recent developments on ACs in a clearer perspective and to also derive new results for ACs. This includes an exponential separation between ACs with and without determinism; completeness and incompleteness results; and tractability results (or lack thereof) when computing most probable explanations (MPEs).

paragraphs: Arithmetic circuits are representations used for tractable probabilistic reasoning. Related representations can impose different combinations of properties, making their capabilities difficult to compare directly. This paper develops a formal basis for such comparisons, aiming to clarify what those properties mean and what computational roles they play.

A central focus is determinism and what changes when that property is relaxed. The authors establish an exponential separation between circuits with and without determinism. They also derive completeness and incompleteness results, using the framework to distinguish capabilities across variants. These results show that seemingly related circuit representations can have substantial formal differences.

The paper additionally examines the computation of most probable explanations, including when this task is tractable and when it is not. Its significance is that tractability must be understood in relation to both a representation’s properties and the inference task being performed. The framework places earlier developments in a common perspective while supporting new results about arithmetic circuits themselves.
summary.tldr: A formal comparison framework clarifies how arithmetic-circuit properties, especially determinism, affect representational capabilities and the tractability of most probable explanations.

title: On Relaxing Determinism in Arithmetic Circuits

abstract: We develop a framework for combining differentiable programming languages with neural networks. Using this framework we create end-to-end trainable systems that learn to write interpretable algorithms with perceptual components. We explore the benefits of inductive biases for strong generalization and modularity that come from the program-like structure of our models. In particular, modularity allows us to learn a library of (neural) functions which grows and improves as more tasks are solved. Empirically, we show that this leads to lifelong learning systems that transfer knowledge to new tasks more effectively than baselines.
originalAbstract: We develop a framework for combining differentiable programming languages with neural networks. Using this framework we create end-to-end trainable systems that learn to write interpretable algorithms with perceptual components. We explore the benefits of inductive biases for strong generalization and modularity that come from the program-like structure of our models. In particular, modularity allows us to learn a library of (neural) functions which grows and improves as more tasks are solved. Empirically, we show that this leads to lifelong learning systems that transfer knowledge to new tasks more effectively than baselines.

paragraphs: The paper develops a framework that combines differentiable programming languages with neural networks. The resulting systems can be trained end to end to write interpretable algorithms that include perceptual components. This brings program structure into the learning process while retaining neural components for parts of the task that require perception.

The authors examine how that structure can encourage generalization and modularity. An algorithm organized into reusable functions provides a way to separate pieces of a learned solution. In their framework, neural functions form a library that can expand and improve as the system solves more tasks, making earlier learning available for later problems.

The empirical result is that these lifelong learning systems transfer knowledge to new tasks more effectively than the baselines studied. The significance lies in treating accumulated learning as reusable components within programs, rather than only as a completed solution to one task. The paper connects the interpretability of learned algorithms with a concrete mechanism for sharing learned capabilities across tasks.
summary.tldr: Differentiable programs with reusable neural-function libraries learn interpretable algorithms and improve knowledge transfer across tasks.

title: Differentiable Programs with Neural Libraries

abstract: A major challenge in contextual bandits is to design general-purpose algorithms that are both practically useful and theoretically well-founded. We present a new technique that has the empirical and computational advantages of realizability-based approaches combined with the flexibility of agnostic methods. Our algorithms leverage the availability of a regression oracle for the value-function class, a more realistic and reasonable oracle than the classification oracles over policies typically assumed by agnostic methods. Our approach generalizes both UCB and LinUCB to far more expressive possible model classes and achieves low regret under certain distributional assumptions. In an extensive empirical evaluation, we find that our approach typically matches or outperforms both realizability-based and agnostic baselines.
originalAbstract: A major challenge in contextual bandits is to design general-purpose algorithms that are both practically useful and theoretically well-founded. We present a new technique that has the empirical and computational advantages of realizability-based approaches combined with the flexibility of agnostic methods. Our algorithms leverage the availability of a regression oracle for the value-function class, a more realistic and reasonable oracle than the classification oracles over policies typically assumed by agnostic methods. Our approach generalizes both UCB and LinUCB to far more expressive possible model classes and achieves low regret under certain distributional assumptions. In an extensive empirical evaluation, we find that our approach typically matches or outperforms both realizability-based and agnostic baselines.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms need to make effective decisions while learning from limited feedback. This paper seeks methods that combine practical usefulness with theoretical support. It brings together the empirical and computational advantages associated with realizability-based approaches and the flexibility associated with agnostic approaches.

The algorithms use a regression oracle for a class of value functions. This is presented as a more realistic computational building block than the classification oracles over policies commonly assumed by agnostic methods. The approach extends UCB and LinUCB to substantially more expressive model classes, allowing those familiar approaches to work within a broader modeling framework.

The authors establish low regret under certain distributional assumptions and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation. Their approach typically matches or exceeds the performance of both realizability-based and agnostic baselines. The theory is conditional on the stated kind of distributional assumptions, while the experiments support practical competitiveness rather than uniform superiority. Together, these results motivate regression as a useful foundation for general-purpose contextual bandit learning.
summary.tldr: Regression-oracle contextual bandits support expressive models, conditional low-regret guarantees, and competitive empirical performance.

title: Practical Contextual Bandits with Regression Oracles

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is widely used in machine learning. Although being commonly viewed as a fast but not accurate version of gradient descent (GD), it always finds better solutions than GD for modern neural networks. In order to understand this phenomenon, we take an alternative view that SGD is working on the convolved (thus smoothed) version of the loss function. We show that, even if the function $f$ has many bad local minima or saddle points, as long as for every point $x$, the weighted average of the gradients of its neighborhoods is one point convex with respect to the desired solution $x^*$, SGD will get close to, and then stay around $x^*$ with constant probability. Our result identifies a set of functions that SGD provably works, which is much larger than the set of convex functions. Empirically, we observe that the loss surface of neural networks enjoys nice one point convexity properties locally, therefore our theorem helps explain why SGD works so well for neural networks.

Although being commonly viewed as a fast but not accurate version of gradient descent (GD), it always finds better solutions than GD for modern neural networks. In order to understand this phenomenon, we take an alternative view that SGD is working on the convolved (thus smoothed) version of the loss function. We show that, even if the function $f$ has many bad local minima or saddle points, as long as for every point $x$, the weighted average of the gradients of its neighborhoods is one point convex with respect to the desired solution $x^*$, SGD will get close to, and then stay around $x^*$ with constant probability. Our result identifies a set of functions that SGD provably works, which is much larger than the set of convex functions. Empirically, we observe that the loss surface of neural networks enjoys nice one point convexity properties locally, therefore our theorem helps explain why SGD works so well for neural networks.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent uses noisy gradient information, yet it can work remarkably well on neural network objectives with complicated geometry. This paper studies that behavior by viewing SGD as operating on a smoothed version of the loss. The relevant landscape is therefore shaped by averages over neighborhoods, rather than solely by the gradient at an individual point.

The main guarantee requires a particular condition: at every point, a weighted average of nearby gradients must satisfy one-point convexity relative to the desired solution. Under that condition, SGD approaches the solution and then remains nearby with constant probability. The original objective may still contain many poor local minima or saddle points, so the result covers a substantially broader class than convex functions.

The authors also observe favorable local one-point convexity properties in neural network loss surfaces. This empirical finding helps connect their theorem to neural network training. It supports an explanation for SGD's effectiveness, while preserving the distinction between locally observed geometry and the theorem's condition across every point.
summary.tldr: Viewing SGD through a smoothed loss yields a conditional guarantee that it can approach and remain near a desired solution despite bad local minima.

title: An Alternative View: When Does SGD Escape Local Minima?

abstract: We present an algorithm, HOMER, for exploration and reinforcement learning in rich observation environments that are summarizable by an unknown latent state space. The algorithm interleaves representation learning to identify a new notion of kinematic state abstraction with strategic exploration to reach new states using the learned abstraction. The algorithm provably explores the environment with sample complexity scaling polynomially in the number of latent states and the time horizon, and, crucially, with no dependence on the size of the observation space, which could be infinitely large. This exploration guarantee further enables sample-efficient global policy optimization for any reward function. On the computational side, we show that the algorithm can be implemented efficiently whenever certain supervised learning problems are tractable. Empirically, we evaluate HOMER on a challenging exploration problem, where we show that the algorithm is more sample efficient than standard reinforcement learning baselines.
originalAbstract: We present an algorithm, HOMER, for exploration and reinforcement learning in rich observation environments that are summarizable by an unknown latent state space. The algorithm interleaves representation learning to identify a new notion of kinematic state abstraction with strategic exploration to reach new states using the learned abstraction. The algorithm provably explores the environment with sample complexity scaling polynomially in the number of latent states and the time horizon, and, crucially, with no dependence on the size of the observation space, which could be infinitely large. This exploration guarantee further enables sample-efficient global policy optimization for any reward function. On the computational side, we show that the algorithm can be implemented efficiently whenever certain supervised learning problems are tractable. Empirically, we evaluate HOMER on a challenging exploration problem, where we show that the algorithm is more sample efficient than standard reinforcement learning baselines.

paragraphs: An environment can generate an enormous variety of observations while having a much smaller underlying state space. HOMER addresses reinforcement learning in environments that admit such an unknown latent-state description. Its aim is to make exploration depend on the underlying structure rather than on the sheer number of possible observations.

The algorithm alternates between learning a representation, called a kinematic state abstraction, and using that representation to explore strategically. Newly learned abstractions help it reach new states, connecting representation learning directly to exploration. The authors prove that its sample complexity grows polynomially with the number of latent states and the time horizon, without depending on observation-space size, even when that space is infinite.

The exploration guarantee also supports sample-efficient global policy optimization for any reward function in this setting. Efficient implementation is conditional on the tractability of certain supervised learning problems. In a challenging exploration experiment, HOMER uses samples more efficiently than standard reinforcement learning baselines, providing empirical support alongside its theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: HOMER combines learned state abstractions with exploration, achieving sample guarantees independent of observation-space size under the paper’s latent-state setting.

title: Kinematic State Abstraction and Provably Efficient Rich-Observation Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We present a simple analysis of k-means|| (Bahmani et al., PVLDB 2012) - a distributed variant of the k-means++ algorithm (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, SODA 2007). Moreover, the bound on the number of rounds is improved from $O(\log n)$ to $O(\log n / \log\log n)$, which we show to be tight.
originalAbstract: We present a simple analysis of k-means|| (Bahmani et al., PVLDB 2012) - a distributed variant of the k-means++ algorithm (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, SODA 2007). Moreover, the bound on the number of rounds is improved from $O(\log n)$ to $O(\log n / \log\log n)$, which we show to be tight.

paragraphs: This paper provides a simpler analysis of k-means||, a distributed variant of k-means++. Its contribution concerns the number of rounds required by the algorithm. The work revisits an existing algorithm and strengthens the mathematical account of its round complexity, rather than introducing a new clustering procedure.

The authors improve the round bound from O(log n) to O(log n / log log n). The additional denominator gives a smaller asymptotic upper bound as n grows. This is a statement about how the number of rounds scales, so its significance lies in a sharper guarantee for the distributed algorithm rather than a reported measurement of execution time.

The authors also show that the new bound is tight. Thus, the analysis does more than supply a better upper bound: it establishes that the resulting order of growth captures the round requirement in the analyzed setting. Together, simplicity and tightness make the result a clearer characterization of an existing distributed method’s complexity.
summary.tldr: A simpler analysis tightens the k-means|| round bound to O(log n / log log n) and proves it tight.

title: Simple and sharp analysis of k-means||

abstract: We introduce the Graph Mixture Density Networks, a new family of machine learning models that can fit multimodal output distributions conditioned on graphs of arbitrary topology. By combining ideas from mixture models and graph representation learning, we address a broader class of challenging conditional density estimation problems that rely on structured data. In this respect, we evaluate our method on a new benchmark application that leverages random graphs for stochastic epidemic simulations. We show a significant improvement in the likelihood of epidemic outcomes when taking into account both multimodality and structure. The empirical analysis is complemented by two real-world regression tasks showing the effectiveness of our approach in modeling the output prediction uncertainty. Graph Mixture Density Networks open appealing research opportunities in the study of structure-dependent phenomena that exhibit non-trivial conditional output distributions.
originalAbstract: We introduce the Graph Mixture Density Networks, a new family of machine learning models that can fit multimodal output distributions conditioned on graphs of arbitrary topology. By combining ideas from mixture models and graph representation learning, we address a broader class of challenging conditional density estimation problems that rely on structured data. In this respect, we evaluate our method on a new benchmark application that leverages random graphs for stochastic epidemic simulations. We show a significant improvement in the likelihood of epidemic outcomes when taking into account both multimodality and structure. The empirical analysis is complemented by two real-world regression tasks showing the effectiveness of our approach in modeling the output prediction uncertainty. Graph Mixture Density Networks open appealing research opportunities in the study of structure-dependent phenomena that exhibit non-trivial conditional output distributions.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems take a graph as input and have several distinct plausible outcomes. A single predicted value cannot express that structure of uncertainty. This paper introduces Graph Mixture Density Networks, which estimate an output distribution conditioned on a graph and can represent multiple modes, or separate concentrations of likely outcomes.

The models combine graph representation learning with mixture models. Graph representation learning supplies information about the input’s connections, while the mixture component supplies a flexible description of possible outputs. The framework accepts graphs of arbitrary topology, allowing it to address conditional density estimation problems where connectivity and the form of uncertainty both matter.

The authors evaluate the approach on a new benchmark using random graphs and stochastic epidemic simulations. Accounting for both graph structure and multiple outcome modes significantly improves the likelihood assigned to epidemic outcomes. Two real-world regression tasks further demonstrate its ability to model predictive uncertainty. These findings support treating uncertainty as a distribution shaped by the input graph, rather than reducing the task to a single outcome estimate.
summary.tldr: Graph Mixture Density Networks combine graph representations with mixture models to predict multimodal outcome distributions and model uncertainty.

title: Graph Mixture Density Networks

abstract: State-of-the-art methods for scalable Gaussian processes use iterative algorithms, requiring fast matrix vector multiplies (MVMs) with the co-variance kernel. The Structured Kernel Interpolation (SKI) framework accelerates these MVMs by performing efficient MVMs on a grid and interpolating back to the original space. In this work, we develop a connection between SKI and the permutohedral lattice used for high-dimensional fast bilateral filtering. Using a sparse simplicial grid instead of a dense rectangular one, we can perform GP inference exponentially faster in the dimension than SKI. Our approach, Simplex-GP, enables scaling SKI to high dimensions, while maintaining strong predictive performance. We additionally provide a CUDA implementation of Simplex-GP, which enables significant GPU acceleration of MVM based inference.

paragraphs: Scalable Gaussian process inference often uses iterative algorithms whose speed depends on multiplying the covariance kernel matrix by vectors. Structured Kernel Interpolation accelerates this operation by working on a grid and interpolating back to the original inputs. The grid representation therefore plays a central role in the cost of inference.

The paper connects this framework to the permutohedral lattice, a structure used in high-dimensional fast bilateral filtering. Its Simplex-GP method replaces a dense rectangular grid with a sparse simplicial grid. The authors state that this change enables Gaussian process inference that is exponentially faster in input dimension than the original SKI approach.

Simplex-GP extends structured kernel interpolation to higher dimensions while maintaining strong predictive performance. The authors also provide a CUDA implementation that substantially accelerates matrix-vector-based inference on GPUs. The contribution combines a different interpolation geometry with an implementation suited to that computation, addressing both dimensional scaling and execution speed. The dimensional claim describes the comparison with SKI, while the reported predictive results support the usefulness of the resulting approximation.
summary.tldr: Simplex-GP uses a sparse simplicial lattice to improve the dimensional scaling of Gaussian process kernel interpolation.

title: SKIing on Simplices: Kernel Interpolation on the Permutohedral Lattice for Scalable Gaussian Processes

abstract: Evaluating the quality of learned representations without relying on a downstream task remains one of the challenges in representation learning. In this work, we present Geometric Component Analysis (GeomCA) algorithm that evaluates representation spaces based on their geometric and topological properties. GeomCA can be applied to representations of any dimension, independently of the model that generated them. We demonstrate its applicability by analyzing representations obtained from a variety of scenarios, such as contrastive learning models, generative models and supervised learning models.

We demonstrate its applicability by analyzing representations obtained from a variety of scenarios, such as contrastive learning models, generative models and supervised learning models.

paragraphs: A learned representation turns data into a space in which relationships between examples can be examined. Evaluating that representation commonly requires a downstream task, but doing so ties the assessment to a particular use. This paper addresses the challenge of assessing representations through the structure of the representation space itself.

The proposed algorithm, Geometric Component Analysis, or GeomCA, uses geometric and topological properties for that assessment. In plain language, it examines aspects of the space's shape and organization. Its stated scope includes representations of any dimension, and its applicability does not depend on which model produced them.

The authors demonstrate GeomCA on representations from contrastive learning, generative modeling, and supervised learning. These examples establish its applicability across several learning settings rather than restricting it to one model family. The contribution is a common structural approach to representation evaluation: instead of making a downstream task the basis of assessment, it examines properties of the representations that can be analyzed across different sources.
summary.tldr: GeomCA evaluates learned representations through their geometry and topology, independently of representation dimension or the model that produced them.

title: GeomCA: Geometric Evaluation of Data Representations

abstract: Off-policy evaluation learns a target policy’s value with a historical dataset generated by a different behavior policy. In addition to a point estimate, many applications would benefit significantly from having a confidence interval (CI) that quantifies the uncertainty of the point estimate. In this paper, we propose a novel procedure to construct an efficient, robust, and flexible CI on a target policy’s value. Our method is justified by theoretical results and numerical experiments. A Python implementation of the proposed procedure is available at https://github.com/ RunzheStat/D2OPE.
originalAbstract: Off-policy evaluation learns a target policy’s value with a historical dataset generated by a different behavior policy. In addition to a point estimate, many applications would benefit significantly from having a confidence interval (CI) that quantifies the uncertainty of the point estimate. In this paper, we propose a novel procedure to construct an efficient, robust, and flexible CI on a target policy’s value. Our method is justified by theoretical results and numerical experiments. A Python implementation of the proposed procedure is available at https://github.com/ RunzheStat/D2OPE.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how well a target policy would perform using historical data collected by a different behavior policy. The central challenge is that the available observations come from decisions made under another policy. This paper focuses on expressing uncertainty about the resulting value estimate, rather than reporting only a single number.

The proposed procedure constructs a confidence interval for the target policy’s value. Such an interval makes uncertainty part of the evaluation output: the estimated value is accompanied by a range intended to quantify its statistical uncertainty. This distinction matters whenever the usefulness of an evaluation depends on how precisely the available historical data support it.

The authors describe their interval procedure as efficient, robust, and flexible, and support it through theoretical results and numerical experiments. They also provide a Python implementation. The stated contribution is a method for uncertainty quantification in off-policy evaluation, with both mathematical and experimental justification, making confidence intervals a central part of evaluating a policy from previously collected data.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a theoretically and numerically supported procedure for confidence intervals on policy values estimated from historical off-policy data.

title: Deeply-Debiased Off-Policy Interval Estimation

abstract: In performative prediction, the deployment of a predictive model triggers a shift in the data distribution. As these shifts are typically unknown ahead of time, the learner needs to deploy a model to get feedback about the distribution it induces. We study the problem of finding near-optimal models under performativity while maintaining low regret. On the surface, this problem might seem equivalent to a bandit problem. However, it exhibits a fundamentally richer feedback structure that we refer to as performative feedback: after every deployment, the learner receives samples from the shifted distribution rather than bandit feedback about the reward. Our main contribution is regret bounds that scale only with the complexity of the distribution shifts and not that of the reward function. The key algorithmic idea is careful exploration of the distribution shifts that informs a novel construction of confidence bounds on the risk of unexplored models. The construction only relies on smoothness of the shifts and does not assume convexity. More broadly, our work establishes a conceptual approach for leveraging tools from the bandits literature for the purpose of regret minimization with performative feedback.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, deploying a model changes the data distribution on which it operates. A learner must therefore discover the consequences of its own choices while searching for a good model. This paper studies how to keep cumulative regret low during that search, when the distribution changes caused by deployment are initially unknown.

The key distinction from ordinary bandit feedback is what deployment reveals. The learner receives samples from the induced distribution, giving it more information than a reward observation alone. The proposed approach carefully explores how distributions shift and uses that information to construct confidence bounds on the risk of models that have not yet been deployed.

The main regret bounds depend on the complexity of the distribution shifts rather than the complexity of the reward function. This separates the difficulty of learning deployment effects from the difficulty of describing rewards. The confidence-bound construction relies on smoothness of the shifts and does not require convexity. The work shows how bandit-style exploration tools can exploit this richer feedback structure under those conditions.
summary.tldr: Learning how deployments shift data enables regret bounds governed by shift complexity rather than reward-function complexity.

title: Regret Minimization with Performative Feedback

abstract: Pruning, the task of sparsifying deep neural networks, received increasing attention recently. Although state-of-the-art pruning methods extract highly sparse models, they neglect two main challenges: (1) the process of finding these sparse models is often very expensive; (2) unstructured pruning does not provide benefits in terms of GPU memory, training time, or carbon emissions. We propose Early Compression via Gradient Flow Preservation (EarlyCroP), which efficiently extracts state-of-the-art sparse models before or early in training addressing challenge (1), and can be applied in a structured manner addressing challenge (2). This enables us to train sparse networks on commodity GPUs whose dense versions would be too large, thereby saving costs and reducing hardware requirements. We empirically show that EarlyCroP outperforms a rich set of baselines for many tasks (incl. classification, regression) and domains (incl. computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcment learning). EarlyCroP leads to accuracy comparable to dense training while outperforming pruning baselines.

paragraphs: Pruning can produce sparse neural networks, but finding them may itself require expensive training. The paper also highlights that unstructured sparsity does not provide the desired GPU memory, training-time, or emissions benefits. These are separate practical obstacles: reducing the number of retained weights and reducing the resources needed to obtain and train a model.

Early Compression via Gradient Flow Preservation, or EarlyCroP, extracts sparse models before training or early in the process. It can also be applied in a structured manner to address the resource problem. This makes it possible to train sparse networks on commodity GPUs even when their dense versions would be too large for that hardware.

The authors evaluate EarlyCroP across classification and regression, with domains including computer vision, language processing, and reinforcement learning. They report performance exceeding a broad set of pruning baselines while retaining accuracy comparable to dense training. The findings connect early model compression with practical training feasibility, rather than judging pruning solely by how sparse the final network becomes.
summary.tldr: EarlyCroP finds sparse networks before or early in training, with a structured form that enables practical resource savings and reported accuracy comparable to dense training.

title: Winning the Lottery Ahead of Time: Efficient Early Network Pruning

abstract: Probabilistic modeling is a central task in machine learning. Probabilistic models should be tractable, i.e., allowing tractable probabilistic inference, but also efficient, i.e., being able to represent a large set of probability distributions. Zhang et al. (ICML 2021) recently proposed a new model, probabilistic generating circuits. They raised the question whether every strongly Rayleigh distribution can be efficiently represented by such circuits. We prove that this question has a negative answer, there are strongly Rayleigh distributions that cannot be represented by polynomial-sized probabilistic generating circuits, assuming a widely accepted complexity theoretic conjecture.
originalAbstract: Probabilistic modeling is a central task in machine learning. Probabilistic models should be tractable, i.e., allowing tractable probabilistic inference, but also efficient, i.e., being able to represent a large set of probability distributions. Zhang et al. (ICML 2021) recently proposed a new model, probabilistic generating circuits. They raised the question whether every strongly Rayleigh distribution can be efficiently represented by such circuits. We prove that this question has a negative answer, there are strongly Rayleigh distributions that cannot be represented by polynomial-sized probabilistic generating circuits, assuming a widely accepted complexity theoretic conjecture.

paragraphs: A useful probabilistic model needs both manageable inference and the ability to represent many distributions compactly. These are separate requirements: a representation can support tractable inference yet require too much space for some distributions. This paper investigates that representational issue for probabilistic generating circuits.

The specific question is whether every strongly Rayleigh distribution can be represented by a circuit whose size grows only polynomially with the problem size. The authors give a negative answer under a widely accepted conjecture from complexity theory. Their result establishes that some distributions in this class cannot have polynomial-sized probabilistic generating circuit representations if that conjecture holds.

This is a conditional boundary on the expressive efficiency of the model family. It rules out the proposed coverage of the entire strongly Rayleigh class under the stated assumption, while leaving room for compact representations of particular members. The contribution clarifies what tractable circuit-based modelling can promise: convenient inference does not by itself imply efficient representation of every distribution in a mathematically structured class.
summary.tldr: Assuming a standard complexity conjecture, some strongly Rayleigh distributions require more than polynomial-sized probabilistic generating circuits.

title: Not all Strongly Rayleigh Distributions Have Small Probabilistic Generating Circuits

abstract: We present new algorithms for optimizing non-smooth, non-convex stochastic objectives based on a novel analysis technique. This improves the current best-known complexity for finding a $(\delta,\epsilon)$-stationary point from $O(\epsilon^{-4}\delta^{-1})$ stochastic gradient queries to $O(\epsilon^{-3}\delta^{-1})$, which we also show to be optimal. Our primary technique is a reduction from non-smooth non-convex optimization to online learning , after which our results follow from standard regret bounds in online learning. For deterministic and second-order smooth objectives, applying more advanced optimistic online learning techniques enables a new complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-1.5}\delta^{-0.5})$. Our improved non-smooth analysis also immediately recovers all optimal or best-known results for finding $\epsilon$ stationary points of smooth or second-order smooth objectives in both stochastic and deterministic settings.
