Our improved non-smooth analysis also immediately recovers all optimal or best-known results for finding $\epsilon$ stationary points of smooth or second-order smooth objectives in both stochastic and deterministic settings.

paragraphs: The paper develops algorithms for stochastic optimization when an objective is both nonsmooth and nonconvex. Its target is a (delta, epsilon)-stationary point, an approximate stationarity criterion controlled by two accuracy parameters. The main question is how many stochastic gradient queries are needed to reach such a point, rather than how to guarantee a global optimum.

The authors reduce this optimization problem to online learning, allowing standard regret bounds to yield optimization guarantees. Their analysis improves the query complexity from O(epsilon⁻⁴ delta⁻¹) to O(epsilon⁻³ delta⁻¹), and they show that the improved rate is optimal. This makes the connection to online learning a tool for obtaining a sharper complexity result.

For deterministic objectives with second-order smoothness, more advanced optimistic online learning techniques yield O(epsilon⁻¹·⁵ delta⁻⁰·⁵) complexity. The nonsmooth analysis also recovers optimal or best-known rates for epsilon-stationarity in smooth and second-order smooth problems, in stochastic and deterministic settings. The framework thus connects several regularity regimes through one analysis strategy, while the stronger rates depend on the stated additional structure.
summary.tldr: A reduction to online learning yields optimal stochastic gradient-query complexity for nonsmooth, nonconvex approximate stationarity.

title: Optimal Stochastic Non-smooth Non-convex Optimization through Online-to-Non-convex Conversion

abstract: We propose a simple algorithm to learn optimal decision trees of bounded depth. This algorithm is essentially an anytime version of the state-of-the-art dynamic programming approach. It has virtually no overhead compared to heuristic methods and is comparable to the best exact methods to prove optimality on most data sets. Experiments show that whereas existing exact methods hardly scale to deep trees, this algorithm learns trees comparable to standard heuristics without computational overhead, and can significantly improve their accuracy when given more computation time, even for deep trees.
originalAbstract: We propose a simple algorithm to learn optimal decision trees of bounded depth. This algorithm is essentially an anytime version of the state-of-the-art dynamic programming approach. It has virtually no overhead compared to heuristic methods and is comparable to the best exact methods to prove optimality on most data sets. Experiments show that whereas existing exact methods hardly scale to deep trees, this algorithm learns trees comparable to standard heuristics without computational overhead, and can significantly improve their accuracy when given more computation time, even for deep trees.

paragraphs: Learning a decision tree involves choosing a sequence of splits, and finding the best tree within a depth bound can require substantial computation. This paper introduces Blossom, an algorithm designed to provide useful trees quickly while continuing to search for better ones when more computation is available.

Blossom adapts a leading dynamic programming approach into an anytime algorithm. The significance of this design is that practical use does not depend on waiting until an optimality proof is complete. The algorithm can produce a candidate tree along the way, while retaining the ability to establish optimality through further search.

In experiments, Blossom learns trees comparable to those produced by standard heuristics with virtually no computational overhead. Additional computation can substantially improve accuracy, including for deep trees that existing exact methods struggle to handle. On most datasets, its ability to prove optimality is comparable to the best exact methods. These results suggest a useful connection between fast heuristic-style results and the more demanding search for an optimal bounded-depth tree.
summary.tldr: Blossom quickly produces competitive decision trees and can improve them toward bounded-depth optimality with additional computation.

title: Blossom: an Anytime Algorithm for Computing Optimal Decision Trees

abstract: Agents that can build temporally abstract representations of their environment are better able to understand their world and make plans on extended time scales, with limited computational power and modeling capacity. However, existing methods for automatically learning temporally abstract world models usually require millions of online environmental interactions and incentivize agents to reach every accessible environmental state, which is infeasible for most real-world robots both in terms of data efficiency and hardware safety. In this paper, we present an approach for simultaneously learning sets of skills and temporally abstract, skill-conditioned world models purely from offline data, enabling agents to perform zero-shot online planning of skill sequences for new tasks. We show that our approach performs comparably to or better than a wide array of state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms on a number of simulated robotics locomotion and manipulation benchmarks, while offering a higher degree of adaptability to new goals. Finally, we show that our approach offers a much higher degree of robustness to perturbations in environmental dynamics, compared to policy-based methods.

Finally, we show that our approach offers a much higher degree of robustness to perturbations in environmental dynamics, compared to policy-based methods.

paragraphs: Planning over extended periods becomes easier when an agent can reason in terms of skills and their effects. However, learning such temporally abstract world models often requires extensive interaction with an environment. For robots, the paper identifies both data efficiency and hardware safety as obstacles to that style of exploration.

The proposed approach learns a set of skills and a world model conditioned on those skills together, using only offline data. The model describes the environment at the time scale of skills, enabling the agent to plan sequences of them. After learning, it supports zero-shot online planning for new tasks without requiring online experimentation to construct the skills and model.

On simulated robotics locomotion and manipulation benchmarks, the approach performs comparably to or better than a broad range of state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning methods. It also offers greater adaptability to new goals and substantially greater robustness to changes in environmental dynamics than policy-based methods. These findings connect offline skill learning to flexible planning, particularly when the goal or dynamics differ from the conditions a fixed policy handles well.
summary.tldr: Learning skills and skill-conditioned world models from offline data enables adaptable planning for new tasks without online model-learning experiments.

title: Learning Temporally AbstractWorld Models without Online Experimentation

abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are one of the deep generative models that have experienced enormous success over the past decades. However, in practice, they suffer from a problem called posterior collapse, which occurs when the posterior distribution coincides, or collapses, with the prior taking no information from the latent structure of the input data into consideration. In this work, we introduce an inverse Lipschitz neural network into the decoder and, based on this architecture, provide a new method that can control in a simple and clear manner the degree of posterior collapse for a wide range of VAE models equipped with a concrete theoretical guarantee. We also illustrate the effectiveness of our method through several numerical experiments.
originalAbstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are one of the deep generative models that have experienced enormous success over the past decades. However, in practice, they suffer from a problem called posterior collapse, which occurs when the posterior distribution coincides, or collapses, with the prior taking no information from the latent structure of the input data into consideration. In this work, we introduce an inverse Lipschitz neural network into the decoder and, based on this architecture, provide a new method that can control in a simple and clear manner the degree of posterior collapse for a wide range of VAE models equipped with a concrete theoretical guarantee. We also illustrate the effectiveness of our method through several numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can suffer from posterior collapse: the distribution inferred from an input becomes the same as the prior distribution. In that situation, the inferred representation does not capture the input’s latent structure. This paper addresses how to control the degree of that collapse, rather than simply treating it as an all-or-nothing outcome.

The proposed intervention is architectural. The authors place an inverse Lipschitz neural network in the decoder, the part of the model that maps latent representations toward generated data. An inverse Lipschitz constraint limits how much differences between latent inputs can be compressed by that mapping. This gives the decoder a controlled sensitivity to changes in the latent representation.

Building on this decoder design, the paper presents a method for controlling posterior collapse across a wide range of VAE models, supported by a concrete theoretical guarantee. Several numerical experiments also illustrate its effectiveness. The contribution is a direct connection between a property of the decoder and control over collapse, giving the architectural constraint an explicit role in preserving informative latent structure.
summary.tldr: An inverse Lipschitz constraint on a VAE decoder provides theoretically supported control over the degree of posterior collapse.

title: Controlling Posterior Collapse by an Inverse Lipschitz Constraint on the Decoder Network

abstract: We propose a new method for optimistic planning in infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision processes based on the idea of adding regularization to the updates of an otherwise standard approximate value iteration procedure. This technique allows us to avoid contraction and monotonicity arguments typically required by existing analyses of approximate dynamic programming methods, and in particular to use approximate transition functions estimated via least-squares procedures in MDPs with linear function approximation. We use our method to recover known guarantees in tabular MDPs and to provide a computationally efficient algorithm for learning near-optimal policies in discounted linear mixture MDPs from a single stream of experience, and show it achieves near-optimal statistical guarantees.

We use our method to recover known guarantees in tabular MDPs and to provide a computationally efficient algorithm for learning near-optimal policies in discounted linear mixture MDPs from a single stream of experience, and show it achieves near-optimal statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper develops optimistic planning for discounted Markov decision processes with an infinite horizon. Its starting point is approximate value iteration, a procedure for repeatedly updating estimates of future value. The proposed change adds regularization to those updates, creating a planning method with a different route to theoretical guarantees.

This route avoids relying on the contraction and monotonicity arguments commonly used to analyze approximate dynamic programming. A concrete consequence is that the planner can use approximate transition functions estimated by least squares in MDPs with linear function approximation. The regularized update therefore supports a useful combination of statistical estimation and planning.

The authors recover known guarantees in tabular MDPs and develop a computationally efficient learning algorithm for discounted linear mixture MDPs. That algorithm learns near-optimal policies from a single stream of experience and achieves near-optimal statistical guarantees. The result joins three concerns within the stated setting: making the planning computation efficient, working with estimated transitions, and controlling how much experience is needed to learn a good policy.
summary.tldr: Regularized value updates enable efficient optimistic planning with near-optimal statistical guarantees in discounted linear mixture MDPs.

title: Optimistic Planning by Regularized Dynamic Programming

abstract: We present Kernel QuantTree (KQT), a non-parametric change detection algorithm that monitors multivariate data through a histogram. KQT constructs a nonlinear partition of the input space that matches pre-defined target probabilities and specifically promotes compact bins adhering to the data distribution, resulting in a powerful detection algorithm. We prove two key theoretical advantages of KQT: i ) statistics defined over the KQT histogram do not depend on the stationary data distribution $\phi_0$, so detection thresholds can be set a priori to control false positive rate, and ii ) thanks to the kernel functions adopted, the KQT monitoring scheme is invariant to the roto-translation of the input data. Consequently, KQT does not require any preprocessing step like PCA. Our experiments show that KQT achieves superior detection power than non-parametric state-of-the-art change detection methods, and can reliably control the false positive rate.

KQT constructs a nonlinear partition of the input space that matches pre-defined target probabilities and specifically promotes compact bins adhering to the data distribution, resulting in a powerful detection algorithm. We prove two key theoretical advantages of KQT: i ) statistics defined over the KQT histogram do not depend on the stationary data distribution $\phi_0$, so detection thresholds can be set a priori to control false positive rate, and ii ) thanks to the kernel functions adopted, the KQT monitoring scheme is invariant to the roto-translation of the input data. paragraphs: Kernel QuantTree detects changes in multivariate data by monitoring a histogram. Its bins come from a nonlinear partition of the input space, designed to match specified target probabilities. The partition also encourages compact bins that follow the data distribution, making the histogram responsive to changes in how observations are distributed.

The paper proves that statistics defined over this histogram do not depend on the particular stationary data distribution. This allows detection thresholds to be chosen in advance to control false positives. The kernel construction also makes monitoring invariant to rotations and translations of the input, so changing the coordinate orientation or position does not change the monitoring behavior.

These properties matter because a detector must distinguish real distribution changes from artifacts of its representation and threshold choice. The authors state that KQT needs no preprocessing such as PCA. Experiments show stronger detection power than the compared nonparametric state-of-the-art methods, together with reliable false-positive control. The contribution combines a distribution-independent thresholding result with an empirically effective nonlinear partition.
summary.tldr: Kernel QuantTree uses nonlinear histogram bins to detect distribution changes with theoretically controlled thresholds and rotation-and-translation invariance.

title: Kernel QuantTree

abstract: Prior knowledge and symbolic rules in machine learning are often expressed in the form of label constraints, especially in structured prediction problems. In this work, we compare two common strategies for encoding label constraints in a machine learning pipeline, regularization with constraints and constrained inference , by quantifying their impact on model performance. For regularization, we show that it narrows the generalization gap by precluding models that are inconsistent with the constraints. However, its preference for small violations introduces a bias toward a suboptimal model. For constrained inference, we show that it reduces the population risk by correcting a model’s violation, and hence turns the violation into an advantage. Given these differences, we further explore the use of two approaches together and propose conditions for constrained inference to compensate for the bias introduced by regularization, aiming to improve both the model complexity and optimal risk.

However, its preference for small violations introduces a bias toward a suboptimal model. For constrained inference, we show that it reduces the population risk by correcting a model’s violation, and hence turns the violation into an advantage. Given these differences, we further explore the use of two approaches together and propose conditions for constrained inference to compensate for the bias introduced by regularization, aiming to improve both the model complexity and optimal risk.

paragraphs: Prior knowledge can be expressed as rules restricting which labels are consistent with one another. This paper compares two ways to use such constraints: encouraging compliance during training through regularization and enforcing constraints when making predictions. It analyzes how each choice affects model performance.

Constraint-based regularization excludes models inconsistent with the rules, which narrows the gap between training and generalization performance. However, favoring small violations also introduces a bias toward a suboptimal model. Constrained inference has a different effect: by correcting violations in a model’s predictions, it reduces population risk. In that sense, violations provide opportunities for correction at prediction time.

The authors then study using both approaches together. They propose conditions under which constrained inference can compensate for the bias introduced by regularization, aiming to improve model complexity and optimal risk simultaneously. The contribution explains why the stage at which a rule is applied matters. Restricting model learning and correcting predictions have distinct statistical effects, and their combination benefits from conditions that account for those differences.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how label constraints affect training and inference differently and gives conditions for inference corrections to offset regularization bias.

title: On Regularization and Inference with Label Constraints

abstract: In this work, we address the problem of Hessian inversion bias in distributed second-order optimization algorithms. We introduce a novel shrinkage-based estimator for the resolvent of gram matrices which is asymptotically unbiased, and characterize its non-asymptotic convergence rate in the isotropic case. We apply this estimator to bias correction of Newton steps in distributed second-order optimization algorithms, as well as randomized sketching based methods. We examine the bias present in the naive averaging-based distributed Newton’s method using analytical expressions and contrast it with our proposed biasfree approach. Our approach leads to significant improvements in convergence rate compared to standard baselines and recent proposals, as shown through experiments on both real and synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: Second-order optimization uses curvature information to choose updates, often through an inverse Hessian. In distributed algorithms, estimating these quantities locally and combining them can introduce Hessian inversion bias. The paper studies this bias in distributed Newton methods and develops a correction based on shrinkage.

The central tool is an estimator for the resolvent of Gram matrices, an inverse-type matrix quantity relevant to the correction. The estimator is asymptotically unbiased, meaning its bias vanishes in the limiting regime considered by the analysis. The authors also characterize a finite-sample convergence rate in the isotropic case, providing a more specific guarantee under that condition.

They apply the estimator to correct Newton steps in distributed optimization and in methods based on randomized sketching. Analytical expressions expose the bias in naive averaging-based distributed Newton updates and allow comparison with the proposed approach. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets show substantial convergence improvements over standard baselines and recent proposals. The findings support correcting how inverse curvature is estimated as a useful route to faster optimization, while the unbiasedness guarantee is explicitly asymptotic.
summary.tldr: A shrinkage-based, asymptotically unbiased matrix estimator corrects distributed Newton-step bias and improves convergence in experiments.

title: Optimal Shrinkage for Distributed Second-Order Optimization

abstract: Unbiased Learning to Rank (ULTR) aims to train unbiased ranking models from biased click logs, by explicitly modeling a generation process for user behavior and fitting click data based on examination hypothesis. Previous research found empirically that the true latent relevance is mostly recoverable through click fitting. However, we demonstrate that this is not always achievable, resulting in a significant reduction in ranking performance. This research investigates the conditions under which relevance can be recovered from click data in the first principle. We initially characterize a ranking model as identifiable if it can recover the true relevance up to a scaling transformation, a criterion sufficient for the pairwise ranking objective. Subsequently, we investigate an equivalent condition for identifiability, articulated as a graph connectivity test problem: the recovery of relevance is feasible if and only if the identifiability graph (IG), derived from the underlying structure of the dataset, is connected. The presence of a disconnected IG may lead to degenerate cases and suboptimal ranking performance. To tackle this challenge, we introduce two methods, namely node intervention and node merging, designed to modify the dataset and restore the connectivity of the IG. Empirical results derived from a simulated dataset and two real-world LTR benchmark datasets not only validate our proposed theory, but also demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods in alleviating data bias when the relevance model is unidentifiable.

This paper shows that fitting clicks does not always recover the underlying relevance, despite earlier empirical successes, and that the failure can substantially harm ranking performance.

The authors define identifiability as recovering true relevance up to a scaling transformation, which is sufficient for the pairwise ranking objective. Within their analysis, they establish an exact criterion: relevance is recoverable if and only if an identifiability graph derived from the dataset is connected. A disconnected graph can leave the model unable to recover the relevant relationships.

The practical message is that the structure of the available click data matters, alongside how well a model fits those clicks.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes relevance recovery through graph connectivity and proposes dataset interventions for otherwise unidentifiable ranking problems.

title: Identifiability Matters: Revealing the Hidden Recoverable Condition in Unbiased Learning to Rank

abstract: Causal inferences from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) may not pertain to a target population where some effect modifiers have a different distribution. Prior work studies generalizing the results of a trial to a target population with no outcome but covariate data available. We show how the limited size of trials makes generalization a statistically infeasible task, as it requires estimating complex nuisance functions. We develop generalization algorithms that supplement the trial data with a prediction model learned from an additional observational study (OS), without making any assumptions on the OS. We theoretically and empirically show that our methods facilitate better generalization when the OS is "high-quality", and remain robust when it is not, and e.g., have unmeasured confounding.

paragraphs: An effect measured in a randomized trial may differ from the effect in a target population when characteristics that modify treatment effects have different distributions. Generalizing trial results is particularly difficult when the target population has covariate data but no observed outcomes. Limited trial sizes make estimating the complex supporting functions statistically infeasible in the problem studied.

The authors develop algorithms that supplement trial data with a prediction model trained on an additional observational study. Their approach does not require assumptions about that observational study. This allows the extra data to contribute predictions without requiring the observational source itself to satisfy conditions that would justify treating its associations as causal effects.

Theoretical and empirical results show improved generalization when the observational study is high-quality and robustness when it is not, including when it contains unmeasured confounding. The improvement is conditional on the usefulness of the additional source. The central contribution is a way to gain from observational predictions while protecting the generalization procedure against a poor observational study.
summary.tldr: Observational prediction models can improve the generalization of trial effects to a target population while preserving robustness to poor observational data.

title: Prediction-powered Generalization of Causal Inferences

abstract: Recent advancements in differentiable simulators highlight the potential of policy optimization using simulation gradients. Yet, these approaches are largely contingent on the continuity and smoothness of the simulation, which precludes the use of certain simulation engines, such as Mujoco. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the adaptive analytic gradient. This method views the Q function as a surrogate for future returns, consistent with the Bellman equation. By analyzing the variance of batched gradients, our method can autonomously opt for a more resilient Q function to compute the gradient when encountering rough simulation transitions. We also put forth the Adaptive-Gradient Policy Optimization (AGPO) algorithm, which leverages our proposed method for policy learning. On the theoretical side, we demonstrate AGPO’s convergence, emphasizing its stable performance under non-smooth dynamics due to low variance. On the empirical side, our results show that AGPO effectively mitigates the challenges posed by non-smoothness in policy learning through differentiable simulation.

paragraphs: Differentiable simulators can provide gradients that tell a policy how changes in its actions affect outcomes. This offers a direct route to policy optimization, but existing approaches depend heavily on smooth simulation dynamics. Abrupt or rough transitions can undermine that route, restricting which simulation engines those approaches can use.

The paper introduces an adaptive analytic gradient that uses a Q function as a substitute for future returns, following the Bellman equation. It examines the variability of gradients across a batch and can choose the more resilient Q-function route when simulation transitions become rough. The key idea is to adapt the source of gradient information to its observed stability.

The authors build Adaptive-Gradient Policy Optimization, or AGPO, around this mechanism and establish its convergence theoretically. Their analysis emphasizes low gradient variance as a source of stability under nonsmooth dynamics. Experiments also show that AGPO mitigates the difficulties caused by nonsmooth simulation, supporting adaptive gradient computation as a practical policy-learning strategy.
summary.tldr: AGPO adapts its gradient computation using a Q function to stabilize policy learning when differentiable simulations have rough transitions.

title: Adaptive-Gradient Policy Optimization: Enhancing Policy Learning in Non-Smooth Differentiable Simulations

abstract: Distinguishing causal connections from correlations is important in many scenarios. However, the presence of unobserved variables, such as the latent confounder, can introduce bias in conditional independence testing commonly employed in constraint-based causal discovery for identifying causal relations. To address this issue, existing methods introduced proxy variables to adjust for the bias caused by unobserveness. However, these methods were either limited to categorical variables or relied on strong parametric assumptions for identification. In this paper, we propose a novel hypothesis-testing procedure that can effectively examine the existence of the causal relationship over continuous variables, without any parametric constraint. Our procedure is based on discretization, which under completeness conditions, is able to asymptotically establish a linear equation whose coefficient vector is identifiable under the causal null hypothesis. Based on this, we introduce our test statistic and demonstrate its asymptotic level and power. We validate the effectiveness of our procedure using both synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Causal discovery often uses conditional independence tests to investigate whether observed relationships could reflect causal connections. Hidden variables can distort these tests, particularly when an unobserved factor influences multiple measured variables. Proxy variables provide indirect information about what is hidden, but previous proxy-based approaches restricted the variable types or imposed strong assumptions about functional form.

This paper introduces a hypothesis test for causal relationships between continuous variables without parametric constraints. Its central step is discretization: converting continuous observations into a form that supports a linear equation. Under completeness conditions, this equation emerges asymptotically, and its coefficient vector can be identified when the causal null hypothesis holds.

The authors build their test statistic around that identifiable structure and establish its asymptotic level and power, addressing false-positive control and detection ability as sample sizes grow. Synthetic and real-world evaluations support the procedure’s effectiveness. The contribution is a less parametrically restrictive route to proxy-assisted causal testing, while retaining the stated completeness conditions and asymptotic nature of its guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a nonparametric proxy-based test for causal relationships among continuous variables, with asymptotic guarantees under completeness conditions.

title: Causal Discovery via Conditional Independence Testing with Proxy Variables

abstract: Effective motion planning in high dimensional spaces is a long-standing open problem in robotics. One class of traditional motion planning algorithms corresponds to potential-based motion planning. An advantage of potential based motion planning is composability – different motion constraints can easily combined by adding corresponding potentials. However, constructing motion paths from potentials requires solving a global optimization across configuration space potential landscape, which is often prone to local minima. We propose a new approach towards learning potential based motion planning, where we train a neural network to capture and learn an easily optimizable potentials over motion planning trajectories. We illustrate the effectiveness of such approach, significantly outperforming both classical and recent learned motion planning approaches and avoiding issues with local minima. We further illustrate its inherent composability, enabling us to generalize to a multitude of different motion constraints. Project website at https://energy-based-model.github.io/potential-motion-plan.

paragraphs: Potential-based motion planning represents motion constraints through functions that can be added together. This makes it convenient to combine different requirements for a robot's movement. The difficulty is finding a good path through the resulting potential landscape, especially in high-dimensional spaces where optimization can become trapped in local minima.

The proposed approach learns potentials over complete motion-planning trajectories with a neural network. The goal is to obtain potentials that are easier to optimize, addressing the difficulty of constructing paths from a challenging configuration-space landscape. It retains the compositional structure that makes potential-based planning attractive while learning the functions used to guide planning.

The authors demonstrate substantial improvements over both classical and recent learned planning approaches, along with avoidance of local-minimum problems in their evaluations. They also demonstrate generalization to many different motion constraints through composition. The stated findings support learning an optimization-friendly trajectory potential as a way to combine flexible constraints with more effective path construction.
summary.tldr: Learning easily optimized potentials over motion trajectories improves planning while preserving the ability to combine different motion constraints.

title: Potential Based Diffusion Motion Planning

abstract: Crystalline materials are a fundamental component in next-generation technologies, yet modeling their distribution presents unique computational challenges. Of the plausible arrangements of atoms in a periodic lattice only a vanishingly small percentage are thermodynamically stable, which is a key indicator of the materials that can be experimentally realized. Two fundamental tasks in this area are to (a) predict the stable crystal structure of a known composition of elements and (b) propose novel compositions along with their stable structures. We present FlowMM, a pair of generative models that achieve state-of-the-art performance on both tasks while being more efficient and more flexible than competing methods. We extend Riemannian Flow Matching to suit the symmetries inherent to crystals: translation, rotation, permutation, and periodic boundary conditions. Our framework enables the freedom to choose the flow base distributions, drastically simplifying the problem of learning crystal structures compared with diffusion models. In addition to standard benchmarks, we validate FlowMM’s generated structures with quantum chemistry calculations, demonstrating that it is $\sim$3x more efficient, in terms of integration steps, at finding stable materials compared to previous open methods.

paragraphs: Generating plausible crystals is difficult because only a tiny fraction of atomic arrangements in periodic lattices are thermodynamically stable. FlowMM addresses two related tasks: finding a stable structure for a specified chemical composition, and proposing both new compositions and their structures. It supplies a pair of generative models for these different forms of materials discovery.

These properties matter because different representations can describe equivalent crystal structures. The framework also permits different choices of starting distributions for the flow, which the authors report substantially simplifies learning crystal structures compared with diffusion approaches.

They find that FlowMM requires roughly three times fewer integration steps to find stable materials than previous open methods. That efficiency result specifically concerns integration steps, while the calculations provide evidence about the generated structures' stability.
summary.tldr: FlowMM adapts flow matching to crystal symmetries, delivering leading generation results and finding stable materials with roughly threefold better integration-step efficiency.

title: FlowMM: Generating Materials with Riemannian Flow Matching

abstract: Machine learning often aims to produce latent embeddings of inputs which lie in a larger, abstract mathematical space. For example, in the field of 3D modeling, subsets of Euclidean space can be embedded as vectors using implicit neural representations. Such subsets also have a natural algebraic structure including operations (e.g., union) and corresponding laws (e.g., associativity). How can we learn to "union" two sets using only their latent embeddings while respecting associativity? We propose a general procedure for parameterizing latent space operations that are provably consistent with the laws on the input space. This is achieved by learning a bijection from the latent space to a carefully designed mirrored algebra which is constructed on Euclidean space in accordance with desired laws. We evaluate these structural transport nets for a range of mirrored algebras against baselines that operate directly on the latent space. Our experiments provide strong evidence that respecting the underlying algebraic structure of the input space is key for learning accurate and self-consistent operations.

paragraphs: Latent embeddings represent complex objects as vectors, but the original objects may support operations with mathematical rules. Sets, for example, can be combined by union, and union obeys associativity. The paper asks how an operation performed on embeddings can respect these rules rather than merely approximate individual examples of the operation.

The proposed procedure learns a bijection between latent space and a carefully constructed mirrored algebra on Euclidean space. Operations are carried through this mapping, using the algebra's designed rules. The resulting parameterization is provably consistent with the desired laws, making structural consistency part of how the operation is built.

The authors evaluate these structural transport networks across several mirrored algebras against methods that operate directly in latent space. Their experiments provide strong evidence that respecting the input objects' algebraic structure helps learn accurate and self-consistent operations. The theoretical guarantee concerns the laws, while the experiments assess how this structured construction performs when learning the operations.
summary.tldr: Structural transport networks build latent operations that provably respect algebraic laws and show improved accuracy and consistency in experiments.

title: Transport of Algebraic Structure to Latent Embeddings

abstract: With the increasing computational costs associated with deep learning, automated hyperparameter optimization methods, strongly relying on black-box Bayesian optimization (BO), face limitations. Freeze-thaw BO offers a promising grey-box alternative, strategically allocating scarce resources incrementally to different configurations. However, the frequent surrogate model updates inherent to this approach pose challenges for existing methods, requiring retraining or fine-tuning their neural network surrogates online, introducing overhead, instability, and hyper-hyperparameters. In this work, we propose FT-PFN, a novel surrogate for Freeze-thaw style BO. FT-PFN is a prior-data fitted network (PFN) that leverages the transformers’ in-context learning ability to efficiently and reliably do Bayesian learning curve extrapolation in a single forward pass. Our empirical analysis across three benchmark suites shows that the predictions made by FT-PFN are more accurate and 10-100 times faster than those of the deep Gaussian process and deep ensemble surrogates used in previous work. Furthermore, we show that, when combined with our novel acquisition mechanism (MFPI-random), the resulting in-context freeze-thaw BO method (ifBO), yields new state-of-the-art performance in the same three families of deep learning HPO benchmarks considered in prior work.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization can consume substantial computation because candidate configurations require training. Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization allocates resources incrementally across configurations, using partial learning curves to guide further investment. Its predictive surrogate must be updated frequently, however, and online retraining or fine-tuning can add overhead, instability, and another layer of settings to manage.

FT-PFN replaces those repeated neural-surrogate updates with in-context prediction. This prior-data fitted network uses a transformer's ability to condition on supplied observations to extrapolate learning curves through Bayesian prediction in a single forward pass. The aim is to make the predictions needed for incremental resource allocation both fast and reliable.

Combined with the authors' MFPI-random acquisition mechanism, it forms ifBO, which achieves reported state-of-the-art results in those benchmark families. The findings connect better surrogate predictions with improved decisions about where to spend training resources.
summary.tldr: FT-PFN predicts learning curves in one forward pass, enabling faster surrogate updates and stronger freeze-thaw hyperparameter optimization in the evaluated benchmarks.

title: In-Context Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization for Hyperparameter Optimization

abstract: The widespread practice of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific data faces two major challenges in memory and privacy. First, as the size of LLMs continues to grow, the memory demands of gradient-based training methods via backpropagation become prohibitively high. Second, given the tendency of LLMs to memorize training data, it is important to protect potentially sensitive information in the fine-tuning data from being regurgitated. Zeroth-order methods, which rely solely on forward passes, substantially reduce memory consumption during training. However, directly combining them with standard differentially private gradient descent suffers more as model size grows. To bridge this gap, we introduce DPZero, a novel private zeroth-order algorithm with nearly dimension-independent rates. The memory efficiency of DPZero is demonstrated in privately fine-tuning RoBERTa and OPT on several downstream tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/Liang137/DPZero.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning language models on specialized data creates two linked challenges. Backpropagation can require substantial memory, while models can memorize sensitive information from their training examples. Zeroth-order optimization addresses the memory side by relying on forward passes. However, the authors explain that directly combining this approach with standard differentially private gradient descent becomes less effective as the model grows.

DPZero is a private zeroth-order algorithm designed to address that scaling problem. Its central theoretical result is a set of nearly dimension-independent rates. This means the reported rates largely avoid the unfavorable dependence on model dimensionality that motivates the work. The qualifier matters: the claim is nearly independent of dimension, not that every cost of fine-tuning is independent of model size.

The paper demonstrates the algorithm’s memory efficiency by privately fine-tuning RoBERTa and OPT on several downstream tasks. Its contribution is to bring privacy and memory-efficient optimization into the same training method, rather than addressing either concern alone. The theoretical result supports its treatment of dimensionality, and the experiments demonstrate memory-efficient private adaptation in the evaluated language models.
summary.tldr: DPZero combines private fine-tuning with forward-pass-only optimization and achieves nearly dimension-independent theoretical rates.

title: DPZero: Private Fine-Tuning of Language Models without Backpropagation

abstract: Different from the context-independent (CI) concepts such as human, car, and airplane, context-dependent (CD) concepts require higher visual understanding ability, such as camouflaged object and medical lesion. Despite the rapid advance of many CD understanding tasks in respective branches, the isolated evolution leads to their limited cross-domain generalisation and repetitive technique innovation. Since there is a strong coupling relationship between foreground and background context in CD tasks, existing methods require to train separate models in their focused domains. This restricts their real-world CD concept understanding towards artificial general intelligence (AGI). We propose a unified model with a single set of parameters, Spider, which only needs to be trained once. With the help of the proposed concept filter driven by the image-mask group prompt, Spider is able to understand and distinguish diverse strong context-dependent concepts to accurately capture the Prompter’s intention. Without bells and whistles, Spider significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art specialized models in 8 different context-dependent segmentation tasks, including 4 natural scenes (salient, camouflaged, and transparent objects and shadow) and 4 medical lesions (COVID-19, polyp, breast, and skin lesion with color colonoscopy, CT, ultrasound, and dermoscopy modalities). Besides, Spider shows obvious advantages in continuous learning. It can easily complete the training of new tasks by fine-tuning parameters less than 1% and bring a tolerable performance degradation of less than 5% for all old tasks. The source code will be publicly available at https://github.com/Xiaoqi-Zhao-DLUT/Spider-UniCDSeg.

paragraphs: Some segmentation targets depend strongly on their surroundings: recognizing camouflage, shadows, or lesions requires interpreting the relationship between foreground and background. Separate research communities have developed specialized models for these tasks. Spider brings them into one model with a shared parameter set, aiming to reduce the need for independently trained systems for each domain.

Spider uses a concept filter driven by a prompt consisting of grouped images and masks. This prompt helps the model determine which context-dependent concept the user intends to segment. The shared model is trained once and evaluated across eight tasks, covering salient, camouflaged, and transparent objects, shadows, and four kinds of medical lesions.

The authors report significant improvements over specialized state-of-the-art models across those tasks. They also examine adding new tasks: fine-tuning less than 1% of the parameters produces less than 5% performance degradation on all old tasks. These findings support both shared context-dependent segmentation and the ability to extend the model while limiting disruption to previously learned tasks.
summary.tldr: Spider uses image-and-mask prompts to unify eight context-dependent segmentation tasks and supports new tasks through limited parameter fine-tuning.

title: Spider: A Unified Framework for Context-dependent Concept Segmentation

abstract: Curriculum learning is a training paradigm where machine learning models are trained in a meaningful order, inspired by the way humans learn curricula. Due to its capability to improve model generalization and convergence, curriculum learning has gained considerable attention and has been widely applied to various research domains. Nevertheless, as new curriculum learning methods continue to emerge, it remains an open issue to benchmark them fairly. Therefore, we develop CurBench, the first benchmark that supports systematic evaluations for curriculum learning. Specifically, it consists of 15 datasets spanning 3 research domains: computer vision, natural language processing, and graph machine learning, along with 3 settings: standard, noise, and imbalance. To facilitate a comprehensive comparison, we establish the evaluation from 2 dimensions: performance and complexity. CurBench also provides a unified toolkit that plugs automatic curricula into general machine learning processes, enabling the implementation of 15 core curriculum learning methods. On the basis of this benchmark, we conduct comparative experiments and make empirical analyses of existing methods. CurBench is open-source and publicly available at https://github.com/THUMNLab/CurBench.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes the order in which a model encounters training material, aiming to make that order useful for learning. Although many methods have been proposed, comparing them fairly remains difficult. CurBench addresses this evaluation problem by providing a common benchmark and toolkit for studying curriculum-learning methods systematically.

The benchmark contains 15 datasets across computer vision, natural language processing, and graph machine learning. It includes standard training conditions as well as settings with noise and imbalance. This combination lets researchers examine curriculum methods across different kinds of data and training difficulties. Evaluation covers both performance and complexity, making the comparison broader than predictive results alone.

CurBench also supplies a unified way to insert automatic curricula into general machine-learning workflows, with implementations of 15 core methods. The authors use this infrastructure for comparative experiments and empirical analysis. The contribution is a shared basis for understanding how existing curricula behave across settings; the abstract does not identify a single method as the overall winner. The benchmark and toolkit are publicly available as open-source resources.
summary.tldr: CurBench standardizes curriculum-learning evaluation across 15 datasets, three domains, and multiple training conditions.

title: CurBench: Curriculum Learning Benchmark

abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), e.g., CLIP, demonstrate impressive zero-shot capabilities on downstream tasks. Prior research highlights the crucial role of visual augmentation techniques, like random cropping, in alignment with fine-grained class descriptions generated by large language models (LLMs), significantly enhancing zero-shot performance by incorporating multi-view information. However, the inherent randomness of these augmentations can inevitably introduce background artifacts and cause models to overly focus on local details, compromising global semantic understanding. To address these issues, we propose an Attention-Based Selection (ABS) method from local details to global context, which applies attention-guided cropping in both raw images and feature space, supplement global semantic information through strategic feature selection. Additionally, we introduce a soft matching technique to effectively filter LLM descriptions for better alignment. ABS achieves state-of-the-art performance on out-of-distribution generalization and zero-shot classification tasks. Notably, ABS is training-free and even rivals few-shot and test-time adaptation methods.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision-language models can classify images using text descriptions without task-specific training. Multiple image views and detailed language-model-generated descriptions can improve this ability, but randomly chosen crops may introduce distracting backgrounds or emphasize small details at the expense of the whole image. This paper addresses how to select useful visual and textual information more deliberately.

Attention-Based Selection, or ABS, uses attention-guided cropping in both the original image and the model’s feature space. Strategic feature selection supplements local information with global semantic context. The method also introduces soft matching to filter generated descriptions, improving their alignment with the visual information used for classification.

ABS requires no additional training. The authors report state-of-the-art results on zero-shot classification and out-of-distribution generalization, with performance that even rivals few-shot and test-time adaptation methods. These findings support the usefulness of coordinated selection across visual views, features, and descriptions: the contribution lies in how existing representations are used, alongside preserving both detailed and global image information.
summary.tldr: ABS improves training-free vision-language classification through attention-guided visual selection and better matching of generated descriptions.

title: From Local Details to Global Context: Advancing Vision-Language Models with Attention-Based Selection

abstract: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) using neural networks has become a central focus in scientific machine learning. Training neural networks for singularly perturbed problems is particularly challenging due to certain parameters in the PDEs that introduce near-singularities in the loss function. In this study, we overcome this challenge by introducing a novel method based on homotopy dynamics to effectively manipulate these parameters. From a theoretical perspective, we analyze the effects of these parameters on training difficulty in these singularly perturbed problems and establish the convergence of the proposed homotopy dynamics method. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our approach significantly accelerates convergence and improves the accuracy of these singularly perturbed problems. These findings present an efficient optimization strategy leveraging homotopy dynamics, offering a robust framework to extend the applicability of neural networks for solving singularly perturbed differential equations.

paragraphs: Neural networks can be trained to solve partial differential equations, but singularly perturbed equations create a particularly difficult optimization problem. Certain equation parameters introduce near-singular behavior in the loss function. This paper addresses that source of training difficulty through a method based on homotopy dynamics.

The method manipulates the troublesome parameters through the proposed dynamics, making their treatment part of the optimization strategy. The authors analyze how these parameters affect training difficulty and establish convergence of their method. This connects the mathematical source of the difficulty with the mechanism intended to overcome it, giving the approach a theoretical foundation.

Experiments report significantly faster convergence and more accurate solutions for the singularly perturbed problems studied. The findings indicate that managing the perturbation parameters can improve neural-network solvers where the original training objective is difficult to optimize. The contribution is an optimization framework for this class of differential equations, supported by both convergence analysis and empirical improvements in speed and accuracy.
summary.tldr: A homotopy-dynamics method manages difficult PDE parameters, with convergence theory and reported gains in neural-solver speed and accuracy.

title: Learn Singularly Perturbed Solutions via Homotopy Dynamics

abstract: Open-ended learning agents must efficiently prioritize goals in vast possibility spaces, focusing on those that maximize learning progress (LP). When such autotelic exploration is achieved by LLM agents trained with online RL in high-dimensional and evolving goal spaces, a key challenge for LP prediction is modeling one’s own competence, a form of metacognitive monitoring. Traditional approaches either require extensive sampling or rely on brittle expert-defined goal groupings. We introduce MAGELLAN, a metacognitive framework that lets LLM agents learn to predict their competence and learning progress online. By capturing semantic relationships between goals, MAGELLAN enables sample-efficient LP estimation and dynamic adaptation to evolving goal spaces through generalization. In an interactive learning environment, we show that MAGELLAN improves LP prediction efficiency and goal prioritization, being the only method allowing the agent to fully master a large and evolving goal space. These results demonstrate how augmenting LLM agents with a metacognitive ability for LP predictions can effectively scale curriculum learning to open-ended goal spaces.

paragraphs: An agent that chooses its own goals must decide where further practice will produce the most learning. This becomes difficult when the goal space is large and changes over time. MAGELLAN addresses this problem for language-model agents trained with online reinforcement learning by helping them predict their own competence and learning progress.

The framework learns these predictions during interaction. It captures semantic relationships between goals so that knowledge about some goals can inform estimates for others. This generalization supports more sample-efficient progress estimation and adaptation as the goal space evolves. It also addresses the reliance of earlier approaches on extensive sampling or fragile, expert-defined goal groupings.

In the reported interactive environment, MAGELLAN improves both learning-progress prediction efficiency and goal prioritization. Among the methods compared, it is the only one that enables full mastery of the large, evolving goal space. That finding is specific to the evaluated setting, while supporting the broader idea that learned self-assessment can help agents organize their own curricula when enumerating and testing every possible goal would be costly.
summary.tldr: MAGELLAN helps LLM agents choose productive goals by learning to predict their own competence and progress across related goals.

title: MAGELLAN: Metacognitive predictions of learning progress guide autotelic LLM agents in large goal spaces

abstract: With the rapid advancement of Social Networking Services (SNS), the need for intelligent and efficient interaction within diverse platforms has become more crucial. Large Language Models (LLMs) play an important role in SNS as they possess the potential to revolutionize user experience, content generation, and communication dynamics. However, recent studies focus on isolated SNS tasks rather than a comprehensive evaluation. In this paper, we introduce SNS-Bench, specially constructed for assessing the abilities of large language models from different Social Networking Services, with a wide range of SNS-related information. SNS-Bench encompasses 8 different tasks such as note classification, query content relevance, and highlight words generation in comments. Finally, 6,658 questions of social media text, including subjective questions, single-choice, and multiple-choice questions, are concluded in SNS-Bench. Further, we evaluate the performance of over 25+ current diverse LLMs on our SNS-Bench. Models with different sizes exhibit performance variations, yet adhere to the scaling law. Moreover, we hope provide more insights to revolutionize the techniques of social network services with LLMs.

paragraphs: Language models could support social-network interactions, content generation, and communication, but evaluating these abilities through isolated tasks gives only a partial picture. SNS-Bench brings several social-networking tasks into one benchmark so that models can be assessed across a broader collection of relevant text-based activities.

The benchmark covers eight tasks, including classifying notes, judging whether content is relevant to a query, and generating highlighted words in comments. Its 6,658 questions include subjective responses as well as single-choice and multiple-choice formats. This combination broadens the evaluation beyond one answer style and includes both judging existing content and producing task-specific text.

The authors evaluate more than twenty-five language models and observe performance differences across model sizes, with results following a scaling-law pattern. The reported finding connects model scale with performance within this benchmark. SNS-Bench’s main value is the shared assessment structure: several social-networking abilities can be examined together, providing evidence for further development of language-model techniques for these services.
summary.tldr: SNS-Bench evaluates language models on eight social-networking tasks using 6,658 questions and varied answer formats.

title: SNS-Bench: Defining, Building, and Assessing Capabilities of Large Language Models in Social Networking Services

abstract: Robust high-definition (HD) map construction is vital for autonomous driving, yet existing methods often struggle with incomplete multi-view camera data. This paper presents SafeMap, a novel framework specifically designed to ensure accuracy even when certain camera views are missing. SafeMap integrates two key components: the Gaussian-based Perspective View Reconstruction (G-PVR) module and the Distillation-based Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) Correction (D-BEVC) module. G-PVR leverages prior knowledge of view importance to dynamically prioritize the most informative regions based on the relationships among available camera views. Furthermore, D-BEVC utilizes panoramic BEV features to correct the BEV representations derived from incomplete observations. Together, these components facilitate comprehensive data reconstruction and robust HD map generation. SafeMap is easy to implement and integrates seamlessly into existing systems, offering a plug-and-play solution for enhanced robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that SafeMap significantly outperforms previous methods in both complete and incomplete scenarios, highlighting its superior performance and resilience.

paragraphs: SafeMap addresses high-definition map construction for autonomous driving when some camera views are unavailable. Missing views leave the system with an incomplete account of its surroundings, which existing methods can struggle to handle. The framework combines reconstruction of perspective-view information with correction of the bird’s-eye-view representation used for mapping.

Its Gaussian-based Perspective View Reconstruction module uses prior knowledge about view importance and relationships between the available cameras. It dynamically prioritizes regions that are most informative. The Distillation-based Bird’s-Eye-View Correction module then uses panoramic bird’s-eye-view features to improve representations built from incomplete observations. The two components address missing information at complementary stages of the mapping process.

The authors present SafeMap as a plug-and-play framework that is straightforward to incorporate into existing systems. Experiments report significant improvements over previous methods when camera observations are complete and when some are missing. These results support the value of combining selective reconstruction with representation correction to improve mapping robustness, rather than treating missing-camera cases as a separate mapping task.
summary.tldr: SafeMap combines perspective reconstruction and bird’s-eye-view correction to improve HD mapping when camera views are missing.

title: SafeMap: Robust HD Map Construction from Incomplete Observations

abstract: Gradient-based bilevel optimisation is a powerful technique with applications in hyperparameter optimisation, task adaptation, algorithm discovery, meta-learning more broadly, and beyond. It often requires differentiating through the gradient-based optimisation process itself, leading to "gradient-of-a-gradient" calculations with computationally expensive second-order and mixed derivatives. While modern automatic differentiation libraries provide a convenient way to write programs for calculating these derivatives, they oftentimes cannot fully exploit the specific structure of these problems out-of-the-box, leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we analyse such cases and propose Mixed-Flow Meta-Gradients, or MixFlow-MG – a practical algorithm that uses mixed-mode differentiation to construct more efficient and scalable computational graphs yielding over 10x memory and up to 25% wall-clock time improvements over standard implementations in modern meta-learning setups.

paragraphs: Gradient-based bilevel optimization involves an optimization problem whose outcome feeds into another optimization problem. Applications include tuning hyperparameters, adapting to tasks, and discovering learning algorithms. Computing the outer update can require differentiating through the inner training procedure, creating expensive derivatives of calculations that already contain gradients.

Automatic differentiation makes those calculations convenient to express, but the paper argues that standard implementations often miss opportunities created by the structure of these problems. The authors analyze such cases and introduce Mixed-Flow Meta-Gradients, or MixFlow-MG. It combines differentiation modes to construct more efficient computational graphs for obtaining the required meta-gradients.

In modern meta-learning setups, the authors report memory improvements exceeding a factor of ten and wall-clock time improvements of up to 25% over standard implementations. These are distinct resource benefits: reducing the graph’s memory demands addresses scalability, while reducing elapsed time makes the computation faster. The contribution shows that how a nested derivative calculation is organized can materially affect its practical cost, even when automatic differentiation already provides a working implementation.
summary.tldr: MixFlow-MG reorganizes meta-gradient computation with mixed-mode differentiation, reporting over tenfold memory improvements and up to 25% faster execution.

title: Scalable Meta-Learning via Mixed-Mode Differentiation

abstract: Despite substantial progress in promoting fairness in high-stake applications using machine learning models, existing methods often modify the training process, such as through regularizers or other interventions, but lack formal guarantees that fairness achieved during training will generalize to unseen data. Although overfitting with respect to prediction performance has been extensively studied, overfitting in terms of fairness loss has received far less attention. This paper proposes a theoretical framework for analyzing fairness generalization error through an information-theoretic lens. Our novel bounding technique is based on Efron–Stein inequality, which allows us to derive tight information-theoretic fairness generalization bounds with both Mutual Information (MI) and Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). Our empirical results validate the tightness and practical relevance of these bounds across diverse fairness-aware learning algorithms. Our framework offers valuable insights to guide the design of algorithms improving fairness generalization.

paragraphs: A model can satisfy a fairness objective during training without maintaining that behavior on unseen data. This paper studies that gap as fairness overfitting. The motivation is that many fairness interventions alter training through regularization or other mechanisms, yet do not provide formal guarantees about whether the resulting fairness will generalize.

The authors develop an information-theoretic framework for bounding fairness generalization error. Their bounding technique uses the Efron–Stein inequality and yields bounds involving both mutual information and conditional mutual information. These quantities provide ways to characterize information dependence relevant to the learning process, connecting that dependence to the difference between training and unseen-data fairness.

Empirical evaluations across diverse fairness-aware learning algorithms support the tightness and practical relevance of the bounds. The contribution is therefore both analytical and diagnostic: it supplies a formal way to study fairness overfitting and evidence that the bounds are informative in practice. The framework offers guidance for designing algorithms with better fairness generalization, without itself establishing that every fairness intervention will generalize.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic bounds characterize how fairness achieved during training can fail to generalize, with empirical support across fairness-aware algorithms.

title: Fairness Overfitting in Machine Learning: An Information-Theoretic Perspective

abstract: We consider the max-min eigenvalue augmentation problem: given $n \times n$ symmetric positive semidefinite matrices $M,A_1,\ldots, A_m$ and a positive integer $k < m$, the goal is to choose a subset $I \subset \{1,\ldots,m\}$ of cardinality at most $k$ that maximizes the minimum eigenvalue of the matrix $M + \sum_{i \in I} A_i$. The problem captures both the Bayesian E-optimal design and maximum algebraic connectivity augmentation problems. In contrast to the existing work, we do not assume that the augmentation matrices are rank-one matrices, and we focus on the setting in which $k < n$. We show that a simple randomized rounding method provides a constant-factor approximation if the optimal increase is sufficiently large, specifically, if $\mathrm{OPT} - \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}(M) = \Omega(R \ln k)$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the optimal value, and $R$ is the maximum trace of an augmentation matrix. To establish the guarantee, we derive a matrix concentration inequality that is of independent interest. The inequality can be interpreted as an intrinsic dimension analog of the matrix Chernoff inequality for the minimum eigenvalue of a sum of independent random positive semidefinite matrices; such an inequality has already been established for the maximum eigenvalue, but not for the minimum eigenvalue.

paragraphs: The paper considers choosing a limited number of positive semidefinite matrices to add to an existing matrix, with the goal of maximizing its smallest eigenvalue. This optimization captures Bayesian E-optimal design and algebraic-connectivity augmentation. The authors allow augmentation matrices beyond rank one and focus on a selection budget k smaller than the matrix dimension n.

They show that a simple randomized rounding method achieves a constant-factor approximation when the best possible improvement is sufficiently large. Specifically, the optimal increase above the original minimum eigenvalue must be at least on the order of R log k, where R is the largest trace of any augmentation matrix. This condition is part of the guarantee, so the approximation claim depends on the instance.

The proof introduces a concentration inequality for the minimum eigenvalue of a sum of independent random positive semidefinite matrices. It provides an intrinsic-dimension counterpart to a matrix Chernoff inequality. This mathematical contribution supports the rounding analysis and extends a type of result previously available for the maximum eigenvalue to the minimum-eigenvalue setting.
summary.tldr: Simple randomized rounding gives a constant-factor eigenvalue-augmentation approximation when the optimal improvement is sufficiently large.

title: Simple Randomized Rounding for Max-Min Eigenvalue Augmentation

abstract: Conformal Prediction (CP) has proven to be an effective post-hoc method for improving the trustworthiness of neural networks by providing prediction sets with finite-sample guarantees. However, under adversarial attacks, classical conformal guarantees do not hold anymore: this problem is addressed in the field of Robust Conformal Prediction. Several methods have been proposed to provide robust CP sets with guarantees under adversarial perturbations, but, for large scale problems, these sets are either too large or the methods are too computationally demanding to be deployed in real life scenarios. In this work, we propose a new method that leverages Lipschitz-bounded networks to precisely and efficiently estimate robust CP sets. When combined with a 1-Lipschitz robust network, we demonstrate that our lip-rcp method outperforms state-of-the-art results in both the size of the robust CP sets and computational efficiency in medium and large-scale scenarios such as ImageNet. Taking a different angle, we also study vanilla CP under attack, and derive new worst-case coverage bounds of vanilla CP sets, which are valid simultaneously for all adversarial attack levels. Our lip-rcp method makes this second approach as efficient as vanilla CP while also allowing robustness guarantees.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction equips a neural network with sets of possible answers and finite-sample guarantees. Adversarial changes to inputs can invalidate ordinary conformal guarantees. Existing robust alternatives address this issue, but at large scales they can produce overly large prediction sets or require too much computation for practical deployment.

The paper introduces lip-rcp, which uses networks with bounded sensitivity to input changes to estimate robust prediction sets precisely and efficiently. Combined with a 1-Lipschitz robust network, the method achieves better set sizes and computational efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art approaches in medium- and large-scale settings, including ImageNet. The network condition is part of the stated result.

The authors also examine ordinary conformal prediction under attack. They derive worst-case coverage bounds that apply simultaneously across all adversarial attack levels. Their method makes this second approach as efficient as ordinary conformal prediction while adding robustness guarantees. The work therefore addresses both constructing robust sets and understanding how much coverage ordinary sets retain under adversarial perturbations.
summary.tldr: Lip-rcp uses Lipschitz-bounded networks to make robust conformal prediction sets smaller and more computationally efficient.

title: Efficient Robust Conformal Prediction via Lipschitz-Bounded Networks

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful strategy for training deep neural networks (DNNs). While it was originally proposed to train a more compact “student” model from a large “teacher” model, many recent efforts have focused on adapting it as an effective way to promote generalization of the model itself, such as online KD and self KD. Here, we propose an easy-to-use and compatible strategy named Spaced KD to improve the effectiveness of both online KD and self KD, in which the student model distills knowledge from a teacher model trained with a space interval ahead. This strategy is inspired by a prominent theory named spacing effect in the field of biological learning and memory, positing that appropriate intervals between learning trials can significantly enhance learning performance. We provide an in-depth theoretical and empirical analysis showing that the benefits of the proposed spacing effect in KD stem from seeking a flat minima during stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We perform extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our Spaced KD in improving the learning performance of DNNs (e.g., the additional performance gain is up to 2.31% and 3.34% on Tiny-ImageNet over online KD and self KD, respectively). Our codes have been released on github https://github.com/SunGL001/Spaced-KD.

This strategy is inspired by a prominent theory named spacing effect in the field of biological learning and memory, positing that appropriate intervals between learning trials can significantly enhance learning performance. We perform extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our Spaced KD in improving the learning performance of DNNs (e.g., the additional performance gain is up to 2.31% and 3.34% on Tiny-ImageNet over online KD and self KD, respectively). Our codes have been released on github https://github.com/SunGL001/Spaced-KD.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using guidance from a teacher. Beyond compressing a large model, online and self-distillation use this idea to improve generalization. This paper asks whether the timing of the teacher's learning relative to the student's can make that guidance more useful.

The proposed Spaced KD method lets the student learn from a teacher trained an interval ahead. Its inspiration is the spacing effect in biological learning, where appropriately separated learning episodes can improve learning performance. The method is designed to be easy to incorporate into both online distillation and self-distillation, making timing a reusable part of the training strategy.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical analyses connecting the benefit to finding flatter minima during stochastic gradient descent. Their experiments show additional gains of up to 2.31% over online distillation and 3.34% over self-distillation on Tiny-ImageNet. These findings support the idea that the relative training schedule influences generalization, with the reported improvements reflecting the evaluated models and tasks.
summary.tldr: Spaced KD improves distillation by training the teacher an interval ahead of the student, with benefits linked to flatter minima.

title: Right Time to Learn: Promoting Generalization via Bio-inspired Spacing Effect in Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are prone to hallucinations, i.e., the generated content that is nonsensical or unfaithful to input sources. Unlike in LLMs, hallucinations in MLLMs often stem from the sensitivity of text decoder to visual tokens, leading to a phenomenon akin to "amnesia" about visual information. To address this issue, we propose MemVR, a novel decoding paradigm inspired by common cognition: when the memory of an image seen the moment before is forgotten, people will look at it again for factual answers. Following this principle, we treat visual tokens as supplementary evidence, re-injecting them into the MLLM through Feed Forward Network (FFN) as “key-value memory” at the middle trigger layer. This look-twice mechanism occurs when the model exhibits high uncertainty during inference, effectively enhancing factual alignment. Comprehensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that MemVR significantly mitigates hallucination across various MLLMs and excels in general benchmarks without incurring additional time overhead.
